for all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . From this, a simple dyadic decomposition argument shows that for every $A\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\Delta)(\varphi\ast v)\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty $$

with room to spare (for a similar dyadic decomposition argument, see the proof of Theorem 11.10 at the end of Subsection 15.3). Since $\varphi\ast v$ is $K$ -invariant and satisfies (2.13), it is super-smooth. ∎

This proof shows that in Lemma 2.9, one can take $\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(G)$ . This would not be possible if we required $\varphi\ast v$ to be an analytic vector for $\Delta$ . These subtleties are unimportant for us.

## 3. $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -Adapted bases

We first give a definition-by-construction of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases, and then we prove their most important properties (Propositions 3.2 and 3.3). Once we prove these properties, we can forget about the construction entirely.

Fix once and for all a choice of representative of each isomorphism class of real irreducible unitary representations of $G$ (normally we do not distinguish representations in the same isomorphism class, but in this section it is helpful for clarity). In addition, for each representative $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ with complexification $\pi$ , fix a unit vector $\varphi_{\pi}\in\pi_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}$ if $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is principal series, or fix a unit vector $f_{\pi}$ of lowest positive weight in $\pi$ if $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is discrete series. These unit vectors are analogous to primary states in a CFT. Let $\{\xi_{\pi,n}\}_{n}$ be the following orthonormal basis of $\pi$ .

- • If $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is trivial, define $\xi_{\pi,n}$ for $n=0$ by $\displaystyle\xi_{\pi,n}=\varphi_{\pi}.$

- • If $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is principal series and nontrivial, define $\xi_{\pi,n}$ for $n\in\mathbf{Z}$ by (3.1) $\displaystyle\xi_{\pi,n}=\frac{E^{n}\varphi_{\pi}}{\|E^{n}\varphi_{\pi}\|}\text{ for }n\geq 0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\xi_{\pi,n}=(-1)^{n}\overline{\xi_{\pi,-n}}\text{ for }n\leq 0$ (note that these are consistent for $n=0$ because $\varphi_{\pi}$ is real).

- • If $\pi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is discrete series, let $k=k_{\pi}$ be the weight of $f_{\pi}$ . Define $\xi_{\pi,n}$ for integers $|n|\geq k$ by (3.2) $\displaystyle\xi_{\pi,n}=\frac{E^{n-k}f_{\pi}}{\|E^{n-k}f_{\pi}\|}\text{ for }n\geq k\qquad\text{and}\qquad\xi_{\pi,n}=(-1)^{n}\overline{\xi_{\pi,-n}}\text{ for }n\leq-k.$

In all cases, $\xi_{\pi,n}$ is an automorphic vector of weight $n$ . By the structure theory in Subsection 2.2, $\{\xi_{\pi,n}\}_{n}$ is indeed a well-defined orthonormal basis of $\pi$ . This can be thought of as a basis of primary and descendant states.

Now let $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ be a real unitary representation of $G$ with discrete bi-infinite spectrum. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be its complexification. Assume the trivial representation appears exactly once in $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , i.e., $\dim\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{G}=1$ . Then the Laplace and holomorphic spectra of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ satisfy (1.11) and (1.12), respectively. Assume further that $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{G}$ is generated by a distinguished unit vector $\mathbf{1}$ . The main example to keep in mind is $\mathcal{H}$ a multiplicative representation with bi-infinite spectrum, $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ as in Remark 1.27, and $\mathbf{1}$ the unit in $\mathcal{H}$ .

Let $\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0}$ and $\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1}$ be the Laplace and holomorphic spectra of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\simeq\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbf{Z}}\pi_{r,\mathbf{R}}, $$

where $\pi_{r,\mathbf{R}}$ is the chosen representative of the isomorphism class of

$$ \displaystyle\begin{cases}\text{real principal series representations with Casimir eigenvalue }\lambda_{r}&\text{for }r\geq 0,\\
\text{real discrete series representations with lowest positive weight }k_{-r}&\text{for }r<0.\end{cases} $$

Let $\pi_{r}$ be the complexification of $\pi_{r,\mathbf{R}}$ . Define $I\subseteq\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ in terms of the $k_{r}$ by (1.9). The motivation for (1.9) is that for $(r,n)\in\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ , one has $(r,n)\in I$ if and only if $n$ is in the range in which $\xi_{\pi_{r},n}$ is defined. Note that $I$ depends only on the isomorphism class of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . For $i=(i_{1},i_{2})\in I$ , let

$$ \displaystyle\eta_{i}=\xi_{\pi_{i_{1}},i_{2}}. $$

Then $\{\eta_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbf{Z}}\pi_{r}$ consisting of automorphic vectors. Each $\eta_{i}$ has Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda_{i_{1}}$ and weight $i_{2}$ (here we use the notation (1.13) when $i_{1}<0$ ).

#### Definition 3.1 ( $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -Adapted basis).

A $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis of $\mathcal{H}$ is an orthonormal basis $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{H}$ , such that $\psi_{(0,0)}=\mathbf{1}$ , and such that there exists an isomorphism $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\simeq\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbf{Z}}\pi_{r,\mathbf{R}}$ which (after complexifying) takes $\psi_{i}$ to $\eta_{i}$ for all $i\in I$ .

When we talk about $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases of multiplicative representations, we understand that $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ is as in Remark 1.27 and $\mathbf{1}$ is the unit.

The following proposition is obvious from Definition 3.1.

#### Proposition 3.2 (Existence and uniqueness of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases).

There exists a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{H}$ . Furthermore, if $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime},\mathcal{H}^{\prime},\mathbf{1}^{\prime}$ are also as above, with $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ as real unitary representations, and if $\{\psi_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in I}$ is a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis of $\mathcal{H}^{\prime}$ , then there exists a unique isomorphism $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\simeq\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}$ which (after complexifying) takes $\psi_{i}$ to $\psi_{i}^{\prime}$ .

The properties of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases which we will use to make calculations are the following. We use the notation from Definition 1.21.

#### Proposition 3.3 (Key properties of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases).

Let $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis of $\mathcal{H}$ . Then $\psi_{(0,0)}=\mathbf{1}$ . For $i\in\mathbf{Z}^{2}\setminus I$ , denote $\psi_{i}=0$ . Then the following hold for all $i\in I$ .

- • $\psi_{i}$ has Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda_{i_{1}}$ and weight $i_{2}$ .

- • The complex conjugate of $\psi_{i}$ is (3.3) $\displaystyle\overline{\psi_{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\psi_{\overline{i}}.$

- • The raising operator $E$ acts on $\psi_{i}$ by (3.4) $\displaystyle E\psi_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1)}\,\psi_{i^{+}}.$

- • The lowering operator $\overline{E}$ acts on $\psi_{i}$ by (3.5) $\displaystyle\overline{E}\psi_{i}=-\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,\psi_{i^{-}}.$

#### Proof.

By definition, $\psi_{(0,0)}=\mathbf{1}$ . The first two bullet points are also clear from the definition, but the third and fourth require arguments. To prove (3.4), we first show that

$$ \displaystyle E\psi_{i}=c_{i}\psi_{i^{+}}\qquad\text{for some}\qquad c_{i}\geq 0; $$

we will compute $c_{i}$ afterward by equating norms. We check (3.6) in different ways in different cases.

Case 1: $i=(0,0)$ .

Then $\psi_{i}=\mathbf{1}$ is $G$ -invariant, so $E\psi_{i}=0$ , and we can take $c_{i}=0$ in (3.6).

Case 2: $i_{1}<0$ and $i_{2}=-k_{-i_{1}}$ .

Then $\psi_{i}$ is a highest weight vector, so $E\psi_{i}=0$ , and we can again take $c_{i}=0$ .

Case 3: $i\neq(0,0)$ and $i_{2}\geq 0$ .

Then (3.6) is immediate from (3.1) when $i_{1}>0$ and from (3.2) when $i_{1}<0$ . Moreover, it is implicit in (3.1) and (3.2) that $E\psi_{i}\neq 0$ , so $c_{i}>0$ .

Case 4: ( $i_{1}>0$ and $i_{2}<0$ ) or ( $i_{1}<0$ and $i_{2}<-k_{-i_{1}}$ ).

The conditions on $i$ imply that $i^{+}\in I$ and $(i^{+})_{2}=i_{2}+1\leq 0$ . Since $I$ is preserved by $i\mapsto\overline{i}$ , we have $\overline{i^{+}}\in I$ . We know (3.6) with $\overline{i^{+}}$ in place of $i$ by Case 3, and moreover the proof in Case 3 tells us that $c_{\overline{i^{+}}}>0$ . Combining this with (3.3), and noting that $\overline{i}=(\overline{i^{+}})^{+}$ , we can write

$$ \displaystyle\overline{E\psi_{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\overline{E}\psi_{\overline{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\overline{E}\psi_{(\overline{i^{+}})^{+}}=\frac{(-1)^{i_{2}}}{c_{\overline{i^{+}}}}\overline{E}E\psi_{\overline{i^{+}}}. $$

By the first bullet point in Proposition 3.3, $\psi_{\overline{i^{+}}}$ has Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda_{i_{1}}$ and weight $-i_{2}-1$ . Thus by (2.5),

$$ \displaystyle\overline{E\psi_{i}}=\frac{(-1)^{i_{2}+1}}{c_{\overline{i^{+}}}}(\Delta+H^{2}+H)\psi_{\overline{i^{+}}}=\frac{(-1)^{i_{2}+1}}{c_{\overline{i^{+}}}}(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))\psi_{\overline{i^{+}}}. $$

Taking complex conjugates using (3.3), we get

$$ \displaystyle E\psi_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1)}{c_{\overline{i^{+}}}}\psi_{i^{+}}. $$

The numerator is nonnegative by (1.14), so (3.6) holds.

Cases 1–4 cover all possibilities, so (3.6) holds for all $i\in I$ . To prove (3.4), it remains to show that we can take

$$ \displaystyle c_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1)}. $$

If $i^{+}\not\in I$ , then $\psi_{i^{+}}=0$ , so $E\psi_{i}=0$ by (3.6), and hence (3.6) holds with any choice of $c_{i}$ . Therefore we may assume $i^{+}\in I$ . Then $\|\psi_{i^{+}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ , so taking norms in (3.6) gives $\|E\psi_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=c_{i}$ . We compute

$$ \displaystyle c_{i}^{2}=\|E\psi_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=-\langle\overline{E}E\psi_{i},\psi_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle(\Delta+H^{2}+H)\psi_{i},\psi_{i}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))\|\psi_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Here we have used (2.7), (2.5), and the first bullet point in Proposition 3.3. Since $i\in I$ , we have $\|\psi_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ . Thus we obtain (3.7) upon taking square roots in (3.8). Hence (3.4) is established.

We finally come to the last bullet point. By (3.3) and (3.4),

$$ \displaystyle\overline{\overline{E}\psi_{i}}=E\overline{\psi_{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}E\psi_{\overline{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+(-i_{2})(-i_{2}+1)}\,\psi_{\overline{i}^{+}}. $$

Noting that $(-i_{2})(-i_{2}+1)=i_{2}(i_{2}-1)$ and $\overline{i}^{+}=\overline{i^{-}}$ , taking complex conjugates using (3.3) yields (3.5). This completes the proof of Proposition 3.3. ∎

## 4. Proof of the hyperbolic bootstrap equations

In this section we prove the “only if” direction in Proposition 1.29, namely that if

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}=(\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0},\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1},\{C_{ij}^{\ell}\}_{i,j,\ell\in I}) $$

is the multiplicative spectrum of a multiplicative representation $\mathcal{H}$ with bi-infinite spectrum, with respect to a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ , then $\mathcal{S}$ solves the hyperbolic bootstrap equations.

#### Proof of (HB1).

Since $\psi_{i}\psi_{j}=\psi_{j}\psi_{i}$ , (HB1) is trivial. ∎

#### Proof of (HB2).

By the first bullet point in Proposition 3.3, $\psi_{i}\psi_{j}$ has weight $i_{2}+j_{2}$ , and $\psi_{\ell}$ has weight $\ell_{2}$ . Thus $\psi_{i}\psi_{j}$ and $\psi_{\ell}$ are orthogonal unless $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ . In other words, (HB2) holds. ∎

#### Proof of (HB3).

If $i_{2}+j_{2}\neq\ell_{2}$ , then by (HB2), both sides of (HB3) vanish. Therefore, we may assume $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ . By Remark 1.27 (more specifically Propositions 9.5 and 9.8) and (3.3),

$$ \displaystyle\overline{C_{ij}^{\ell}}=\langle\overline{\psi_{i}}\,\overline{\psi_{j}},\overline{\psi_{\ell}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=(-1)^{i_{2}+j_{2}+\ell_{2}}\langle\psi_{\overline{i}}\psi_{\overline{j}},\psi_{\overline{\ell}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=(-1)^{i_{2}+j_{2}+\ell_{2}}C_{\overline{i}\,\overline{j}}^{\overline{\ell}}. $$

Since $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ , the sign is $+1$ . Thus (HB3) holds. ∎

#### Proof of (HB4).

Since $i=(0,0)$ , we have $\psi_{i}=\mathbf{1}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle C_{ij}^{\ell}=\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\psi_{j},\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathds{1}_{j=\ell}, $$

with the last equality by orthonormality. This is (HB4). ∎

#### Proof of (HB5).

By (3.5),

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:SE5}=-\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\overline{E}\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Moving $\overline{E}$ to the other side via (2.7), applying the product rule, and then evaluating the result using (3.4),

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:SE5}=\langle E(\psi_{i}\psi_{j}),\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle(E\psi_{i})\psi_{j},\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\psi_{i}(E\psi_{j}),\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\RHS\eqref{eqn:SE5}.\qed $$

#### Proof of (HB6).

By (3.3), spectral expansion, (HB3), and (HB2),

$$ \displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\overline{\psi_{i^{\prime}}}\,\overline{\psi_{j^{\prime}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=(-1)^{i_{2}^{\prime}+j_{2}^{\prime}}\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\psi_{\overline{i^{\prime}}}\psi_{\overline{j^{\prime}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=(-1)^{i_{2}^{\prime}+j_{2}^{\prime}}\sum_{\ell\in I}C_{ij}^{\ell}\overline{C_{\overline{i^{\prime}}\,\overline{j^{\prime}}}^{\ell}}=(-1)^{i_{2}^{\prime}+j_{2}^{\prime}}\sum_{\ell\in I}C_{ij}^{\ell}C_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{ij}^{\ell}C_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{\overline{\ell}}, $$

with absolute convergence on the right hand side by Bessel’s inequality. By crossing symmetry in Definition 1.6, the left hand side is unchanged by permutation of the indices, so the right hand side must be as well. In particular, switching $i^{\prime}$ and $j$ preserves the right hand side. This is precisely the content of (HB6). ∎

## 5. Building a multiplicative representation from a solution

In this section we prove the “if” direction in Proposition 1.29, namely that if

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}=(\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0},\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1},\{C_{ij}^{\ell}\}_{i,j,\ell\in I}) $$

is a candidate spectrum solving the hyperbolic bootstrap equations, then $\mathcal{S}$ is the multiplicative spectrum of a multiplicative representation with bi-infinite spectrum, with respect to a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis.

#### Remark 5.1 (Convergence assumptions on $\mathcal{S}$ ).

We only assume $\mathcal{S}$ is a weak solution as defined in Remark 1.36. This means that instead of assuming (HB6) with absolute convergence for all $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in I$ , we only assume the following: if $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in I$ are such that both sides of (HB6) converge in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ in the sense of Definition 1.37, then (HB6) holds as an equality in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ .

### 5.1. Polynomial decay of $C_{ij}^{\ell}$ as $\ell\to\infty$

The main result of this subsection is

#### Proposition 5.2.

Let $i,j\in I$ and $N\geq 0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N}|C_{ij}^{\ell}|^{2}<\infty. $$

The proof of this proposition is by elementary analysis of the hyperbolic bootstrap equations.

#### Remark 5.3 (Weak solutions are solutions).

By Cauchy–Schwarz, the $N=0$ case of Proposition 5.2 implies that both sides of (HB6) converge absolutely for all $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in I$ . In view of Remark 5.1, this is not a circular argument.

We first prove an analog of (HB4) in which $\ell=(0,0)$ rather than $i=(0,0)$ .

#### Lemma 5.4.

For $\ell=(0,0)$ and all $i,j\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{ij}^{\ell}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\mathds{1}_{i=\overline{j}}. $$

#### Proof.

Define $i^{\prime}=j^{\prime}=(0,0)$ . Then by (HB4), followed by (HB6), followed by (HB1) and (HB4),

$$ \displaystyle C_{ij}^{\ell}=\sum_{m\in I}(-1)^{m_{2}}C_{ij}^{m}C_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{\overline{m}}=\sum_{m\in I}(-1)^{m_{2}}C_{ii^{\prime}}^{m}C_{jj^{\prime}}^{\overline{m}}=\sum_{m\in I}(-1)^{m_{2}}\mathds{1}_{i=m}\mathds{1}_{j=\overline{m}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\mathds{1}_{i=\overline{j}}. $$

Here (HB6) is applicable according to Remark 5.1 since at most one term in each sum is nonzero. ∎

We next prove an analog of (HB5) with $\ell^{+},i^{-},j^{-}$ in place of $\ell^{-},i^{+},j^{+}$ .

#### Lemma 5.5.

For all $i,j,\ell\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}+1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell^{+}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{-}j}^{\ell}+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij^{-}}^{\ell}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $I$ is closed under $i\mapsto\overline{i}$ , we can apply (HB5) with $\overline{i},\overline{j},\overline{\ell}$ in place of $i,j,\ell$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}+1)}\,C_{\overline{i}\,\overline{j}}^{\overline{\ell}^{-}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,C_{\overline{i}^{+}\overline{j}}^{\overline{\ell}}+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\,C_{\overline{i}\,\overline{j}^{+}}^{\overline{\ell}}. $$

Taking complex conjugates using (HB3) yields (5.2). ∎

The following lemma is obtained by combining (HB5) with Lemma 5.5.

#### Lemma 5.6.

For all $i,j,\ell\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-\lambda_{i_{1}}-\lambda_{j_{1}}+2i_{2}j_{2})C_{ij}^{\ell}=\, \displaystyle\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1))}\,C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell} \displaystyle+\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1))}\,C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell}. $$

#### Proof.

Let us first verify this when $\ell=(0,0)$ . Then by Lemma 5.4, both sides vanish unless $i=\overline{j}$ , in which case (5.3) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle(-2\lambda_{i_{1}}-2i_{2}^{2})(-1)^{i_{2}}=(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))(-1)^{i_{2}+1}+(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))(-1)^{i_{2}-1}. $$

This is true by elementary algebra.

Suppose now that $\ell\neq(0,0)$ . Then we see from the definition of $I$ that at least one of $\ell^{+}\in I$ or $\ell^{-}\in I$ must hold. We will treat the case where $\ell^{-}\in I$ . The case $\ell^{+}\in I$ can be dealt with by an almost identical computation (writing $\ell=(\ell^{+})^{-}$ instead of $\ell=(\ell^{-})^{+}$ ), or can be deduced from the case $\ell^{-}\in I$ by a “complex conjugation trick” similar to the proof of Lemma 5.5. So assume $\ell^{-}\in I$ . Then writing $\ell=(\ell^{-})^{+}$ and applying Lemma 5.5,

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij}^{(\ell^{-})^{+}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{-}j}^{\ell^{-}}+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij^{-}}^{\ell^{-}}. $$

Multiplying both sides by $\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1))C_{ij}^{\ell} \displaystyle=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{-}j}^{\ell^{-}} \displaystyle+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij^{-}}^{\ell^{-}}. $$

We claim that the first term on the right hand side can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{-}j}^{\ell^{-}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\, \displaystyle\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell} \displaystyle+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1)}\,C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell}\Big). $$

If $i^{-}\in I$ , then (HB5) with $i^{-}$ in place of $i$ implies (5.5). If $i^{-}\not\in I$ , then it follows from the definition of $I$ that either $i_{1}=i_{2}=0$ , or $i_{1}<0$ and $i_{2}=k_{-i_{1}}$ . In the former case, $\lambda_{i_{1}}=0$ , while in the latter case, $\lambda_{i_{1}}=-k_{-i_{1}}(k_{-i_{1}}-1)$ by (1.13). We see that in both cases,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)=0, $$

and hence (5.5) holds with both sides equal to $0$ . Thus (5.5) holds in all cases. Since $i,j$ are arbitrary in (5.5), we can switch $i,j$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij^{-}}^{\ell^{-}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\, \displaystyle\Big(\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell} \displaystyle+\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1)}\,C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell}\Big). $$

Expanding the right hand sides of (5.5) and (5.6), and then inserting (5.5) and (5.6) into (5.4),

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1))C_{ij}^{\ell} \displaystyle=(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))C_{ij}^{\ell}+\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1))}\,C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell} \displaystyle+(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1))C_{ij}^{\ell}+\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1))}\,C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell}. $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-\lambda_{i_{1}}-\lambda_{j_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)-i_{2}(i_{2}-1)-j_{2}(j_{2}-1))C_{ij}^{\ell} \displaystyle=\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1))}\,C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell} \displaystyle+\sqrt{(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1))}\,C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell}. $$

By (HB2), we may assume $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ , or else both sides of (5.3) will be zero. Then

$$ \displaystyle\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)-i_{2}(i_{2}-1)-j_{2}(j_{2}-1)=2i_{2}j_{2}. $$

Inserting this into the equation above yields (5.3). ∎

#### Corollary 5.7.

For all $i,\ell\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1))C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}=(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{i_{1}}-2i_{2}^{2})C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}-(\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1))C_{i^{-}\overline{i^{-}}}^{\ell}. $$

#### Proof.

Take $j=\overline{i}$ in Lemma 5.6 and rearrange. ∎

We will prove the proposition below by iterating Corollary 5.7. Given $i=(i_{1},i_{2})\in\mathbf{Z}^{2}$ and $n\in\mathbf{Z}$ , denote $i^{+n}=(i_{1},i_{2}+n)$ . In the remainder of this subsection, allow all implicit constants to depend on $\mathcal{S}$ .

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Let $i=(r,0)$ and $j=(-r,k_{r})$ . Let $\ell\in I$ with $\ell_{1}>0$ and $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r,n}1$ . Then there are positive quantities

$$ \displaystyle A\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad B\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{n} $$

such that

$$ \displaystyle C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}=AC_{ii}^{\ell}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{j^{+n}\overline{j^{+n}}}^{\ell}=BC_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell} $$

(of course, if $C_{ii}^{\ell}\neq 0$ (resp. $C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}\neq 0$ ), then $A$ (resp. $B$ ) is determined by division).

#### Proof.

Let us note at the outset that $i^{+n},j^{+n}\in I$ for all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . We will induct on $n$ , with base cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ . First, when $n=0$ we can take $A=B=1$ . Next, suppose $n=1$ . Since $i_{2}=0$ , we have by (HB1) that $C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}=C_{i^{-}\overline{i^{-}}}^{\ell}$ . Thus by Corollary 5.7 with the given choices of $i,\ell$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 2\lambda_{i_{1}}C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}=(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{i_{1}})C_{ii}^{\ell}, $$

where we have moved the second term on the right hand side of (5.7) to the left, and used that $\overline{i}=i$ because $i_{2}=0$ . Since $i_{1}=r\geq 1$ , we have $\lambda_{i_{1}}>0$ , so we can divide by $\lambda_{i_{1}}$ and take

$$ \displaystyle A=\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{i_{1}}}{2\lambda_{i_{1}}}. $$

This will be positive and $\sim_{r}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}$ when $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r}1$ . This establishes the first half of (5.8) and (5.9) when $n=1$ . For the second half (still with $n=1$ ), Corollary 5.7 with $j$ in place of $i$ says that

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1))C_{j^{+}\overline{j^{+}}}^{\ell}=(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{j_{1}}-2j_{2}^{2})C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}-(\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1))C_{j^{-}\overline{j^{-}}}^{\ell}. $$

By (1.13), we have $\lambda_{j_{1}}=-k_{r}(k_{r}-1)$ . By the definition of $j$ , we also have $j_{2}=k_{r}$ and $j^{-}\not\in I$ . The latter implies $C_{j^{-}\overline{j^{-}}}^{\ell}=0$ by definition. Therefore (5.10) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle 2k_{r}C_{j^{+}\overline{j^{+}}}^{\ell}=(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2k_{r})C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}. $$

Thus we can take

$$ \displaystyle B=\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2k_{r}}{2k_{r}}. $$

This will be positive and $\sim_{r}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}$ when $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r}1$ . The base cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ are now complete.

For the induction step, let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ , and let us prove the proposition for $n+1$ . By Corollary 5.7 with $i^{+n}=(r,n)$ in place of $i$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{i_{1}}+n(n+1))C_{i^{+(n+1)}\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\ell}=(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{i_{1}}-2n^{2})C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}-(\lambda_{i_{1}}+n(n-1))C_{i^{+(n-1)}\overline{i^{+(n-1)}}}^{\ell}. $$

By induction, for $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r,n}1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}=A^{\prime}C_{ii}^{\ell}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{i^{+(n-1)}\overline{i^{+(n-1)}}}^{\ell}=A^{\prime\prime}C_{ii}^{\ell} $$

for some positive $A^{\prime},A^{\prime\prime}$ with $A^{\prime}\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{n}$ and $A^{\prime\prime}\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{n-1}$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle C_{i^{+(n+1)}\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\ell}=AC_{ii}^{\ell}\qquad\text{with}\qquad A=\frac{(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-2\lambda_{i_{1}}-2n^{2})A^{\prime}-(\lambda_{i_{1}}+n(n-1))A^{\prime\prime}}{\lambda_{i_{1}}+n(n+1)}. $$

For $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r,n}1$ , this $A$ is positive and $\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{n+1}$ . This completes the induction for the first half of the proposition. The induction step for the second half can be carried out in almost exactly the same way, with $j$ replacing $i$ and $B$ replacing $A$ , and with minor differences in algebra. ∎

The proof of Proposition 5.8 shows that $A,B$ obey second-order recurrences in $n$ . We will not need these recurrences in this section, but we will use the recurrence for $B$ in Section 6, so we record it here.

#### Corollary 5.9.

Let $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ and $j=(-r,k_{r})$ . Let $\ell\in I$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{j^{+n}\overline{j^{+n}}}^{\ell}=B_{k_{r},n}(\lambda_{\ell_{1}})C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}, $$

where $B_{k,n}$ is given by the second-order recurrence

$$ \displaystyle B_{k,n+1}(\lambda)=\frac{(\lambda+2k(k-1)-2(n+k)^{2})B_{k,n}(\lambda)-((n+k)(n+k-1)-k(k-1))B_{k,n-1}(\lambda)}{(n+k)(n+k+1)-k(k-1)} $$

for $n\geq 1$ , with initial conditions

$$ \displaystyle B_{k,0}(\lambda)=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_{k,1}(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda}{2k}-1. $$

#### Proof.

The case $n=0$ is trivial. The case $n=1$ is (5.11). If (5.12) holds for $n$ and for $n-1$ , then it holds for $n+1$ because of Corollary 5.7 and the fact that $\lambda_{j_{1}}=-k_{r}(k_{r}-1)$ . ∎

We can now prove the following special case of our goal, Proposition 5.2.

#### Proposition 5.10.

Let $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ . Let $i=(r,0)$ and $j=(-r,k_{r})$ . Let $N\geq 0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N}|C_{ii}^{\ell}|^{2}<\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N}|C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}|^{2}<\infty. $$

#### Proof.

Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . By (HB6), with assumptions as in Remark 5.1, we will have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}i^{+(n+1)}}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i^{+n}}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+(n+1)}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}} $$

as soon as we can show that both sides converge in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ . By (HB2), the summand on the left hand side of (5.14) is zero unless $\ell_{2}=2n+1$ (an odd number), in which case the summand is nonpositive by (HB3). Therefore $\LHS\eqref{eqn:+n_+n+1_crossing}$ converges in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ to a nonpositive value. By (HB2), the summand on the right is zero unless $\ell_{2}=0$ . By (1.10) and (1.11), for all but finitely many $\ell\in I$ with $\ell_{2}=0$ , we have $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{r,n}1$ . For such $\ell$ , Proposition 5.8 tells us that

$$ \displaystyle C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+(n+1)}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}\sim_{r,n}\lambda_{\ell_{1}}^{2n+1}(C_{ii}^{\ell})^{2} $$

(with positive implicit constant). Since $i_{2}=\ell_{2}=0$ , it follows from (HB3) that $C_{ii}^{\ell}\in\mathbf{R}$ . Therefore $\RHS\eqref{eqn:+n_+n+1_asymp}\geq 0$ , and hence $\LHS\eqref{eqn:+n_+n+1_asymp}\geq 0$ . Thus all but finitely many terms in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:+n_+n+1_crossing}$ are nonnegative, and consequently $\RHS\eqref{eqn:+n_+n+1_crossing}$ converges in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ to a value other than $-\infty$ . We now know that the left and right hand sides of (5.14) both converge in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ , so we can apply (HB6) to get that they have the same value in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ . We further know that their common value must be in the interval $(-\infty,0]$ ; in particular, it must be finite. Since all but finitely many terms on each side of (5.14) have the same sign, we conclude that both sides converge absolutely. Absolute convergence on the right hand side means

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell\in I\\
\ell_{2}=0\end{subarray}}|C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+(n+1)}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}|<\infty $$

(we have included the condition $\ell_{2}=0$ in the sum, but this makes no difference because the summand vanishes when $\ell_{2}\neq 0$ ). Plugging (5.15) into (5.16) for all but finitely many $\ell$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\ell\in I\\
\ell_{2}=0\end{subarray}}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{2n+1}|C_{ii}^{\ell}|^{2}<\infty $$

(the absolute values are redundant). We can remove the condition $\ell_{2}=0$ because again, by (HB2), the summand vanishes when $\ell_{2}\neq 0$ . Since $n$ may be taken arbitrarily large, the first half of the proposition follows. The second half can be proved by a very similar argument. ∎

The next proposition is a slight generalization of Proposition 5.10.

#### Proposition 5.11.

Let $m\in I$ and $N\geq 0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N}|C_{m\overline{m}}^{\ell}|^{2}<\infty. $$

#### Proof.

We may assume $m_{2}\geq 0$ by replacing $m$ with $\overline{m}$ if necessary; by (HB1), this will not change (5.17). The case $m=(0,0)$ is trivial by (HB4), so assume furthermore that $m\neq(0,0)$ . Then we see from the definition of $I$ that either $m=i^{+n}$ or $m=j^{+n}$ for some $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , with $i,j$ of the form in Proposition 5.10. We claim that

$$ \displaystyle|C_{m\overline{m}}^{\ell}|\lesssim_{m}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{n}|C_{ii}^{\ell}|\qquad\text{or}\qquad|C_{m\overline{m}}^{\ell}|\lesssim_{m}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{n}|C_{j\overline{j}}^{\ell}| $$

for all but finitely many $\ell\in I$ . If $\ell_{2}\neq 0$ , then by (HB2), we have $C_{m\overline{m}}^{\ell}=0$ , and (5.18) holds trivially. By (1.10) and (1.11), we have $\lambda_{\ell_{1}}\gg_{m}1$ for all but finitely many $\ell\in I$ with $\ell_{2}=0$ . For such $\ell$ , Proposition 5.8 implies (5.18). Thus the claim holds. Inserting (5.18) into (5.17) for all but finitely many $\ell$ , we obtain (5.17) from Proposition 5.10. ∎

We are finally ready to prove the main result of this subsection, Proposition 5.2.

#### Proof of Proposition 5.2.

We will prove (5.1) for nonnegative even integers $N$ by induction. We begin with the base case $N=0$ . By (HB6), with assumptions as in Remark 5.1, we will have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{ij}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i}\,\overline{j}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{j\overline{j}}^{\overline{\ell}} $$

as soon as we can show that both sides converge in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}+i\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ . By (HB2) and (HB3), the terms on the left hand side are either zero or have sign $(-1)^{i_{2}+j_{2}}$ . In particular, they are either all nonnegative or all nonpositive, so the left hand side converges in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ . By Cauchy–Schwarz and the $N=0$ case of Proposition 5.11, the right hand side converges absolutely in $\mathbf{C}$ . Thus (HB6) applies and tells us in particular that the left hand side converges in $\overline{\mathbf{R}}$ to an element of $\overline{\mathbf{R}}\cap\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{R}$ . Therefore the left hand side is finite, and since the terms on the left all have the same sign, the left hand side converges absolutely. By (HB3), this absolute convergence is exactly the same as the $N=0$ case of (5.1). Hence the base case holds.

For the induction step, let $N\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 2}$ , assume Proposition 5.2 holds for $N-2$ , and let us prove the proposition for $N$ . By Lemma 5.6,

$$ \displaystyle|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}C_{ij}^{\ell}|\lesssim_{i,j}|C_{ij}^{\ell}|+|C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell}|+|C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell}|. $$

Squaring this and inserting it in the left hand side of (5.1),

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N}|C_{ij}^{\ell}|^{2}\lesssim_{i,j}\sum_{\ell\in I}|\lambda_{\ell_{1}}|^{N-2}(|C_{ij}^{\ell}|^{2}+|C_{i^{+}j^{-}}^{\ell}|^{2}+|C_{i^{-}j^{+}}^{\ell}|^{2}). $$

The right hand side is finite by induction, so the proof is complete. ∎

### 5.2. Building the multiplicative representation

Let $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ be a real unitary representation of $G$ with Laplace spectrum $\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0}$ and holomorphic spectrum $\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1}$ . By (1.11) and (1.12), $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ has discrete bi-infinite spectrum, and the trivial representation appears exactly once in $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Fix a choice of unit vector $\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{G}$ . Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the complexification of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Let $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis of $\mathcal{H}$ with $\psi_{(0,0)}=\mathbf{1}$ . By Proposition 1.28, $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ is a basis for $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ as an abstract vector space. Define a bilinear multiplication map $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\times\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ by setting

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{i}\psi_{j}=\sum_{\ell\in I}C_{ij}^{\ell}\psi_{\ell} $$

and extending by linearity. The right hand side is in $\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ by Propositions 2.7 and 5.2.

#### Proposition 5.12.

With the above multiplication, $\mathcal{H}$ is a multiplicative representation. Moreover, for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , the complex conjugate of $\alpha$ in the sense of Definition 1.6 coincides with the complex conjugate of $\alpha$ determined by viewing $\mathcal{H}$ as the complexification of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ .

Assuming this proposition, the multiplicative spectrum of $\mathcal{H}$ with respect to $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ is $\mathcal{S}$ by construction, and the “if” direction in Proposition 1.29 holds.

To prove Proposition 5.12, we need to verify the axioms in Definition 1.6: commutativity, existence of a unit, normalization, ergodicity, equivariance, existence of complex conjugates (compatibly with $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\otimes_{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{C}$ ), and crossing symmetry.

Recall from Proposition 3.3 that $\psi_{i}$ has Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda_{i_{1}}$ and weight $i_{2}$ . We shall use this without comment from now on.

#### Proof of commutativity.

By (HB1), we have $\psi_{i}\psi_{j}=\psi_{j}\psi_{i}$ for all $i,j\in I$ . Commutativity follows by linearity. ∎

#### Proof of existence of a unit.

We claim that $\mathbf{1}$ is a unit. To show this, it suffices by linearity to check that $\mathbf{1}\psi_{j}=\psi_{j}$ for all $j\in I$ . Denote $i=(0,0)$ . Then by (HB4),

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{1}\psi_{j}=\psi_{i}\psi_{j}=\sum_{\ell\in I}C_{ij}^{\ell}\psi_{\ell}=\psi_{j}.\qed $$

#### Proof of normalization.

Above, we chose $\mathbf{1}$ to be a unit vector. ∎

#### Proof of ergodicity.

We already saw that the trivial representation appears exactly once in $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . By definition, $\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{G}$ is a unit vector. It follows that $\mathcal{H}^{G}=\mathbf{\mathbf{C}}\mathbf{1}$ . ∎

#### Proof of equivariance.

By linearity, it suffices to prove the product rule

$$ \displaystyle X(\psi_{i}\psi_{j})=(X\psi_{i})\psi_{j}+\psi_{i}(X\psi_{j}) $$

for all $i,j\in I$ and $X\in\{H,E,\overline{E}\}$ . Testing this against $\psi_{\ell}$ , it in fact suffices to prove

$$ \displaystyle-\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\overline{X}\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle(X\psi_{i})\psi_{j},\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\psi_{i}(X\psi_{j}),\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $i,j,\ell\in I$ and $X\in\{H,E,\overline{E}\}$ .

First suppose $X=H$ . Then since $-\overline{H}=H$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=\ell_{2}C_{ij}^{\ell}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\RHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=(i_{2}+j_{2})C_{ij}^{\ell}. $$

By (HB2), both sides are zero unless $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ , in which case both sides are equal.

Next suppose $X=E$ . Then by (3.4) and (3.5),

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell^{-}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}+1)}\,C_{i^{+}j}^{\ell}+\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}+1)}\,C_{ij^{+}}^{\ell}. $$

These are equal by (HB5).

Finally, suppose $X=\overline{E}$ . Then again by (3.4) and (3.5),

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=-\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}+1)}\,C_{ij}^{\ell^{+}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:weak_prod_rule}=-\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+i_{2}(i_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{-}j}^{\ell}-\sqrt{\lambda_{j_{1}}+j_{2}(j_{2}-1)}\,C_{ij^{-}}^{\ell}. $$

These are equal by Lemma 5.5. ∎

#### Proof of existence of complex conjugates (compatibly with $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\otimes_{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{C}$ ).

For $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , let $\overline{\alpha}$ be the complex conjugate of $\alpha$ obtained by viewing $\mathcal{H}$ as the complexification of $\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . We must show that $\overline{\alpha}$ is the complex conjugate of $\alpha$ in the sense of Definition 1.6. By linearity, it suffices to prove this for $\alpha=\psi_{i}$ for $i\in I$ . By linearity again, this is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\psi_{j},\overline{\psi_{i}}\psi_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $j,\ell\in I$ . In summary, we are reduced to proving (5.20) for all $i,j,\ell\in I$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:psi_i_adjoint}=C_{ij}^{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad\RHS\eqref{eqn:psi_i_adjoint}=\overline{\langle\overline{\psi_{i}}\psi_{\ell},\psi_{j}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\overline{\langle\psi_{\overline{i}}\psi_{\ell},\psi_{j}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\overline{C_{\overline{i}\ell}^{j}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}C_{i\overline{\ell}}^{\overline{j}}, $$

where the last equality is by (HB3). Thus it remains to show that

$$ \displaystyle C_{ij}^{\ell}=(-1)^{i_{2}}C_{i\overline{\ell}}^{\overline{j}} $$

for all $i,j,\ell\in I$ . Define $m=(0,0)$ . Then by (HB1) and (HB4), followed by (HB6), followed by (HB1) and (HB4) again,

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{ij}^{\ell}=\sum_{n\in I}(-1)^{n_{2}}C_{ij}^{n}C_{\overline{\ell}m}^{\overline{n}}=\sum_{n\in I}(-1)^{n_{2}}C_{i\overline{\ell}}^{n}C_{jm}^{\overline{n}}=(-1)^{j_{2}}C_{i\overline{\ell}}^{\overline{j}}. $$

By (HB2), both sides of (5.21) vanish unless $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ , so we may assume $i_{2}+j_{2}=\ell_{2}$ . Then (5.22) implies (5.21). ∎

#### Proof of crossing symmetry.

As explained in Remark 1.11, it suffices to check the crossing equation (1.4) for the permutation $\sigma=(23)$ . Therefore, by linearity, it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\overline{\psi_{i^{\prime}}}\,\overline{\psi_{j^{\prime}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{i^{\prime}},\overline{\psi_{j}}\,\overline{\psi_{j^{\prime}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in I$ . By the same computation as in the proof of (HB6) in Section 4, namely (4.1),

$$ \displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}\psi_{j},\overline{\psi_{i^{\prime}}}\,\overline{\psi_{j^{\prime}}}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{ij}^{\ell}C_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}^{\overline{\ell}}. $$

By (HB6), the right hand side is preserved by switching $i^{\prime}$ and $j$ , so the left hand side must be preserved by the same switch. This means that (5.23) holds. ∎

The proof of Proposition 5.12 is complete. Between Section 4 and this section, we have now proved both the “if” and “only if” directions in Proposition 1.29.

## 6. Applications of the hyperbolic bootstrap equations

There have been two strands of applications of the conformal bootstrap in the context of hyperbolic surface spectra. The first, in the low energy regime, is the work [11, 36, 27] on bounds for small eigenvalues. The second, in the high energy regime, is the work [5, 1] on subconvexity for triple product $L$ -functions. To show that the hyperbolic bootstrap equations capture the information used in the conformal bootstrap, in this section we illustrate how the proofs in [36] and [1] can be phrased in terms of these equations. The proofs in [11, 27] and [5] can be phrased similarly (though [27] works with $\SL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ rather than $\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ and thus needs a slight generalization of the hyperbolic bootstrap equations).

### 6.1. Bounds on $\lambda_{1}$

The bass note spectrum of compact hyperbolic 2-orbifolds, defined by Sarnak in [63, Lecture 1], is the set of positive real numbers

$$ \displaystyle\{\lambda_{1}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}):\Gamma\text{ is a cocompact lattice in }G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})\}, $$

i.e., the set of numbers which arise as the first Laplace eigenvalue of a compact hyperbolic 2-orbifold. In [36, Figure 2 and Conjecture 4.2], Kravchuk, Mazáč, and Pal give a conjectural description of the bass note spectrum, and in [36, Theorem 4.3] they prove almost all of the conjecture. The following is a summary of their conjecture.

#### Conjecture 6.1.

The bass note spectrum of compact hyperbolic 2-orbifolds is

$$ \displaystyle(0,15.7902...]\cup\{23.0785...\}\cup\{28.0798...\}\cup\{44.8883...\}, $$

where these four numbers are the first eigenvalues of specific triangle orbifolds given in [36, Conjecture 4.2].

Qualitatively, (6.1) consists of an interval together with three singleton outliers. None of the triangle orbifolds which conjecturally give rise to the three outliers carry holomorphic modular forms of weight 4. Therefore, a sample consequence of Conjecture 6.1 is that if $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ carries a holomorphic form of weight 4, then $\lambda_{1}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})$ lies in the interval. Kravchuk, Mazáč, and Pal almost prove this: they show that $\lambda_{1}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})\leq 15.79144$ (see [36, Table 2]). To prove this bound they used linear programming on a computer. An easier estimate, which can be obtained by hand with the same technique, is the theorem below. The case $k=2$ of the theorem gives $\lambda_{1}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})\leq 16$ for $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ as above.

#### Theorem 6.2.

Let $\lambda_{1}$ be the first eigenvalue of a compact hyperbolic 2-orbifold admitting a nonzero holomorphic modular form of weight $2k$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{1}\leq\frac{\sqrt{33k^{2}+18k+1}+9k+1}{2}. $$

The inequality (6.2) is [36, (2.48)]. Although it is far from the sharpest estimate in [36], it is still remarkably accurate given that it has such a simple form. The quality of (6.2) is illustrated in the table below, which displays the largest known $\lambda_{1}$ of a compact hyperbolic 2-orbifold with a holomorphic form of weight $2k$ . The last two columns in the table come from [36, Table 2].

| $k$ | $\RHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_basic_bd}$ | Largest known $\lambda_{1}$ | Topological type of maximizer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8.6055… | 8.4677… | [1;2] |
| 2 | 16 | 15.7902… | [0;2,2,2,3] |
| 3 | 23.3808… | 23.0785… | [0;3,3,4] |
| 4 | 30.7577… | 28.0798… | [0;2,4,5] |
| 6 | 45.5069… | 44.8883… | [0;2,3,7] |

We note, as explained below Table 2 in [36], that every 2-orbifold admits a holomorphic form of weight $2k$ for some $k\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$ .

We now outline the proof of Theorem 6.2 in the language of this paper. This is not a direct translation from [36], but the general mechanism is the same. Let $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ be a compact hyperbolic 2-orbifold as in Theorem 6.2, and let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}=(\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0},\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1},\{C_{ij}^{\ell}\}_{i,j,\ell\in I}) $$

be the multiplicative spectrum of $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ with respect to some choice of $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis. The only information needed to prove Theorem 6.2 is that $\mathcal{S}$ solves the hyperbolic bootstrap equations. Since $\RHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_basic_bd}$ increases with $k$ , we may assume $k=k_{1}$ . Then in the remainder of this subsection, let $i=(-1,k)\in I$ . Following [36], we will deduce Theorem 6.2 from the two results below.

#### Proposition 6.3.

One has

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\lambda_{r}(\lambda_{r}^{2}-(9k+1)\lambda_{r}+12k^{2})|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}=0. $$

#### Lemma 6.4.

There exists $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ such that $C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}\neq 0$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 6.2 assuming Proposition 6.3 and Lemma 6.4.

The right hand side of (6.2) is the larger of the two roots of the quadratic polynomial $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{2}-(9k+1)\lambda+12k^{2}$ . Thus if (6.2) fails, then $\LHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_(2.47)}$ is nonnegative, and in fact by Lemma 6.4 it is strictly positive. This is a contradiction. ∎

It remains to prove Proposition 6.3 and Lemma 6.4. As in Section 5, denote

$$ \displaystyle i^{+n}=(i_{1},i_{2}+n)=(-1,k+n). $$

We will use the following instances of (HB6): for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}i^{+n}}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i^{+n}}\,\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+(n+1)}\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{i^{+n}i^{+(n+1)}}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i^{+n}}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}. $$

Actually, for Proposition 6.3 we will only use the cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ , and for Lemma 6.4, we will only use the case $n=0$ . Given $N\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and coefficients $a_{0},\dots,a_{N},b_{0},\dots,b_{N}\in\mathbf{R}$ , form the linear combination

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{N}(a_{n}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}}+b_{n}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+(n+1)}\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{N}(a_{n}C_{i^{+n}i^{+n}}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i^{+n}}\,\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}}+b_{n}C_{i^{+n}i^{+(n+1)}}^{\ell}C_{\overline{i^{+n}}\,\overline{i^{+(n+1)}}}^{\overline{\ell}}) $$

of (6.4) and (6.5).

#### Lemma 6.5.

Let $N\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $a_{0},\dots,a_{N}\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then there exist $b_{0},\dots,b_{N}\in\mathbf{R}$ , depending only on $k,N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N}$ , such that $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}=0$ .

The proof is elementary but lengthy, so we only give a sketch.

#### Sketch of proof.

For $\ell\in I$ and $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{i^{+n}i^{+n}}^{\ell^{-}}=2\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+(i_{2}+n)(i_{2}+n+1)}\,C_{i^{+n}i^{+(n+1)}}^{\ell} $$

by (HB5) followed by (HB1), and

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}+1)}\,C_{i^{+n}i^{+n}}^{\ell^{+}}=2\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+(i_{2}+n)(i_{2}+n-1)}\,C_{i^{+(n-1)}i^{+n}}^{\ell} $$

by Lemma 5.5 followed by (HB1). Since $\lambda_{i_{1}}=-k(k-1)$ by (1.13) and $i_{2}=k$ , the square roots on the right hand sides of (6.7) and (6.8) depend only on $k$ and $n$ .

Using (6.7), (6.8), (HB2), and (HB3), all of which are linear relations between the $C$ ’s, one can eliminate variables in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ to the point where $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ is expressed as a linear combination of the $N+1$ quantities $D_{0},\dots,D_{N}$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle D_{n}=\sum_{\ell\in I_{2k+2n}}|C_{i^{+n}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle I_{m}=\{\ell\in I:\ell_{1}<0\text{ and }\ell_{2}=k_{-\ell_{1}}=m\} $$

is the set of indices $\ell$ for which $\psi_{\ell}$ is a lowest weight vector in $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ of weight $m$ .

Now, since we have $N+1$ degrees of freedom in the choice of $b_{0},\dots,b_{N}$ , it is plausible that we can choose the $b_{n}$ such that no matter what values the $N+1$ variables $D_{n}$ take, $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ always vanishes. Indeed, performing the elimination of variables explicitly yields an explicit formula for $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ in terms of the $D_{n}$ , and from this formula one can see that such a choice of $b$ ’s exists. ∎

For use in the proofs of Proposition 6.3 and Lemma 6.4, we record two instances of Lemma 6.5.

#### Lemma 6.6.

If $N=0$ and $a_{0}=1$ , then taking $b_{0}=2$ makes $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ vanish. If $N=1$ , $a_{0}=-1$ , and $a_{1}=1$ , then taking

$$ \displaystyle b_{0}=-\frac{4k+2}{k+1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad b_{1}=\frac{4k+2}{k+1} $$

makes $\RHS\eqref{eqn:s-t_crossing_combo}$ vanish.

#### Sketch of proof.

Carry out the proof of Lemma 6.5 in these two cases. ∎

We can now prove Lemma 6.4.

#### Proof of Lemma 6.4.

Let $N=0$ , $a_{0}=1$ , and $b_{0}=2$ . Then by Lemma 6.6, the equation (6.6) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}(C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}+2C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\overline{\ell}})=0. $$

By the case $n=1$ of Corollary 5.9, this further simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\Big[1+2\Big(\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}}{2k}-1\Big)\Big]C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}=0. $$

When $\ell=(0,0)$ , the expression in brackets is nonzero, so by Lemma 5.4, the summand is nonzero. On the other hand, the sum of all the terms is equal to zero, so at least one term besides $\ell=(0,0)$ must be nonzero. This forces $C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}\neq 0$ for some $\ell\neq(0,0)$ . By (HB2) and (1.10), such an $\ell$ must be of the form $\ell=(r,0)$ for some $r\geq 1$ . ∎

We finally prove Proposition 6.3, completing the proof of Theorem 6.2.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.3.

Let $N=1$ , $a_{0}=-1$ , $a_{1}=1$ , and $b_{0},b_{1}$ as in (6.9). Then by Lemma 6.6, the equation (6.6) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\Big[-C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}-\Big(\frac{4k+2}{k+1}\Big)C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\overline{\ell}}+C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\overline{\ell}}+\Big(\frac{4k+2}{k+1}\Big)C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}C_{i^{+2}\overline{i^{+2}}}^{\overline{\ell}}\Big]=0. $$

By Corollary 5.9, we have that for all $\ell\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{i^{+}\overline{i^{+}}}^{\ell}=\Big(\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}}{2k}-1\Big)C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_{i^{+2}\overline{i^{+2}}}^{\ell}=\frac{1}{4k+2}\Big[(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}-6k-2)\Big(\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}}{2k}-1\Big)-2k\Big]C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}. $$

Inserting these into (6.10),

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}R_{k}(\lambda_{\ell_{1}})C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}=0, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle R_{k}(\lambda)=-1-\Big(\frac{4k+2}{k+1}\Big)\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2k}-1\Big)+\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2k}-1\Big)^{2}+\Big(\frac{1}{k+1}\Big)\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2k}-1\Big)\Big[(\lambda-6k-2)\Big(\frac{\lambda}{2k}-1\Big)-2k\Big]. $$

Expanding this formula,

$$ \displaystyle R_{k}(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda(\lambda^{2}-(9k+1)\lambda+12k^{2})}{4k^{2}(k+1)}. $$

By (HB1) and (HB3), we have $C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}=|C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}|^{2}$ , and by (HB2) and (1.10), we have $C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}=0$ unless $\ell=(r,0)$ for some $r\geq 0$ . Thus multiplying (6.11) by $4k^{2}(k+1)$ yields

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\lambda_{r}(\lambda_{r}^{2}-(9k+1)\lambda_{r}+12k^{2})|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}=0. $$

The term where $r=0$ vanishes, so this is equivalent to (6.3). ∎

The motivation for choosing $a_{0}=-1$ and $a_{1}=1$ above is to make the $r=0$ term in (6.13) vanish; this condition determines $(a_{0},a_{1})$ uniquely up to scalars.

#### Remark 6.7.

The above proof of Theorem 6.2 used (6.6) with $N=1$ . The bounds in [36, Table 2] can be proved using (6.6) with $N$ larger, optimizing the choice of parameters $a_{0},\dots,a_{N}$ and $b_{0},\dots,b_{N}$ (c.f. [36, Section 3.9]). For each $N$ , there is some optimal upper bound on $\lambda_{1}$ that can be obtained from (6.6) in this way, and one can ask if this bound converges as $N\to\infty$ to the largest known $\lambda_{1}$ in the table above. Although [36] found that this bound comes close, [53] gives strong numerical evidence that it does not converge all the way to the largest known $\lambda_{1}$ . Theorem 1.19 suggests that by using more instances of (HB6) than just (6.4) and (6.5), it may be possible to prove sharper bounds which do converge to the truth in the limit as more and more hyperbolic bootstrap equations are used. Inspired by the work [71, 19] and [42, 41] on sphere packing and the 1d conformal bootstrap (which by [29] are closely related), one could even speculate that there is an infinite linear combination of instances of (HB6), playing the role of (6.6), which gives an upper bound exactly saturated by the $\lambda_{1}$ ’s in the table above. Such a linear combination is called an extremal functional in the conformal bootstrap literature. It would be striking if an extremal functional could be found explicitly. Because of the inexplicit nature of Laplace eigenvalues, this seems much harder than the analogous problem of finding a magic function for sphere packing (“magic function” is defined for example in [20]). For further discussion, we refer to [36, Section 5] and [53].

### 6.2. Subconvexity for triple product $L$ -functions

Let $\Gamma$ be a cocompact lattice in $G$ , and let $\psi$ be an automorphic form on $\Gamma\backslash G$ . Then $|\psi|^{2}$ has weight $0$ , so $|\psi|^{2}$ is a function on $\Gamma\backslash G/K=\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ , and thus can be expanded in a Laplace eigenbasis. To express this in our notation, let $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ be a $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted basis of $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , and let

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{S}=(\{\lambda_{r}\}_{r\geq 0},\{k_{r}\}_{r\geq 1},\{C_{ij}^{\ell}\}_{i,j,\ell\in I}) $$

be the multiplicative spectrum of $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ with respect to $\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I}$ . Then $\{\psi_{(r,0)}\}_{r\geq 0}$ is a Laplace eigenbasis of $\Gamma\backslash G/K=\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ . Suppose $\psi=\psi_{i}$ for some $i\in I$ . Then the expansion of $|\psi|^{2}$ in the above eigenbasis is

$$ \displaystyle|\psi|^{2}=\psi_{i}\overline{\psi_{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\psi_{i}\psi_{\overline{i}}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\sum_{\ell\in I}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}\psi_{\ell}=(-1)^{i_{2}}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}\psi_{(r,0)}. $$

Here we have used (3.3) for the second equality and (HB2) and (1.10) for the last equality.

The rate of decay of the coefficients $C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}$ as $r\to\infty$ has been well studied due to the connection to $L$ -functions explained below. For more discussion and references, see [1]. The sharpest estimates on the rate of decay can be recast as applications of the hyperbolic bootstrap equations. These estimates are summarized in the following theorem. In the rest of this subsection, implicit constants may depend on $\Gamma$ .

#### Theorem 6.8.

Let $r,\rho\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}$ (think of $\rho$ as fixed, and think of $r$ as going to infinity).

- • (Maass case; [5]) Let $i=(\rho,0)$ . Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ , (6.14) $\displaystyle|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|\lesssim_{\rho,\varepsilon}\lambda_{r}^{-\frac{1}{12}+\varepsilon}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}}.$

- • (Holomorphic case; [1]) Let $k=k_{\rho}$ and $i=(-\rho,k)$ . Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ , (6.15) $\displaystyle|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|\lesssim_{\rho,\varepsilon}\lambda_{r}^{k-\frac{1}{6}+\varepsilon}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}}.$

In the former case, $\psi_{i}$ is a Maass form, and in the latter case, $\psi_{i}$ is a holomorphic modular form (in both cases viewed as functions on $\Gamma\backslash G$ ).

The exponential decay in $\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}$ is a general phenomenon independent of the constant curvature of $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ (see Subsection 11.2 for a soft argument which gives such exponential decay). However, the fact that $\frac{\pi}{2}$ is the correct constant in the exponent does use constant curvature. This was first established in the generality of Theorem 6.8 by Sarnak [62], who was motivated by applications to number theory as suggested by Selberg [65]. The achievement of [5, 1] is to give the best known polynomial factor in front of the exponential. One can formulate an analog of Theorem 6.8 for non-cocompact $\Gamma$ as well (including Eisenstein series in the Laplace eigenbasis). Then specifically for $\Gamma=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{Z})$ , Blomer, Jana, and Nelson [7] showed that $\RHS\eqref{eqn:triple_bd_Maass}$ can be improved to

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{r}^{-\frac{1}{6}+\varepsilon}e^{-\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}}. $$

Their method should generalize to congruence subgroups of $\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{Z})$ . Aside from [7], no other improvement to (6.14) or (6.15) is known even for any single $\Gamma$ .

Theorem 6.8 is of particular interest when $\Gamma$ is arithmetic in a suitable sense, and when the basis elements $\psi_{j}$ are eigenfunctions for the Hecke operators. Then whenever $C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}$ is nonzero, the Watson–Ichino formula [72, 32] expresses $|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}$ as the central value of a triple product $L$ -function multiplied by an explicit constant of proportionality. The estimates (6.14) and (6.15) translate to subconvex bounds for these $L$ -functions in the spectral aspect, and in the holomorphic case, (6.15) is a bound of Weyl quality (see [45] for an introduction to subconvexity). For those triple product $L$ -functions related to one of the $C$ ’s coming from $\Gamma=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{Z})$ , one also has the Weyl bound in the Maass case by [7]. Experience with subconvexity for lower degree $L$ -functions suggests that to improve upon the Weyl bound would require major new ideas. Thus $\frac{1}{6}$ in (6.15) and (6.16) is a significant threshold.

At a high level, the proofs of (6.14) and (6.15) are similar (see [1, Section 6] for a comparison). Here, we focus on (6.15). So let $k$ and $i$ be as in the holomorphic case of Theorem 6.8. Then the only information about $C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}$ used in the proof of (6.15) is [1, Corollary 3.8], which is equivalent to the following proposition. In the statement, ${}_{2}F_{1}$ is the Gauss hypergeometric function, and $s_{r}$ denotes one of the two solutions to the quadratic equation $s_{r}(1-s_{r})=\lambda_{r}$ (it does not matter which one).

#### Proposition 6.9.

Let $z\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[1,\infty)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}{}_{2}F_{1}(s_{r},1-s_{r},1,z)|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}=\Big(\frac{1}{1-z}\Big)^{2k}\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(s_{r},1-s_{r},1,\frac{z}{z-1}\Big)|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}, $$

with both sides converging absolutely and locally uniformly in $z$ .

From the point of view of the conformal bootstrap, (6.17) can be interpreted as a crossing equation, while from the point of view of the analytic theory of automorphic forms, (6.17) can be interpreted as a spectral reciprocity formula.

The convergence assertion in Proposition 6.9 is powerful by itself — we will see when we prove (6.23) that convergence of $\LHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_crossing}$ implies

$$ \displaystyle|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|\lesssim e^{-(\frac{\pi}{2}-o(1))\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}} $$

as $r\to\infty$ .

The plan for the remainder of this subsection is to give an alternative proof of Proposition 6.9 based on the hyperbolic bootstrap equations. This proof is quite different from the one in [1] (which in turn follows [36]). We will derive (6.17) as a formal identity by taking linear combinations of crossing equations as in the proof of Proposition 6.3. This formal derivation uses only that $\mathcal{S}$ solves the hyperbolic bootstrap equations. Unlike in the proof of Proposition 6.3, we will take an infinite linear combination, and to prove convergence, we will need an additional estimate on the $C$ ’s (“additional” in the sense that we do not assume it in Theorem 1.19). This estimate is the lemma below, and its proof uses that $\mathcal{S}$ comes from a 2-orbifold. Specifically, the proof uses a Sobolev embedding inequality for functions on $\Gamma\backslash G$ .

#### Lemma 6.10.

Let $j,j^{\prime}\in I$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|C_{jj^{\prime}}^{\ell}|^{2}\lesssim_{j_{1},j_{1}^{\prime}}(|j_{2}|+|j_{2}^{\prime}|+1)^{O(1)}. $$

#### Proof.

Write

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}|C_{jj^{\prime}}^{\ell}|^{2}=\|\psi_{j}\psi_{j^{\prime}}\|_{L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)}^{2}\leq\|\psi_{j}\|_{L^{4}(\Gamma\backslash G)}^{2}\|\psi_{j^{\prime}}\|_{L^{4}(\Gamma\backslash G)}^{2}. $$

This reduces us to showing that

$$ \displaystyle\|\psi_{j}\|_{L^{4}(\Gamma\backslash G)}\lesssim_{j_{1}}(|j_{2}|+1)^{O(1)}. $$

By Sobolev embedding, it further suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathcal{D}\psi_{j}\|_{L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)}\lesssim_{\mathcal{D},j_{1}}(|j_{2}|+1)^{O_{\mathcal{D}}(1)} $$

for any differential operator $\mathcal{D}$ in the universal enveloping algebra $\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{g})$ . Since $\mathfrak{g}$ is spanned by $H,E,\overline{E}$ , this follows from Proposition 3.3 by induction on the degree of $\mathcal{D}$ . ∎

To prove Proposition 6.9, we will use the following instances of (HB6), one for each $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{\overline{i}i}^{\ell}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}} $$

(as usual, $i^{+n}=(i_{1},i_{2}+n)$ ). For $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $|z|<1$ , consider the infinite linear combination

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}z^{n}\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}z^{n}\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}C_{\overline{i}i}^{\ell}C_{i^{+n}\overline{i^{+n}}}^{\overline{\ell}} $$

of (6.19), where

$$ \displaystyle(q)_{n}=q(q+1)\cdots(q+n-1) $$

denotes the (rising) Pochhammer symbol (and $(q)_{0}=1$ ). By Cauchy–Schwarz and Lemma 6.10, both sides of (6.20) converge absolutely and locally uniformly in $z$ for $|z|<1$ . Thus, to prove Proposition 6.9 in the case $|z|<1$ , it suffices to prove the two lemmas below.

#### Lemma 6.11.

Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $|z|<1$ . Then $\LHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\LHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_crossing}$ .

#### Lemma 6.12.

Let $z\in\mathbf{C}$ with $|z|<1$ . Then $\RHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\RHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_crossing}$ .

Before we prove these two lemmas, let us see how the full Proposition 6.9 can be deduced once we know it for $|z|<1$ . The key is the following hypergeometric asymptotic.

#### Lemma 6.13.

Fix $z\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[1,\infty)$ . Then there exists $\delta=\delta(z)>0$ , such that if $s\in\mathbf{C}$ satisfies $s(1-s)=\lambda$ with $\lambda\gg_{z}1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle|{}_{2}F_{1}(s,1-s,1,z)|\leq e^{(\pi-\delta)\sqrt{\lambda}}. $$

Furthermore, $\delta(z)$ may be taken to be locally uniformly bounded below as a function of $z$ .

Conversely, for each $\delta>0$ , if $z\in(0,1)$ is sufficiently close to $1$ depending on $\delta$ , and if $s\in\mathbf{C}$ satisfies $s(1-s)=\lambda$ with $\lambda\gg_{\delta}1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle{}_{2}F_{1}(s,1-s,1,z)\geq e^{(\pi-\delta)\sqrt{\lambda}}. $$

#### Idea of proof.

Apply the method of steepest descent to Euler’s integral representation for ${}_{2}F_{1}$ . ∎

We do not give a complete proof of Lemma 6.13 because it is tangential to our main story.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.9 for general $z$ assuming Proposition 6.9 for $|z|<1$ .

By assumption, $\LHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_crossing}$ converges absolutely for $|z|<1$ . It follows from (6.22) that for every $\delta>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}e^{(\pi-\delta)\sqrt{\lambda_{r}}}<\infty. $$

Thus by (6.21), both sides of (6.17) converge absolutely for all $z\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[1,\infty)$ . Since $\delta=\delta(z)$ in (6.21) may be taken locally uniformly bounded below, both sides of (6.17) also converge locally uniformly. Hence both sides of (6.17) are well-defined holomorphic functions on all of $\mathbf{C}\setminus[1,\infty)$ . By assumption, (6.17) holds for $|z|<1$ , so it holds for all $z\in\mathbf{C}\setminus[1,\infty)$ by analytic continuation. ∎

It remains to prove Lemmas 6.11 and 6.12. To do so, we need one final lemma, which will allow us to compute $\LHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}$ .

#### Lemma 6.14.

Let $\ell\in I$ and $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Suppose $C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}\neq 0$ . Then $\ell=(r,n)$ for some $r\geq 0$ , and

$$ \displaystyle|C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}=\frac{(s_{r})_{n}(1-s_{r})_{n}}{n!(2k)_{n}}|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

We induct on $n$ . For the base case, suppose $n=0$ . Then by (HB2) and (1.10), nonvanishing of $C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}$ forces $\ell=(r,0)$ for some $r\geq 0$ . Since $n=0$ , the quotient in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_recurrence_for_Weyl}$ is equal to $1$ . Thus (6.24) holds by (HB1).

For the induction step, suppose $n>0$ . Then by (HB5) and the fact that $\overline{i}^{+}\not\in I$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}\,C_{\overline{i}i^{+(n-1)}}^{\ell^{-}}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i_{1}}+(i_{2}+n-1)(i_{2}+n)}\,C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}. $$

Inserting $\lambda_{i_{1}}=-k(k-1)$ and $i_{2}=k$ , and then squaring both sides,

$$ \displaystyle(\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1))|C_{\overline{i}i^{+(n-1)}}^{\ell^{-}}|^{2}=(-k(k-1)+(k+n-1)(k+n))|C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}. $$

Simplifying the coefficient on the right hand side, and then dividing both sides by this coefficient,

$$ \displaystyle|C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}=\frac{\lambda_{\ell_{1}}+\ell_{2}(\ell_{2}-1)}{n(2k+n-1)}|C_{\overline{i}i^{+(n-1)}}^{\ell^{-}}|^{2}. $$

By assumption, the left hand side is nonzero, so the right hand side must be nonzero. Then by induction, $\ell^{-}=(r,n-1)$ for some $r\geq 0$ , so $\ell=(r,n)$ . Furthermore, by induction, we can rewrite the right hand side using (6.24), to get

$$ \displaystyle|C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}=\frac{\lambda_{r}+n(n-1)}{n(2k+n-1)}\,\frac{(s_{r})_{n-1}(1-s_{r})_{n-1}}{(n-1)!(2k)_{n-1}}|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}. $$

We note that the numerator in the first quotient in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_recurrence_after_induction}$ agrees with the numerator in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_recurrence_before_induction}$ because $\ell_{1}=r$ and $\ell_{2}=n$ . This numerator factors as

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{r}+n(n-1)=s_{r}(1-s_{r})+n(n-1)=(s_{r}+n-1)(1-s_{r}+(n-1)). $$

Inserting this into (6.26) yields (6.24). ∎

We are finally ready to prove Lemmas 6.11 and 6.12.

#### Proof of Lemma 6.11.

By (HB3),

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}z^{n}\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}|C_{\overline{i}i^{+n}}^{\ell}|^{2}. $$

By Lemma 6.14, this simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\Big[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(s_{r})_{n}(1-s_{r})_{n}}{n!^{2}}z^{n}\Big]|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}. $$

The expression in brackets is the standard power series expansion of the hypergeometric which appears in $\LHS\eqref{eqn:KMP_crossing}$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 6.12.

Let $B_{k,n}$ be as in Corollary 5.9. Then

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\sum_{\ell\in I}(-1)^{\ell_{2}}\Big[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}B_{k,n}(\lambda_{\ell_{1}})z^{n}\Big]C_{\overline{i}i}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}. $$

By (HB1) and (HB3), we have $C_{\overline{i}i}^{\ell}C_{i\overline{i}}^{\overline{\ell}}=|C_{i\overline{i}}^{\ell}|^{2}$ . By (HB2) and (1.10), we get

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:u-t_crossing_combo}=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\Big[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}B_{k,n}(\lambda_{r})z^{n}\Big]|C_{i\overline{i}}^{(r,0)}|^{2}. $$

Thus to prove Lemma 6.12, we just need to show that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^{n}\frac{(2k)_{n}}{n!}B_{k,n}(\lambda_{r})z^{n}=\Big(\frac{1}{1-z}\Big)^{2k}{}_{2}F_{1}\Big(s_{r},1-s_{r},1,\frac{z}{z-1}\Big). $$

This can be done by using the recurrence (5.13) and the hypergeometric ODE to check that both sides of (6.27) obey the same ODE, with the same initial conditions at $z=0$ . We omit the details. ∎

The proof of Proposition 6.9 is now complete.

## 7. Preliminaries on C*-algebras

A C*-algebra is a complex Banach algebra $\mathcal{A}$ with an antilinear involution $A\mapsto A^{*}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle(AB)^{*}=B^{*}A^{*}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|A^{*}A\|=\|A\|^{2} $$

for all $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ . A morphism of C*-algebras (or C*-homomorphism) is a norm-decreasing map which respects both the algebra structure and the involution. For us, the two most important examples of C*-algebras are:

- • Let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space. Then $C(X)$ is a commutative unital C*-algebra with the uniform norm and with complex conjugation as the involution.

- • Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space. Then $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is a C*-algebra with the operator norm and with the adjoint as the involution. If $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is a subalgebra which is closed in the operator norm topology and closed under taking adjoints, then $\mathcal{A}$ is a C*-subalgebra.

Commutative unital C*-algebras were classified by Gelfand. There are many textbook accounts of the classification, such as [26, Chapter 1].

#### Theorem 7.1 (Gelfand duality).

The functor $X\mapsto C(X)$ is an equivalence from the opposite category of compact Hausdorff spaces to the category of commutative unital C*-algebras.

Concretely, this means the following two things. The first says that $X\mapsto C(X)$ is fully faithful, and the second says that $X\mapsto C(X)$ is essentially surjective.

- (1) If $X,Y$ are compact Hausdorff spaces and $\Phi\colon C(X)\to C(Y)$ is a C*-homomorphism, then there is a unique continuous map $T\colon Y\to X$ such that $\Phi(f)=f\circ T$ for all $f\in C(X)$ .

- (2) Every commutative unital C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is isomorphic to $C(X)$ for some compact Hausdorff space $X$ . It follows from (1) that $X$ is unique up to homeomorphism. The space $X$ is called the spectrum of $\mathcal{A}$ .

The book [26] cited above only proves essential surjectivity, but full faithfulness is easy to see from the proof of essential surjectivity.

A compact Hausdorff space $X$ is metrizable if and only if $C(X)$ is separable (i.e., has a countable dense subset). Therefore, the spectrum of a commutative unital C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is metrizable if and only if $\mathcal{A}$ is separable.

A state on a C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a positive linear functional of norm $1$ . Positivity means that the functional takes a nonnegative value on $A^{*}A$ for all $A\in\mathcal{A}$ . Given a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ , a unital C*-subalgebra $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ , and a vector $v\in\mathcal{H}$ of norm $1$ , the Gelfand–Naimark–Segal (GNS) state on $\mathcal{A}$ associated to $v$ is the functional $A\mapsto\langle Av,v\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}$ .

## 8. Proofs of uniqueness results

In this section we prove Propositions 1.9 and 1.20. Proposition 1.20 is essentially a corollary of Proposition 1.9, so we start with Proposition 1.9. Recall the statement:

#### Proposition (Restatement of Proposition 1.9).

Let $\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime}$ be cocompact lattices in $G$ . Suppose $\Phi\colon L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)\to L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)$ is an isomorphism of multiplicative representations. Then there exists a unique element $g\in G/\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma^{\prime}=g\Gamma g^{-1}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(f)(x)=f(g^{-1}x) $$

for all $f\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

We first prove a sequence of lemmas with notation as in Proposition 1.9. Recall that $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $C^{\infty}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , and in particular dense in $C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ with respect to the uniform norm.

#### Lemma 8.1.

Let $f\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $\|\Phi(f)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}$ .

#### Proof.

Using that $L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)$ , that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, and that $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Phi(f)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\sup_{v}\|\Phi(f)v\|_{L^{2}}=\sup_{w}\|\Phi(f)\Phi(w)\|_{L^{2}}=\sup_{w}\|fw\|_{L^{2}}=\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}, $$

with suprema over $v\in L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with $\|v\|_{L^{2}}\leq 1$ and $w\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with $\|w\|_{L^{2}}\leq 1$ . ∎

#### Lemma 8.2.

Let $f\in C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Then $\Phi(f)\in C(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)$ , and $\|\Phi(f)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , there is a sequence $f_{n}\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ converging uniformly to $f$ . Since $\Phi$ is an isometry of $L^{2}$ spaces, $\Phi(f_{n})\to\Phi(f)$ in $L^{2}$ . By Lemma 8.1, the sequence $\Phi(f_{n})$ is Cauchy with respect to the uniform norm, so in fact $\Phi(f_{n})\to\Phi(f)$ uniformly. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous, so $\Phi(f)$ is continuous. Lemma 8.1 together with the uniform convergence of $\Phi(f_{n})$ to $\Phi(f)$ implies that $\|\Phi(f)\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 8.3.

Let $f,h\in C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Then $\Phi(fh)=\Phi(f)\Phi(h)$ .

#### Proof.

Let $f_{n},h_{n}\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with $f_{n}\to f$ and $h_{n}\to h$ uniformly. Then $f_{n}h_{n}\to fh$ uniformly. It follows from Lemma 8.2 that $\Phi(f_{n})$ , $\Phi(h_{n})$ , and $\Phi(f_{n}h_{n})$ converge uniformly to $f$ , $h$ , and $fh$ , respectively. Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\Phi(fh)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi(f_{n}h_{n})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi(f_{n})\Phi(h_{n})=\Phi(f)\Phi(h). $$

Here the second equality is because $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of multiplicative representations. ∎

#### Lemma 8.4.

Let $f\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Then $\Phi(\overline{f})=\overline{\Phi(f)}$ .

#### Proof.

By continuity, it suffices to prove this for $f$ in $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then since $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of multiplicative representations, $\Phi(\overline{f})$ is the complex conjugate of $\Phi(f)$ in the sense of Definition 1.6. Complex conjugation on $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ as a multiplicative representation coincides with complex conjugation of functions, so $\Phi(\overline{f})=\overline{\Phi(f)}$ . ∎

We are now ready to prove Proposition 1.9.

#### Proof of Proposition 1.9.

By Lemmas 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4, $\Phi$ is a C*-homomorphism from $C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ to $C(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G)$ . Applying the same argument to $\Phi^{-1}$ shows that $\Phi$ is a C*-isomorphism. Thus by Gelfand duality (Theorem 7.1), there is a unique homeomorphism $T\colon\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G\to\Gamma\backslash G$ such that $\Phi(f)=f\circ T$ for all $f\in C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Since $\Phi$ is $G$ -equivariant, Gelfand duality implies that $T$ is $G$ -equivariant. Let $e$ denote the identity coset in $\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G$ , and set $g=T(e)^{-1}\in G/\Gamma$ . Then for $x\in G$ ,

$$ \displaystyle T(x)=T(ex)=T(e)x=g^{-1}x, $$

where the second equality is because $T$ is equivariant. In words, (8.2) says that $T$ is given by left-translation by $g^{-1}$ . Thus we have the following equality in $\Gamma\backslash G$ :

$$ \displaystyle g^{-1}\Gamma^{\prime}=T(\Gamma^{\prime})=T(e)=g^{-1}. $$

The fact that this holds in $\Gamma\backslash G$ means that $g^{-1}\Gamma^{\prime}\subseteq\Gamma g^{-1}$ as subsets of $G$ . Rearranging, $\Gamma^{\prime}\subseteq g\Gamma g^{-1}$ . Since $T$ , given by (8.2), is a homeomorphism, we must have $\Gamma^{\prime}=g\Gamma g^{-1}$ . The formula (8.2) implies (8.1) for all $f\in C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Since $\Phi$ is an isometry of $L^{2}$ spaces, (8.1) extends to all $f\in L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ by continuity. Since $T$ is unique, the uniqueness of $g$ in Proposition 1.9 is clear. ∎

Proposition 1.20 follows easily from Proposition 1.9. Recall the statement of Proposition 1.20:

#### Proposition (Restatement of Proposition 1.20).

Let $(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H},\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I})$ and $(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbf{H},\{\psi_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in I^{\prime}})$ be compact hyperbolic 2-orbifolds equipped with $(\mathfrak{g},K)$ -adapted bases. If both have the same multiplicative spectrum, then $I=I^{\prime}$ , and there exists a unique element $g\in G/\Gamma$ such that $\Gamma^{\prime}=g\Gamma g^{-1}$ and

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{i}^{\prime}(x)=\psi_{i}(g^{-1}x) $$

for all $i\in I$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbf{H}$ have the same Laplace and holomorphic spectra, $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G,\mathbf{R})$ and $L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G,\mathbf{R})$ are isomorphic as real unitary representations, and $I=I^{\prime}$ . Thus by Proposition 3.2, there exists a unique isomorphism $\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}\colon L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G,\mathbf{R})\to L^{2}(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash G,\mathbf{R})$ whose complexification $\Phi$ satisfies $\Phi(\psi_{i})=\psi_{i}^{\prime}$ for all $i\in I$ . Since $(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H},\{\psi_{i}\}_{i\in I})$ and $(\Gamma^{\prime}\backslash\mathbf{H},\{\psi_{i}^{\prime}\}_{i\in I})$ have the same multiplication table, $\Phi$ is an isomorphism of multiplicative representations. Therefore Proposition 1.9 implies that there exists an element $g\in G/\Gamma$ satisfying the desired properties. Since $\Phi_{\mathbf{R}}$ is unique, $g$ is unique. ∎

## 9. Elementary properties of complex conjugation on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$

The remainder of the paper is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 1.8. So from now on, let $\mathcal{H}$ be a multiplicative representation.

We show in this section that complex conjugation on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , as defined by the “existence of complex conjugates” axiom in Definition 1.6, obeys the expected properties.
