In particular, we verify all the assertions in Remark 1.27. These properties will be used freely without comment later on.

#### Proposition 9.1.

One has $\overline{\mathbf{1}}=\mathbf{1}$ .

#### Proof.

For all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\mathbf{1}\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\alpha,\overline{\mathbf{1}}\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ , it follows that $\beta=\overline{\mathbf{1}}\beta$ . Thus $\overline{\mathbf{1}}$ is a unit, and hence $\overline{\mathbf{1}}=\mathbf{1}$ because the unit is unique. ∎

#### Proposition 9.2.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $\overline{\overline{\alpha}}=\alpha$ .

#### Proof.

For all $\beta,\gamma\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{\alpha}\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\overline{\langle\gamma,\overline{\alpha}\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\overline{\langle\alpha\gamma,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\langle\beta,\alpha\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

This shows that $\alpha$ satisfies the adjointness property characterizing $\overline{\overline{\alpha}}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 9.3.

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{\alpha},\overline{\beta}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\overline{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}. $$

#### Proof.

Using that $\overline{\overline{\alpha}}=\alpha$ by Proposition 9.2,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{\alpha},\overline{\beta}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\overline{\alpha},\overline{\beta}\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\overline{\alpha}\beta,\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\beta,\alpha\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\overline{\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}.\qed $$

#### Proposition 9.4.

Complex conjugation is antilinear, i.e., for all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ and $c\in\mathbf{C}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\overline{c\alpha+\beta}=\overline{c}\,\overline{\alpha}+\overline{\beta}. $$

#### Proof.

Clearly $\overline{c}\,\overline{\alpha}+\overline{\beta}$ obeys the adjointness property characterizing $\overline{c\alpha+\beta}$ . ∎

Putting Propositions 9.2, 9.3, and 9.4 together, we obtain

#### Proposition 9.5.

Complex conjugation extends by continuity to an antilinear involution on $\mathcal{H}$ , denoted $v\mapsto\overline{v}$ , with

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{v},\overline{w}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\overline{\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}\qquad\text{and in particular}\qquad\|\overline{v}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $v,w\in\mathcal{H}$ .

#### Proof.

By Propositions 9.3 and 9.4, complex conjugation on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is norm-preserving and antilinear, so it extends by continuity to $\mathcal{H}$ . The stated properties of complex conjugation on $\mathcal{H}$ then follow by continuity from the analogous properties on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , which are due to Propositions 9.2, 9.3, and 9.4. ∎

From now on, whenever we use complex conjugation on $\mathcal{H}$ , we understand that it is defined through Proposition 9.5. Given a linear subspace $\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{H}$ , denote

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\mathbf{R}}=\{v\in\mathcal{E}:\overline{v}=v\}. $$

This is an $\mathbf{R}$ -linear subspace of $\mathcal{E}$ . For each $v\in\mathcal{H}$ , there is a unique way to write $v=\re v+i\im v$ for some $\re v,\im v\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , namely by taking

$$ \displaystyle\re v=\frac{1}{2}(v+\overline{v})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\im v=\frac{1}{2i}(v-\overline{v}). $$

The existence and uniqueness of this decomposition into real and imaginary parts means that $\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\otimes_{\mathbf{R}}\mathbf{C}$ as vector spaces.

An immediate corollary of (9.1) in Proposition 9.5 is

#### Corollary 9.6.

Let $v,w\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Then $\langle v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\in\mathbf{R}$ .

#### Proposition 9.7.

Let $v\in\mathcal{H}$ . Then $\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\|\re v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}+\|\im v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}$ .

#### Proof.

Expand $\|\re v+i\im v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}$ and note that the cross terms vanish because of Corollary 9.6. ∎

#### Proposition 9.8.

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $\overline{\alpha\beta}=\overline{\alpha}\overline{\beta}$ . In particular if $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , then $\alpha\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\infty}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\gamma\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be arbitrary. Then by (9.1) in Proposition 9.5,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{\alpha\beta},\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\overline{\langle\alpha\beta,\overline{\gamma}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\overline{\langle\beta,\overline{\alpha}\,\overline{\gamma}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\overline{\langle\beta\gamma,\overline{\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\overline{\langle\gamma,\overline{\alpha}\overline{\beta}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}}=\langle\overline{\alpha}\overline{\beta},\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $\gamma$ was arbitrary, it follows by density that $\overline{\alpha\beta}=\overline{\alpha}\overline{\beta}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 9.9.

The $G$ -action respects complex conjugation, i.e., $\overline{gv}=g\overline{v}$ for all $g\in G$ and $v\in\mathcal{H}$ . Consequently $\overline{Xv}=\overline{X}\overline{v}$ for all $X\in\mathfrak{g}$ and $v\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove these two assertions in the reverse order, so we start with $\overline{Xv}=\overline{X}\overline{v}$ . By density, it suffices to show that $\overline{X\alpha}=\overline{X}\overline{\alpha}$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be arbitrary. Since $\mathbf{1}$ is $G$ -invariant, we have $\overline{X}\mathbf{1}=0$ , so using (2.7) and the product rule, we can write

$$ \displaystyle 0=-\langle\alpha\beta,\overline{X}\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle X(\alpha\beta),\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle(X\alpha)\beta,\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\alpha(X\beta),\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle\beta,\overline{X\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle X\beta,\overline{\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle\beta,\overline{X\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle\beta,\overline{X}\overline{\alpha}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $\beta$ was arbitrary, it follows by density that $\overline{X\alpha}=\overline{X}\overline{\alpha}$ , as desired.

We now show that $\overline{gv}=g\overline{v}$ for all $g\in G$ and $v\in\mathcal{H}$ . By density, it suffices to prove this for $v$ a real analytic vector, i.e., such that $g\mapsto gv$ is a real analytic function from $G$ to $\mathcal{H}$ . So fix $v\in\mathcal{H}$ real analytic. Consider $\Omega=\{g\in G:\overline{gv}=g\overline{v}\}$ . This is evidently a closed subset of $G$ . We claim that it is also open. To see this, let $g_{0}\in\Omega$ , and denote $w=g_{0}v$ . We must show $g\in\Omega$ for $g$ sufficiently close to $g_{0}$ . Write $g=\exp(X)g_{0}$ with $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ sufficiently small. Then

$$ \displaystyle g\in\Omega\qquad\iff\qquad\overline{\exp(X)w}=\exp(X)\overline{w}. $$

Since $v$ is real analytic and $w$ is a translate of $v$ , we have that $w$ is also real analytic, so for $X$ sufficiently small, we can Taylor expand both sides to get

$$ \displaystyle g\in\Omega\qquad\iff\qquad\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\overline{X^{n}w}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}X^{n}\overline{w}. $$

Noting that $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , this is true by the previous paragraph. Thus $\Omega$ is indeed open. Since $G$ is connected, we conclude that $\Omega=G$ , so $\overline{gv}=g\overline{v}$ for all $g\in G$ . ∎

## 10. $L^{\infty}$ and $L^{4}$ norms on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$

For each $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , let $M_{\alpha}$ denote the densely defined operator on $\mathcal{H}$ , with domain $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , given by multiplication by $\alpha$ . Define $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}$ to be the operator norm of $M_{\alpha}$ , that is, the smallest constant $C\in[0,\infty]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq C\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}. $$

The motivation for this definition is that whenever $f$ is a function on a measure space, the $L^{\infty}$ norm of $f$ can be characterized as the operator norm of multiplication-by- $f$ acting on $L^{2}$ (we already used this idea in the proof of Lemma 8.1). Indeed, in the case $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , the $L^{\infty}$ norm on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ coincides with the usual $L^{\infty}$ norm on functions on $\Gamma\backslash G$ . In general, it is not at all clear that $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ for $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . This finiteness is the $n=0$ case of Theorem 11.6.

Define the $L^{4}$ norm of $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}=\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

This evidently agrees with the usual $L^{4}$ norm when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . In general, for $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , we have $\alpha^{2}\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}\subseteq\mathcal{H}$ , so $\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}<\infty$ . By crossing symmetry (the last axiom in Definition 1.6),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{4}=\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Since complex conjugation commutes with multiplication and preserves the Hilbert space norm,

$$ \displaystyle\|\overline{\alpha}\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\overline{\alpha}\|_{L^{4}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}} $$

for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Since $M_{\alpha+\beta}=M_{\alpha}+M_{\beta}$ , the $L^{\infty}$ norm satisfies the triangle inequality

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha+\beta\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|\beta\|_{L^{\infty}} $$

for all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . The triangle inequality for the $L^{4}$ norm is Proposition 10.2 below.

#### Proposition 10.1 ( $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz).

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}. $$

#### Proof.

By crossing symmetry, Cauchy–Schwarz, and (10.1),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle|\alpha|^{2},|\beta|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\||\beta|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{2}.\qed $$

#### Proposition 10.2 (Triangle inequality for the $L^{4}$ norm).

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha+\beta\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}+\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}. $$

#### Proof.

Write

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha+\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{2}=\|(\alpha+\beta)^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}+2\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\beta^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{2}+2\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}+\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{2}=(\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}+\|\beta\|_{L^{4}})^{2}, $$

where the inequality between the first and second lines is by $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz. ∎

#### Proposition 10.3 (Comparison of norms).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}. $$

#### Proof.

By $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz and the normalization axiom in Definition 1.6,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\alpha\mathbf{1}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\mathbf{1}\|_{L^{4}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}. $$

This gives the first inequality. For the second, write

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{2}=\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\|\alpha\mathbf{1}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\|\mathbf{1}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}.\qed $$

## 11. Outline of proof of the converse theorem for multiplicative representations

Theorem 1.8 says that if $\mathcal{H}$ is nontrivial, then $\mathcal{H}\simeq L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ for some cocompact lattice $\Gamma$ in $G$ . In this section, we outline the proof of this theorem.

We will use the notation for the functional calculus for the Casimir from Subsection 2.3, as well as the $L^{\infty}$ and $L^{4}$ norms on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ defined in Section 10.

### 11.1. Roadmap

The purpose of this subsection is to describe the structure of the proof and to state the most important intermediate results. For each of these intermediate results, we will either give some intuition as to why it is true, or in the next subsection we will explain why it is true in the case $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . Of course, by Theorem 1.8, this is the only nontrivial case, but it would be circular to use this. The proofs of these intermediate results in the general case are outlined in Subsections 11.3–11.7.

We break the proof of Theorem 1.8 into five steps. The first two are quantitative, and the last three are qualitative.

#### Step 1.

Given $\lambda\geq 0$ and approximate Casimir eigenvectors $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ with approximate eigenvalue $\lambda$ (meaning that $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I}^{K}$ for some small interval $I$ around $\lambda$ ), estimate the product $\alpha\beta$ . More precisely, bound the Hilbert space norm of both the “bulk” $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim\lambda}(\alpha\beta)$ and the “tail” $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg\lambda}(\alpha\beta)$ . In addition, given a lowest weight vector $f$ , bound the tail of $|f|^{2}$ .

These three bounds correspond to Theorems 11.9, 11.11, and 11.10, respectively. They are proved in Sections 15 and 16.

#### Step 2.

From the results of Step 1, deduce two estimates on $L^{\infty}$ norms of automorphic vectors, the first with explicit dependence on the weight, and the second with explicit dependence on the Casimir eigenvalue.

These two estimates correspond to Theorems 11.6 and 11.7, and they are proved in Section 14. Importantly, both of these theorems apply not just to automorphic vectors, but more generally to elements of $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . The case $n=0$ of Theorem 11.6 says that the $L^{\infty}$ norm is finite-valued on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Thus for each $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , the multiplication operator $M_{\alpha}$ extends from $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ to a bounded linear operator on $\mathcal{H}$ . We thereby view $M_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ .

#### Step 3.

Let $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ be the closed subalgebra generated by $\{M_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\}$ . Show that $\mathcal{A}$ is closed under taking adjoints, so $\mathcal{A}$ is a C*-algebra. Show that $\mathcal{A}$ is commutative, unital, and separable. The unitary group $\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H})$ acts on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ by conjugation; pull this action back along the representation $G\to U(\mathcal{H})$ to obtain an action of $G$ on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ . Use Theorem 11.6 from Step 2 to show that this $G$ -action preserves $\mathcal{A}$ , and that the action map $G\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}$ is continuous.

This is all done in Subsection 13.1.

#### Step 4.

By Gelfand duality, $\mathcal{A}\simeq C(X)$ for a unique compact Hausdorff space $X$ , and the $G$ -action on $\mathcal{A}$ induces a $G$ -action on $X$ . Since $\mathcal{A}$ is separable, $X$ is metrizable. Using that $G\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}$ is continuous, show that $G\times X\to X$ is continuous. Consider the GNS state on $\mathcal{A}\simeq C(X)$ associated to $\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{H}$ . By the Riesz representation theorem, this state is given by integration against a probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ . Show that $\mu$ is $G$ -invariant and has full support. Show that $\mathcal{H}$ identifies with $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ as unitary $G$ -representations, in such a way that multiplication on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is given by pointwise multiplication on $X$ . Translate known properties of $\mathcal{H}$ as a multiplicative representation into properties of $(X,\mu)$ . In particular, translate Corollary 11.8 of Theorem 11.7 from Step 2 into the qualitative Sobolev embedding property (Definition 11.1) for $(X,\mu)$ .

This is all done in Subsection 13.2.

#### Step 5.

Deduce from the qualitative Sobolev embedding property that $X\simeq\Gamma\backslash G$ as $G$ -spaces for some cocompact lattice $\Gamma$ , and that $\mu$ is Haar measure.

This deduction is Theorem 11.3, proved in Section 12.

As can be seen from the section numbering, we present these five steps almost backward, in the order 5, 3, 4, 2, 1. This way, the end goal is always in sight.

We now indicate the main results that make up each step (in the above order). The key definition for Step 5 is

#### Definition 11.1 (Qualitative Sobolev embedding property).

Let $X$ be a $G$ -space equipped with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ . We say that $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property if there exist $1\leq p<q\leq\infty$ and a nonnegative continuous function $\varphi\in L^{1}(G)$ , not identically zero, such that for all $f\in L^{p}(X,\mu)$ , the convolution

$$ \displaystyle\varphi\ast f(x)=\int_{G}\varphi(g)f(g^{-1}x)\,dg $$

lies in $L^{q}(X,\mu)$ .

One should think of the operator $f\mapsto\varphi\ast f$ as “smoothing along $G$ -orbits.” Then the slogan for the qualitative Sobolev embedding property is that “smoothing along $G$ -orbits improves integrability.” One might worry that the source of improvement of integrability is cancellation in the integral (11.1), not smoothing. We require $\varphi$ to be nonnegative so that when $f$ is also nonnegative, there can be no cancellation in (11.1). We require $\varphi$ to be continuous (and not identically zero) so that it is not just positive somewhere, but positive on a nonempty open set.

By the end of Step 4, we will have established the following weak version of the converse theorem for multiplicative representations.

#### Theorem 11.2 (Weak converse theorem).

There exists a connected compact metrizable $G$ -space $X$ together with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ of full support, such that $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property, $\mathcal{H}$ identifies with $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ as unitary representations of $G$ , and the multiplication $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\times\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ is given by pointwise multiplication of functions on $X$ .

Connectedness of $X$ will come from the ergodicity axiom in the definition of a multiplicative representation. The proof of Theorem 11.2 shows that $(X,\mu)$ obeys the qualitative Sobolev embedding property with $p=2$ and $q=\infty$ . Given Theorem 11.2, it essentially remains to prove

#### Theorem 11.3 (Sobolev embedding implies $X\simeq\Gamma\backslash G$ ).

As usual, let $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ . Let $X$ be a connected Hausdorff $G$ -space equipped with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ of full support. Assume $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property. Then either $X$ is a point, or $X\simeq\Gamma\backslash G$ as $G$ -spaces for some cocompact lattice $\Gamma$ in $G$ .

The case where $X$ is a point corresponds to the trivial multiplicative representation. The nontriviality assumption in Theorem 1.8 is used to eliminate this case. It would suffice to prove Theorem 11.3 for $X$ connected compact metrizable, but the proof only requires that $X$ is connected and Hausdorff. On the other hand, Theorem 11.3 does use something specific about $G$ , namely that $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ is a noncompact simple Lie group. What is true in general is

#### Theorem 11.4 (Sobolev embedding implies homogeneity).

Let $G$ be a connected Lie group, and let $X$ be a connected Hausdorff $G$ -space equipped with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ of full support. Assume $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property. Then $X\simeq H\backslash G$ as $G$ -spaces for some closed cocompact subgroup $H\subseteq G$ .

This combined with the following known proposition implies Theorem 11.3.

#### Proposition 11.5.

Let $G$ be a noncompact simple Lie group (e.g., $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ ). Let $H\subseteq G$ be a closed cocompact subgroup such that $H\backslash G$ admits a $G$ -invariant probability measure. Then either $H$ is discrete or $H=G$ .

For completeness, we provide a short self-contained proof of this proposition in Subsection 12.3.

To summarize, Step 5 reduces to proving Theorem 11.4. The intuition for this theorem is as follows. Recall the slogan for the qualitative Sobolev embedding property is that “smoothing along $G$ -orbits improves integrability.” If $X$ is not locally homogeneous, then smoothing along $G$ -orbits amounts to smoothing along some (but not all) directions in $X$ . It should then be possible to build a function $f$ which is smooth in these directions but which blows up in a transverse direction. Convolving $f$ with $\varphi$ will not qualitatively affect $f$ , because $f$ is already smooth along $G$ -orbits. This means that the integrability of $f$ will not improve, contradicting the qualitative Sobolev embedding property. We conclude, at least heuristically, that $X$ is locally homogeneous. A connectedness argument then allows us to upgrade local homogeneity to global homogeneity. An example of this heuristic at work is given in Subsection 11.3.

At this point, let $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ once more, and consider Steps 3 and 4. Although these two steps have a lot of components, almost all are reasonably straightforward. The only difficult thing to show is that the $G$ -action on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ preserves $\mathcal{A}$ (this is Theorem 13.3). In other words, the restriction of the $G$ -action on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ to $\mathcal{A}$ is a map $G\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ , and we wish to show that the image of this map is $\mathcal{A}$ . The reason this is difficult is that $\mathcal{A}$ is generated by (the multiplication operators corresponding to elements of) $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is closed under the $\mathfrak{g}$ -action but not the $G$ -action. To overcome this issue, we show that $G\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is obtained by exponentiating the $\mathfrak{g}$ -action on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We thus need the Taylor series for the appropriate exponential map to converge. In general, the Taylor series at $0$ for a function $f$ on the real line has a positive radius of convergence if and only if $f$ obeys the derivative bounds

$$ \displaystyle|f^{(n)}(x)|\lesssim_{f}O_{f}(n)^{n} $$

for $x$ in an interval around $0$ , where the interval is independent of $n$ . With this in mind, it is natural that we obtain convergence of the exponential Taylor series from the similar looking derivative bounds in Theorem 11.6 below, which is the first of the two main results of Step 2. We defer a more detailed explanation to Subsection 11.4.

We now come to Step 2, which consists of the following two theorems. To state Theorem 11.6, fix once and for all a norm $\|\cdot\|_{\mathfrak{g}}$ on the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ . Up to constants, it doesn’t matter which one we choose.

#### Theorem 11.6 (Derivative bounds in $L^{\infty}$ ).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , let $X\in\mathfrak{g}$ , and let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|X^{n}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(n\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}})^{n}. $$

We emphasize that the $O$ -constant, which is raised to the $n$ th power, is independent of $\alpha$ .

#### Theorem 11.7 (Quasi-Sobolev embedding into $L^{\infty}$ ).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

We add the prefix “quasi-” because the right hand side involves $f(\Delta)$ with $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbf{R}$ a function of quasipolynomial rather than polynomial growth. As we will see in the next subsection, when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , it is possible to replace $\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))$ with $(\Delta+1)^{O(1)}$ in (11.2). I do not know how to do this for a general multiplicative representation without going through Theorem 1.8. Fortunately, most of the time we will be dealing in exponentials, so the difference between polynomial and quasipolynomial will be irrelevant.

If $\alpha$ is an automorphic vector of nonnegative weight and $X=E$ is the raising operator, then the $L^{\infty}$ bounds on the automorphic vectors $E^{n}\alpha$ given by Theorem 11.6 have explicit dependence on the weight $n$ , because the implicit and $O$ -constants are independent of $n$ . On the other hand, if $\alpha$ is an automorphic vector to which Theorem 11.7 applies, then $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ has weight $0$ , and the bound on $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}$ given by Theorem 11.7 depends explicitly on the Casimir eigenvalue of $\alpha$ . This justifies the description of these two estimates in the statement of Step 2 above. The proofs of Theorems 11.6 and 11.7 are outlined in Subsection 11.5.

We have explained that Theorem 11.6 is used to exponentiate the $\mathfrak{g}$ -action on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ to a $G$ -action on $\mathcal{A}$ , and in Step 4 it is stated that a corollary of Theorem 11.7 is used to prove the qualitative Sobolev embedding property for $(X,\mu)$ . Theorem 11.6 and this corollary are the only results from Steps 1 and 2 which are used in Steps 3, 4, and 5. This corollary is the following. In the statement, $\mathcal{C}$ is the dense subspace of $\mathcal{H}$ consisting of vectors which are limits in $\mathcal{H}$ of $L^{\infty}$ -Cauchy sequences in $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . So if $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , then $\mathcal{C}=C(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

#### Corollary 11.8 (Qualitative Sobolev embedding into $L^{\infty}$ ).

There exists a nonnegative continuous function $\varphi\in L^{1}(G)$ , not identically zero, such that for all $v\in\mathcal{H}$ , the convolution

$$ \displaystyle\varphi\ast v=\int_{G}\varphi(g)gv\,dg $$

lies in $\mathcal{C}$ .

#### Proof of Corollary 11.8 assuming Theorem 11.7.

Let $\varphi$ be as in Lemma 2.9. Let $v\in\mathcal{H}$ be arbitrary, and denote $w=\varphi\ast v$ . By Lemma 2.9, $w$ is super-smooth. We wish to show that $w\in\mathcal{C}$ , i.e., that there is a sequence $\alpha_{n}\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ which is Cauchy with respect to the $L^{\infty}$ norm and which converges to $w$ in $\mathcal{H}$ . Let $\alpha_{n}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq n}w$ . Clearly $\alpha_{n}\to w$ in $\mathcal{H}$ . Super-smooth vectors are $K$ -invariant, so $w\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ . Thus $\alpha_{n}\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq n}^{K}$ , and hence $\alpha_{n}\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Therefore we can apply Theorem 11.7 to see that for $m\leq n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha_{n}-\alpha_{m}\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))(\alpha_{n}-\alpha_{m})\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in(m,n]}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))w\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

The right hand side goes to zero as $m,n\to\infty$ because $w$ is super-smooth. Thus the $\alpha_{n}$ are indeed Cauchy in $L^{\infty}$ , and we conclude that $w\in\mathcal{C}$ as required. ∎

This completes our discussion of Step 2. The three main results of Step 1 are

#### Theorem 11.9 (Quasi-Sobolev embedding into $L^{4}$ ).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Theorem 11.10 (Exponential decay in the tail, part I).

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that whenever $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is a lowest weight vector,

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty. $$

#### Theorem 11.11 (Exponential decay in the tail, part II).

There are positive constants $C\lesssim 1$ and $c\gtrsim 1$ , a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals $I_{i}$ of length $\lesssim 1$ , and points $\lambda_{i}\in I_{i}$ for each $i$ , such that the partition has polynomial growth in the sense that

$$ \displaystyle\#\{i:\lambda_{i}\leq X\}\lesssim X^{O(1)}\qquad\text{for}\qquad X\geq 1, $$

and such that for all $i$ and all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Remark 11.12 (Comparison with Theorem 6.8).

When $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , the holomorphic case of Theorem 6.8 is much stronger than Theorem 11.10. For example, it implies that (11.3) holds for any $c<\frac{\pi}{2}$ . Since Theorem 6.8 is proved using the hyperbolic bootstrap equations, it seems at first glance that one should be able to generalize Theorem 6.8 to arbitrary multiplicative representations (without appealing to Theorem 1.8). However, the proof of Theorem 6.8 uses an extra bit of analytic input which is not available for general multiplicative representations; for the holomorphic case of Theorem 6.8, this input is Lemma 6.10.

The statement of Theorem 11.11 is more complicated than that of Theorem 11.10, but it has a simple corollary which is more closely analogous to Theorem 11.10:

#### Corollary 11.13.

Let $c$ and $I_{i}$ be as in Theorem 11.11. Then for all $i$ and all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty. $$

In particular, this holds whenever $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ are Casimir eigenvectors with the same eigenvalue.

#### Proof of Corollary 11.13 assuming Theorem 11.11.

Let $C$ and $\lambda_{i}$ also be as in Theorem 11.11. Splitting $\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq C\lambda_{i}}+\mathds{1}_{\Delta>C\lambda_{i}}$ and using (11.5),

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(c\sqrt{C\lambda_{i}})\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

and the right hand side is finite. ∎

Theorem 11.11 clearly matches its description in the statement of Step 1 as a bound on the “tail” $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg\lambda_{i}}(\alpha\beta)$ . Taking into account the similarity between Theorem 11.10 and Corollary 11.13, Theorem 11.10 matches its description as well. It is perhaps less clear how Theorem 11.9 fits into the picture. The connection is as follows. According to the statement of Step 1, given $\lambda\geq 0$ and approximate eigenvectors $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ with approximate eigenvalue $\lambda$ , Theorem 11.9 should give a bound on the “bulk” $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim\lambda}(\alpha\beta)$ . By Theorem 11.11, the tail $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg\lambda}(\alpha\beta)$ is negligible, so bounding the bulk is equivalent to bounding $\alpha\beta$ itself. Of course, even without Theorem 11.11, any upper bound for $\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ is trivially also an upper bound for $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim\lambda}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ . Now, by $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz (Proposition 10.1), Theorem 11.9, and the fact that $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\lambda+O(1)}^{K}$ (which follows from $\alpha,\beta$ being approximate $\lambda$ -eigenvectors),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Thus indeed Theorem 11.9 yields a bound on the bulk $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim\lambda}(\alpha\beta)$ . This sort of combination of Theorem 11.9 with $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz will be used repeatedly.

The proofs of Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11 are outlined in Subsection 11.6 in the case where $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, and in Subsection 11.7 in the general case.

### 11.2. Proofs/heuristics for $L^{\infty}$ , bulk, and tail bounds when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$

To get a feel for the $L^{\infty}$ bounds in Theorems 11.6 and 11.7 and the bulk and tail bounds in Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11, it is helpful to see why they are true when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . This also serves as a sanity check. Technically, nothing from this subsection is used in the proof of Theorem 1.8, but it may provide some intuition.

In this subsection, let $\Gamma$ be a cocompact lattice in $G$ , and let $\mathcal{H}$ be the multiplicative representation $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . In this setting, we have access to tools from analysis on manifolds which make the above theorems much easier. The two most useful such tools are (crude) Sobolev inequalities and elliptic regularity. We will use elliptic regularity both in the smooth category and in the real analytic category. A precise form of the latter is

#### Lemma 11.14 (Elliptic regularity in the real analytic category [13]).

Let $M$ be a closed real analytic manifold, and embed $M$ as a totally real submanifold of a complex manifold $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ . Given a neighborhood $U$ of $M$ in $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ , let $\Hol(U)|_{M}$ denote the space of functions on $M$ obtained as restrictions of holomorphic functions on $U$ . Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a second order elliptic linear differential operator on $M$ with real analytic coefficients. Assume $\mathcal{L}$ is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite on $L^{2}(M)$ (where the $L^{2}$ inner product is defined with respect to a real analytic density on $M$ ). Then for each $\varepsilon>0$ , the functional calculus defines a bounded linear operator $\exp(-\varepsilon\sqrt{\mathcal{L}})$ on $L^{2}(M)$ . These operators obey the following properties (i) and (ii).

- (i) For each $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $M$ in $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ such that the image of $\exp(-\varepsilon\sqrt{\mathcal{L}})$ is contained in $\Hol(U)|_{M}$ .

- (ii) For each neighborhood $U$ of $M$ in $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ , there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that the image of $\exp(-\varepsilon\sqrt{\mathcal{L}})$ contains $\Hol(U)|_{M}$ .

In particular, by (i), there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $M$ in $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ (depending only on $M,M_{\mathbf{C}},\mathcal{L}$ ), such that every eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$ is contained in $\Hol(U)|_{M}$ .

A neighborhood $U$ as in the last sentence of the lemma is called a Grauert tube (see, e.g., [73]).

It is instructive to verify Lemma 11.14 using Fourier analysis in the case where $M=(\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z})^{d}$ , $M_{\mathbf{C}}=(\mathbf{C}/\mathbf{Z})^{d}$ , and $\mathcal{L}$ is the Laplacian. The only misleading feature of this example is that the Grauert tube can be taken to be all of $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ . In general, this is usually not possible.

The sharpest form of Lemma 11.14 is an application of the theory of Fourier integral operators with complex phase [13].

We now prove or give heuristic arguments for the five theorems above in the present setting where $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . All the arguments are soft in the sense that the key analytic tools, like Lemma 11.14, use nothing about the structure of $\Gamma\backslash G$ except that it is compact and real analytic.

#### Proof of Theorem 11.6 when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

Let $M$ denote the closed real analytic manifold $\Gamma\backslash G$ , and embed $M$ as a totally real submanifold of a complex manifold $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ (e.g., $M_{\mathbf{C}}=\Gamma\backslash\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{C})$ ). View $\mathcal{P}$ , defined by (2.8), as a differential operator on $M$ . Then $\mathcal{P}$ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 11.14, and all automorphic forms are eigenfunctions for $\mathcal{P}$ . Thus by Lemma 11.14, there is a neighborhood $U$ of $M$ in $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ such that all automorphic forms on $M$ extend to holomorphic functions on $U$ .

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . By Proposition 2.5, $\alpha$ is a finite linear combination of automorphic forms, so $\alpha$ extends holomorphically to $U$ . There is a neighborhood $\Omega$ of the origin in $\mathfrak{g}$ such that the map $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}\times M\to M$ by

$$ \displaystyle(X,\Gamma g)\mapsto\Gamma g\exp(X) $$

extends holomorphically in $X$ to a map $\Omega\times M\to U$ . We denote this extension also by (11.6). Define $h\colon\Omega\to L^{\infty}(M)$ by

$$ \displaystyle h(X)(\Gamma g)=\alpha(\Gamma g\exp(X)). $$

Then $h$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$ (as a function valued in a Banach space). It follows from Cauchy’s estimate for derivatives of holomorphic functions that for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $X\in\mathfrak{g}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Big\|\frac{d^{n}}{dt^{n}}\Big|_{t=0}h(tX)\Big\|_{L^{\infty}(M)}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(n\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}})^{n} $$

(the $O$ -constant depends only on $\Omega$ , which ultimately depends only on $\mathcal{H}$ ). The $n$ th derivative at $t=0$ on the left hand side is just $X^{n}\alpha$ . Thus we have the desired bound. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 11.7 when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

The condition that $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ means that $\alpha$ is a function on $\Gamma\backslash G/K=\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ . Let $s\gg 1$ be a sufficiently large constant. Then by Sobolev embedding and elliptic regularity,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})}\lesssim\|\alpha\|_{H^{s}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})}\sim_{s}\|(\Delta+1)^{\frac{s}{2}}\alpha\|_{L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H})}=\|(\Delta+1)^{\frac{s}{2}}\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Thus in particular

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

and $\lesssim$ can be replaced by $\leq$ at the cost of increasing the $O$ -constant. ∎

As referred to earlier, this argument gives the improved estimate $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|(\Delta+1)^{O(1)}\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ , with polynomial rather than quasipolynomial dependence on $\Delta$ in the right hand side.

#### Proof of Theorem 11.9 when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

The $L^{4}$ norm is bounded by the $L^{\infty}$ norm, so Theorem 11.9 follows from Theorem 11.7, which we proved above in the case $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 11.10 when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

Let $M,M_{\mathbf{C}},U$ be as in the proof of Theorem 11.6 above, so $U$ is a neighborhood of $M$ in the complexification $M_{\mathbf{C}}$ such that all automorphic forms on $\Gamma\backslash G$ extend holomorphically to $U$ . Let $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a lowest weight vector. Then $f,\overline{f}$ are both automorphic forms, so they both extend holomorphically to $U$ . Thus $|f|^{2}\in\Hol(U)|_{M}$ . By (ii) in Lemma 11.14, there exists $c>0$ depending only on $U$ , such that $|f|^{2}$ is in the image of $\exp(-c\sqrt{\mathcal{P}})$ (in the lemma $c$ is called $\varepsilon$ ). This means that

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\mathcal{P}})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty. $$

Since $|f|^{2}$ has weight $0$ and $\mathcal{P}|_{\mathcal{H}^{K}}=\Delta|_{\mathcal{H}^{K}}$ , we have $\exp(c\sqrt{\mathcal{P}})(|f|^{2})=\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})$ . Thus (11.7) gives the desired finiteness. It remains to check that $c\gtrsim 1$ . Indeed, $c$ depends only on $U$ and hence only on $\mathcal{H}$ . ∎

This argument shows more generally that if $F\in C^{\infty}(\Gamma\backslash G/K)$ is any polynomial combination of automorphic forms on $\Gamma\backslash G$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})F\|_{L^{2}}<\infty. $$

A very similar argument shows that if $F$ is any polynomial combination of Laplace eigenfunctions on any closed real analytic Riemannian manifold, then (11.8) holds for some $c>0$ , with $\Delta$ interpreted as the Laplacian. Sarnak showed that when the manifold is a hyperbolic surface, any $c<\frac{\pi}{2}$ works [62]. This crucially uses constant curvature.

#### Heuristic for Theorem 11.11 when $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

It suffices to prove the stronger statement that there are positive constants $C\lesssim 1$ and $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that for all $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\lambda}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Normalize $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ , so we want to show that the left hand side is at most $1$ . By the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 11.10 above, we see that $\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty$ for $c$ sufficiently small. By definition, this finiteness means that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\mu\geq 0}\exp(2c\sqrt{\mu})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}<\infty. $$

Therefore $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ decays exponentially in $\sqrt{\mu}$ as $\mu\to\infty$ . However, the rate of decay will not be uniform in $\alpha,\beta$ . One should imagine that there is some threshold $\mu_{0}$ depending on $\alpha,\beta$ , such that $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)$ is small for $\mu\gg\mu_{0}$ , but not necessarily for $\mu\lesssim\mu_{0}$ . The content of Theorem 11.11 is that $\mu_{0}$ can be taken to be $\lambda$ . This can be understood heuristically as follows. The condition that $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\lambda}^{K}$ means that $\alpha,\beta$ are linear combinations of Laplace eigenfunctions on $\Gamma\backslash G/K=\Gamma\backslash\mathbf{H}$ with eigenvalues $\leq\lambda$ . In general, a Laplace eigenfunction of eigenvalue $\mu$ on a fixed closed Riemannian manifold is smooth at scales $\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}$ and oscillatory at scales $\gg\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}$ . For example, when the manifold is a flat torus, this can be seen explicitly by Fourier analysis. In our setting, it follows that $\alpha,\beta$ are smooth at scales $\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ . Therefore the product $\alpha\beta$ is also smooth at scales $\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ . Now $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)$ is a Laplace eigenfunction of eigenvalue $\mu$ , so $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)$ should be oscillatory at scales $\gg\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}$ . Suppose $\mu\gg\lambda$ . Then let $\nu$ be the geometric mean of $\lambda,\mu$ , so $\lambda\ll\nu\ll\mu$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}}\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu}}\ll\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$ . At the intermediate scale $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\nu}}$ , we have that $\alpha\beta$ is smooth and $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)$ is oscillatory. Thus $\alpha\beta$ and $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)$ are almost orthogonal in $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)=\mathcal{H}$ . Consequently

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle\alpha\beta,\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

is small. In summary, we have argued that if $\mu\gg\mu_{0}:=\lambda$ , then $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\mu}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ is small. As discussed above, this is morally the content of Theorem 11.11. ∎

It is notable that the bounds in Theorems 11.6, 11.10, and 11.11 for general multiplicative representations are of the same strength as those given by Lemma 11.14 for $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ .

### 11.3. Main ideas in Section 12

Section 12 carries out Step 5. As discussed in the roadmap above (Subsection 11.1), Step 5 boils down to proving Theorem 11.4. So in this subsection, allow $G$ to be an arbitrary connected Lie group. We prove Theorem 11.4 in the contrapositive, so (in the notation of the theorem) we show that if $X$ is not a compact homogeneous $G$ -space, then $(X,\mu)$ does not have the qualitative Sobolev embedding property. Let us illustrate this in an example.

#### Example 11.15 (Irrational flow on a 2-torus).

Let $G=\mathbf{R}$ . Let $X=(\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z})^{2}$ with Lebesgue measure $\mu$ . Fix a point $\omega\in S^{1}\subseteq\mathbf{R}^{2}$ on the unit circle, and let $G$ act on $X$ by $t\cdot x=x+t\omega$ for $t\in\mathbf{R}=G$ . If the line $L_{\omega}\subseteq\mathbf{R}^{2}$ through the origin and $\omega$ has irrational slope, then this action is uniquely ergodic with invariant measure $\mu$ , but no matter what $\omega$ is, $X$ is never homogeneous as a $G$ -space. We must therefore construct a counterexample to qualitative Sobolev embedding for $(X,\mu)$ . Let $1\leq p<q\leq\infty$ , and let $\varphi\in L^{1}(G)$ be a nonnegative continuous function which is not identically zero. Then a counterexample is, by definition, a function $f\in L^{p}(X,\mu)$ with $\varphi\ast f\not\in L^{q}(X,\mu)$ . We construct such a function $f$ explicitly below. The geometry underlying the construction is depicted in Figure 1.

Let $W\subseteq X$ be the projection to $(\mathbf{R}/\mathbf{Z})^{2}$ of the disc of radius $0.2$ around the origin in $\mathbf{R}^{2}$ . Then $W$ is foliated by line segments parallel to $L_{\omega}$ . We think of these line segments as “local $G$ -orbits.” Let $\omega^{\perp}\in S^{1}$ be a point orthogonal to $\omega$ , and let $\{I_{i}\}$ be an infinite collection of disjoint nonempty open subintervals of $(-0.1,0.1)$ . Then let

$$ \displaystyle R_{i}=\{t\omega+u\omega^{\perp}:t\in(-0.1,0.1)\text{ and }u\in I_{i}\}\mod\mathbf{Z}^{2}. $$

These $R_{i}$ are open rectangles in $W$ , and they are disjoint because each local orbit intersects at most one $R_{i}$ . In addition, each $R_{i}$ has length $0.2$ in the direction $\omega$ . Let $f=\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathds{1}_{R_{i}}$ , where the $c_{i}$ are nonnegative coefficients such that $f\in L^{p}(X,\mu)$ but $f\not\in L^{q}(X,\mu)$ .

It remains to check that $\varphi\ast f\not\in L^{q}(X,\mu)$ . By translation symmetry, we may assume $\varphi(0)>0$ . Then since $\varphi$ is nonnegative and continuous, $\varphi(t)\geq\varepsilon\mathds{1}_{|t|\leq\varepsilon}$ for some small $\varepsilon>0$ . Since the $R_{i}$ have uniform length in the direction $\omega$ , in particular length $\geq\varepsilon$ , we have $\varphi\ast\mathds{1}_{R_{i}}\geq\varepsilon^{2}\mathds{1}_{R_{i}}$ pointwise. Therefore $\varphi\ast f\geq\varepsilon^{2}f$ , and hence $\varphi\ast f\not\in L^{q}(X,\mu)$ . This completes Example 11.15.

*Figure 1. This is an illustration of Example 11.15. The disc is $W$ . The blue lines are the local orbits. The red and orange rectangles are the $R_{i}$ . In reality, there are of course infinitely many local orbits and rectangles $R_{i}$ .*

The two key ingredients in Example 11.15 are

- (1) There is a nonempty open subset $W\subseteq X$ foliated by local orbits; moreover, this foliation is non-pathological in the sense that the space of local orbits is Hausdorff.

- (2) There are infinitely many disjoint open sets $R_{i}$ in $X$ which have “uniform length in the direction of the $G$ -action.”

The purpose of (1) is to show that the $R_{i}$ in (2) are disjoint. Then (2) is used to build $f$ .

To prove Theorem 11.4 in the general case, $W$ is constructed in Lemma 12.4, and the $R_{i}$ can be taken to be the product sets $UV_{i}$ appearing in Proposition 12.1. For technical reasons, we take $f$ to be of the form $\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathds{1}_{U}\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}}$ rather than $\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathds{1}_{UV_{i}}$ . Besides this, the proof in the general case proceeds in exactly the same way given these two ingredients.

### 11.4. Main ideas in Section 13

Let $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ again. Section 13 is split into two subsections which perform Steps 3 and 4, respectively. As discussed in the roadmap, the only difficult part of either of these two steps is the construction of the $G$ -action on the C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ . Recall that $\mathcal{A}$ is the closed subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ generated by $\{M_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\}$ . We want $g\in G$ to act on $\mathcal{A}$ by $A\mapsto gAg^{-1}$ , where this product is interpreted as a product of operators on $\mathcal{H}$ . This will give a well-defined action as soon as we can show that $gAg^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ ; a priori $gAg^{-1}$ is just an arbitrary bounded operator on $\mathcal{H}$ . Since $G$ is connected, it is generated by any neighborhood of the identity, so it suffices to show that for $g$ sufficiently small, one has $gAg^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ for all $A\in\mathcal{A}$ . Furthermore, since $\mathcal{A}$ is generated by the $M_{\alpha}$ , it suffices to show that $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . If $\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , then one can check that $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}=M_{g\alpha}$ , where $M_{g\alpha}$ is the operator on $L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ given by pointwise multiplication by $g\alpha$ . Writing $g=\exp(X)$ for some $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ sufficiently small, and formally Taylor expanding in $X$ ,

$$ \displaystyle gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}=M_{g\alpha}=M_{\exp(X)\alpha}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}M_{X^{n}\alpha}. $$

For a general multiplicative representation, $M_{g\alpha}$ is not defined because $g\alpha\not\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , but both the left and right hand sides of the above equation are well-defined. We show in Proposition 13.6 that equality of the left and right hand sides holds generally, with absolute convergence in operator norm on the right hand side by Theorem 11.6 from Step 2 (we use that $X$ is small to get convergence). This exhibits $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}$ as a limit of elements of $\mathcal{A}$ , so $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ as desired.

### 11.5. Main ideas in Section 14

Section 14 carries out Step 2, which consists of the $L^{\infty}$ bounds in Theorems 11.6 and 11.7. We prove Theorem 11.7 first in Subsection 14.1, and then prove Theorem 11.6 in Subsection 14.3 using some algebraic identities from Subsection 14.2.

Let us begin by sketching the proof of Theorem 11.7, the quasi-Sobolev embedding theorem. Let $I_{i},\lambda_{i}$ be as in Theorem 11.11 from Step 1, so $\{I_{i}\}$ is a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals of length $\lesssim 1$ , and $\lambda_{i}\in I_{i}$ . Then a short reduction using the triangle inequality shows that to prove Theorem 11.7, it is enough to prove (11.2) when $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ for some $i$ . In this case, (11.2) simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i}))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

This simplified estimate is Proposition 14.1, and this is the technical core of Subsection 14.1. If the $L^{\infty}$ norm were replaced by the $L^{4}$ norm, then we would already have (11.9) by Theorem 11.9 from Step 1. With this in mind, the idea of the proof is to obtain $L^{\infty}$ control from $L^{4}$ control by an iterative process where at each step, $L^{p}$ control is boosted to $L^{2p}$ control. To make this precise, we need a good notion of $L^{p}$ norm on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ for $p>4$ a power of $2$ . The naive guess, extrapolating from the definition of the $L^{4}$ norm, would be to define $\|\alpha\|_{L^{p}}=\|\alpha^{\frac{p}{2}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{\frac{2}{p}}$ . This unfortunately doesn’t make sense, because $\alpha^{\frac{p}{2}}$ is a product of at least three elements of $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ when $p>4$ , which typically is not defined. Indeed, as discussed above (1.5), the product of two elements of $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is typically not in $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and so cannot be multiplied by a third element. Nevertheless, let us pretend for now that we do have $L^{p}$ norms not just on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ but on $\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ , and that these $L^{p}$ norms satisfy the usual properties. Then $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}=\lim_{p\to\infty}\|\alpha\|_{L^{p}}$ , and for each $p$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{2p}}^{2}=\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{L^{p}}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg\lambda_{i}}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{L^{p}}+\sum_{j\colon\lambda_{j}\lesssim\lambda_{i}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{j}}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{L^{p}}, $$

where the inequality is by the triangle inequality. Assume by induction on $p$ that we already know (11.9) with $L^{\infty}$ replaced by $L^{p}$ (with the implicit and $O$ -constants independent of $p$ ) for all $i$ and all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ . Then in (11.10), the tail $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg\lambda_{i}}(|\alpha|^{2})$ can be discarded by induction and Theorem 11.11, and the bulk terms $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{j}}(|\alpha|^{2})$ for $\lambda_{j}\lesssim\lambda_{i}$ can be estimated by induction and Theorem 11.9. This recovers (11.9) with $L^{\infty}$ replaced by $L^{2p}$ (with the same implicit and $O$ -constants as for $L^{p}$ ). Taking $p\to\infty$ , and using the independence of the constants from $p$ , yields (11.9). In practice, we will be able to run this argument using certain ad hoc “modified $L^{p}$ norms” on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . The reason we wanted the $L^{p}$ norms above to be defined on all of $\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ instead of just $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is so that we could make sense of $\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{L^{p}}$ for $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We get around this by interpreting $\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{L^{p}}$ as $\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{L^{p}}$ , using that $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We will see that the modified $L^{p}$ norms share enough of the usual properties of $L^{p}$ norms to make the above argument go through more or less unchanged.

Let us now turn to Theorem 11.6. The $n=0$ case of Theorem 11.6 says that $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and the proof gives some information on how $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}$ depends on $\alpha$ . In particular, applying the $n=0$ case of Theorem 11.6 to $X^{n}\alpha$ for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , we get $\|X^{n}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ , and the proof gives a bound on $\|X^{n}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}$ in terms of $n$ and $\alpha$ . This bound is the general case of Theorem 11.6. Therefore, to understand the general case, it essentially suffices to understand the $n=0$ case. So let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and let us explain why $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ (see the proof of Proposition 14.10 for details). By Proposition 2.5 and the triangle inequality, we may assume $\alpha$ is an automorphic vector, and by complex conjugation symmetry, we may assume $\alpha$ has nonnegative weight. Then Proposition 2.6 gives two alternatives for the structure of $\alpha$ , and both are treated in the same way. Suppose for concreteness that the first alternative holds, so $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ for some automorphic vector $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ and some $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Splitting $\varphi$ into real and imaginary parts, we may assume $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . If $n=0$ , then $\alpha=\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ and Theorem 11.7 gives $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ , so the first new case is $n=1$ , i.e., $\alpha=E\varphi$ . Let us explain this case first.

In general, we will show that for any $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , one has

$$ \displaystyle\|\beta\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\||\beta|^{2}\|_{L^{\infty}} $$

(again, technically $\||\beta|^{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}$ is not defined because $|\beta|^{2}\not\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , but we interpret $\||\beta|^{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}$ as $\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\beta|^{2})\|_{L^{\infty}}$ ). Of course, one expects equality in (11.11), but $\leq$ suffices.

Now, we want to use (11.11) to show that $\alpha=E\varphi$ has finite $L^{\infty}$ norm. So we want to show $\||E\varphi|^{2}\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ (with the left hand side interpreted as above). Since $|E\varphi|^{2}$ has weight zero, it suffices by quasi-Sobolev embedding (Theorem 11.7) to check that

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))(|E\varphi|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty. $$

If $|E\varphi|^{2}$ were replaced by $\varphi^{2}$ , then this finiteness would follow from Corollary 11.13 from Step 1. More generally, if $|E\varphi|^{2}$ were replaced by $\Delta^{m}(\varphi^{2})$ for any $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , then we would still have finiteness, because $\Delta^{m}$ could be absorbed into $\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))$ . The key observation which gives (11.12) is that $|E\varphi|^{2}$ is a finite linear combination of the $\Delta^{m}(\varphi^{2})$ for $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Indeed, by the formula (2.6) for the Casimir restricted to $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ , and by the product rule,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(\varphi^{2})=-\overline{E}E(\varphi^{2})=-2\overline{E}(\varphi E\varphi)=-2E\varphi\overline{E}\varphi-2\varphi\overline{E}E\varphi=-2|E\varphi|^{2}+2\varphi\Delta\varphi=-2|E\varphi|^{2}+2\lambda\varphi^{2}, $$

where $\lambda$ is the Casimir eigenvalue of $\varphi$ (we used $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ to write $E\varphi\overline{E}\varphi=|E\varphi|^{2}$ ). Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle|E\varphi|^{2}=\Big(\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Big)(\varphi^{2}). $$

From this we obtain (11.12) and hence $\|E\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ as explained above.

Recall that earlier we had $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ for some $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . The above handles the case $n=1$ . To get $\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ for all $n$ , the same method works, except that at the end we need to express $|E^{n}\varphi|^{2}$ as a linear combination of the $\Delta^{m}(\varphi^{2})$ for $m\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . This is done in Subsection 14.2, where we write down explicit polynomials $p_{n}$ in two variables with real coefficients such that

$$ \displaystyle|E^{n}\varphi|^{2}=p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}) $$

(see Proposition 14.5). For example, $p_{0}(\lambda,\mu)=1$ because $|E^{0}\varphi|^{2}=|\varphi|^{2}=\varphi^{2}$ (remember $\varphi$ is real), and $p_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\mu$ corresponding to (11.13). This concludes our discussion of Theorem 11.6.

### 11.6. Main ideas in Section 15

Sections 15 and 16 do Step 1, which consists of the bulk and tail estimates in Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11. The proofs of these three theorems are quite technical, especially Theorems 11.9 and 11.11. Therefore, as a warmup, Section 15 gives proofs which at various points make the simplifying assumption that $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law (Definition 1.33). We note, however, that the proof of Theorem 11.10 in Section 15 is unconditional.

In this subsection, assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. The proof of Theorem 11.10 is similar and easier than that of Theorem 11.11, so let us focus on Theorems 11.9 and 11.11. A major benefit of the polynomial Weyl law is that there exists a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals $I_{i}$ of length $\lesssim 1$ , which has polynomial growth in the sense of (11.4), and such that each $I_{i}$ contains at most one Casimir eigenvalue (not counting multiplicity). Take the $I_{i}$ in Theorem 11.11 to be such a partition. Then Theorem 11.11 simplifies to the statement that there exists $c\gtrsim 1$ such that for all $\lambda\geq 0$ , all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta=\lambda}^{K}$ , and any $M\gg\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By splitting $\alpha,\beta$ into real and imaginary parts, and then applying the polarization identity to express $\alpha\beta$ as a linear combination of squares, it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} $$

for all $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta=\lambda}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . This is Proposition 15.18. An immediate corollary of (11.15) would be

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Conversely, a dyadic decomposition argument shows that if one knows (11.16) for all $M\gg\lambda+1$ , then one obtains (11.15) for $M\gg\lambda+1$ (after increasing the implicit constant in $M\gg\lambda+1$ and decreasing $c$ ). Thus it suffices to show (11.16). This is (15.15) in Proposition 15.17. It is easier to show the same inequality with $\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}$ on the right hand side instead of $\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}, $$

and in fact we will prove this without the polynomial Weyl law assumption. Once we have established Theorem 11.9 (quasi-Sobolev embedding into $L^{4}$ ), it will be easy to deduce (11.16) from (11.17), again after increasing the implicit constant in $M\gg\lambda+1$ and decreasing $c$ . The inequality (11.17) is (15.14) in Proposition 15.17. To illustrate the method of proof for this inequality, let us derive the weaker estimate

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq M^{-m}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad M\gg_{m,\varepsilon}\lambda^{1+\varepsilon}+1, $$

for any fixed $m\geq 0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ . Let $n$ be a large positive integer to be chosen later. By crossing symmetry and (11.14), we can write

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} \displaystyle=\langle E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E^{n}\varphi},E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E^{n}\varphi}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle|E^{n}\varphi|^{2},|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Negating both sides, and using that $\Delta$ is self-adjoint and the $p_{n}$ have real coefficients, we get

$$ \displaystyle-\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0. $$

The inequality (11.20) is Proposition 15.1. Isolating the tail by moving the bulk to the right hand side in (11.20),

$$ \displaystyle-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg_{n}\lambda+1}\,p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim_{n}\lambda+1}\,p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

(where the spectral cutoffs on both sides are taken at the same point). It follows from the construction of $p_{n}$ that $p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)$ is a polynomial in $\lambda,\mu$ of total degree $n$ , and for $n\geq 1$ , when viewed as a polynomial in $\mu$ with $\lambda$ fixed, $p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $(-1)^{n}\frac{1}{2}$ . We can see this already for $n=0,1$ , because as explained after (11.14), we have $p_{0}(\lambda,\mu)=1$ and $p_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\mu$ . Consequently, for $n\geq 1$ , the polynomial $-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)$ has total degree $2n+1$ in $\lambda,\mu$ , and has degree $2n+1$ with leading coefficient $\frac{1}{4}$ in $\mu$ . Thus the leading term will dominate when $\mu\gg_{n}\lambda+1$ . To be precise, for $\mu\gg_{n}\lambda+1$ , we have $-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0$ and in fact $-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)\sim\mu^{2n+1}$ . Consequently,

$$ \displaystyle M^{2n+1}\mathds{1}_{\mu\geq M}\lesssim-\mathds{1}_{\mu\gg_{n}\lambda+1}\,p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)\qquad\text{for all}\qquad M\gg_{n}\lambda+1\text{ and }\mu\geq 0. $$

Thus for $M\gg_{n}\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle M^{2n+1}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle M^{2n+1}\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\gg_{n}\lambda+1}\,p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Applying (11.21),

$$ \displaystyle M^{2n+1}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\lesssim\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim_{n}\lambda+1}\,p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $p_{n}$ has total degree $n$ , we have $|p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)|\lesssim_{n}(\lambda+1)^{n}$ for $\mu\lesssim_{n}\lambda+1$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle M^{2n+1}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\lesssim_{n}(\lambda+1)^{2n+1}\langle\varphi^{2},\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=(\lambda+1)^{2n+1}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{4}. $$

Dividing both sides by $M^{2n+1}$ and taking square roots,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{n}\Big(\frac{\lambda+1}{M}\Big)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Restricting to $M\gg_{m,\varepsilon}\lambda^{1+\varepsilon}+1$ and fixing $n$ sufficiently large depending on $m,\varepsilon$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{m,\varepsilon}M^{-m}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

This is almost the desired bound (11.18), except we have $\lesssim_{m,\varepsilon}$ instead of $\leq$ . This is fixed by applying the same bound with $m+1$ in place of $m$ , and then increasing $M$ to absorb the implicit constant. We have now established (11.18). To get (11.17) we squeeze a little more out of the same argument, analyzing $p_{n}$ more carefully and then optimizing the choice of $n$ in terms of $\lambda$ and $M$ . This finishes our outline of the proof of Theorem 11.11, and by extension the proof of Theorem 11.10 which is similar.

Let us now move on to Theorem 11.9, the qualitative Sobolev embedding theorem. Recall that Theorem 11.9 is used in the proof of Theorem 11.11 to pass from (11.17) to (11.16), so in Section 15 we will actually prove Theorem 11.9 first. A special case of Theorem 11.9 is that when $\alpha=\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is an automorphic vector,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

where $\lambda\geq 0$ is the Casimir eigenvalue of $\varphi$ . Conversely, if one knows (11.22) for all $K$ -invariant automorphic vectors $\varphi$ , then one can recover Theorem 11.9 by writing

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{\lambda\geq 0}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}\alpha\|_{L^{4}} $$

and then estimating the right hand side by applying (11.22) with $\varphi=\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}\alpha$ . In order for the application of the triangle inequality in (11.23) not to be too lossy, it is crucial that we are assuming $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, or else the sum on the right hand side of (11.23) would contain too many terms. The reduction of Theorem 11.9 to (11.22) takes place after the statement of Proposition 15.8. It remains to prove (11.22). By splitting $\varphi$ into real and imaginary parts, we may assume $\varphi$ is real. We then prove (11.22) by a sort of induction on $\lambda$ . The base case $\lambda\lesssim 1$ is easy (see Lemma 15.6), so let $\lambda\gg 1$ . Then make the inductive assumption that (11.22) holds for all automorphic vectors $\tilde{\varphi}\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\tilde{\lambda}\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda$ , and let us sketch the proof of (11.22) for $\varphi,\lambda$ . One of course has to be careful about implicit constants in inductive arguments, but in this outline we will be deliberately vague. Split

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}=\|\varphi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Although it is not immediately apparent, we will be able to deal with the first term $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ by induction and a little extra massaging. Let us focus on the second term $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ . Above, we estimated $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ for $M\gg\lambda$ (our final estimate was conditional on Theorem 11.9, but (11.17) was not). If we could push $M$ down to $\frac{1}{2}\lambda$ , we would win. This is not possible if we ask for the same quality bound as in (11.17), but we will be able to get a weaker (but sufficient) bound by a similar method. Above, the key inequality was (11.20), which after rearranging allowed us to relate the tail to the bulk via (11.21). The first step in the derivation of (11.20) is the first inequality in (11.19), which trivially lower bounds $\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}$ by $0$ . In the second half of Subsection 15.1 we find a nontrivial lower bound, which leads to the following modification of (11.20):

$$ \displaystyle\langle r_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0, $$

where $r_{n}(\lambda,\mu)$ is an explicit real-valued function of two variables defined by (15.2). We then define a new function $R(\lambda,\mu)$ which is a positive linear combination of the $r_{n}$ . By positivity,

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0. $$

Rearranging as in (11.21),

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda}R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

The key property of $R(\lambda,\mu)$ is that for $\mu>\frac{1}{2}\lambda$ , one has $R(\lambda,\mu)\gtrsim 1$ (see Lemma 15.9). One also has the trivial bound $|R(\lambda,\mu)|\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}$ for $\mu\lesssim\lambda$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\lesssim\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta>\frac{1}{2}\lambda}R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda}R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\frac{1}{2}\lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

This says that the second term in (11.24) is bounded by $\lambda^{O(1)}$ times the first term. As mentioned after (11.24), the first term can be treated by induction with a little work.

At each step of the induction, we lose a factor of $\lambda^{O(1)}$ . In general, if $C(\lambda)$ is a function of $\lambda\geq 0$ satisfying $C(\lambda)\lesssim 1$ for $\lambda\lesssim 1$ and $C(\lambda)\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}C(\frac{1}{2}\lambda)$ for $\lambda\gg 1$ , then

$$ \displaystyle C(\lambda)\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)). $$

This explains the quasipolynomial dependence on $\lambda$ in Theorem 11.9.

### 11.7. Main ideas in Section 16

Section 16 proves Theorems 11.9 and 11.11 unconditionally, completing Step 1 (recall that the proof of Theorem 11.10 in Section 15 is already unconditional). The overall structure of the proofs of Theorems 11.9 and 11.11 is the same as in Section 15, but there are additional technical difficulties when $\mathcal{H}$ is not required to obey a polynomial Weyl law. We describe these difficulties and hint at how they are resolved below.

We often want bounds on some $v\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ . If $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, then a typical strategy is to decompose

$$ \displaystyle v=\sum_{\lambda\geq 0}\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}v, $$

estimate $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}v$ using that it is a $K$ -invariant Casimir eigenvector, and then use the triangle inequality to recover a bound on $v$ . Without the polynomial Weyl law, this application of the triangle inequality is unacceptably lossy. Therefore, in general, we instead decompose

$$ \displaystyle v=\sum_{i}\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v $$

as a sum of $K$ -invariant approximate Casimir eigenvectors, where the $I_{i}$ are as in Theorem 11.11. The condition in Theorem 11.11 that the partition $\{I_{i}\}$ of $[0,\infty)$ has polynomial growth serves as a substitute for the polynomial Weyl law. However, to estimate $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v$ , all of our machinery from Subsection 14.2 and Section 15 for controlling $K$ -invariant Casimir eigenvectors must be extended to approximate eigenvectors. In particular, the identity (11.14) was crucial, and we need a generalization of (11.14) for approximate eigenvectors $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . In fact, we need a formula not just for $|E^{n}\alpha|^{2}$ , but for the real part of $E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta$ whenever $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ are approximate eigenvectors with the same approximate eigenvalue. Let $\lambda\geq 0$ be a common approximate eigenvalue of $\alpha,\beta$ . In Proposition 16.1, we will show that

$$ \displaystyle\re E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta=p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha\beta)+\text{correction terms}, $$

where $p_{n}$ is as in (11.14), and where the correction terms are $\mathbf{R}[\lambda,\Delta]$ -linear combinations of the products $(\Delta-\lambda)^{i}\alpha(\Delta-\lambda)^{j}\beta$ for $i+j>0$ . This identity is true for all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ and all $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ , but the correction terms are only small when $\alpha,\beta$ are approximate $\lambda$ -eigenvectors. When $\alpha,\beta$ are exact $\lambda$ -eigenvectors, the correction terms vanish, and when in addition $\alpha=\beta$ , the above identity reduces to (11.14).

We have not yet explained where the discrete spectrum condition in Definition 1.6 is used; by Remark 1.30, it must be used somewhere. It is used superficially in several places, but the first time it is used in an unavoidable way is in Section 16. This is perhaps surprising, because discrete spectrum is a qualitative hypothesis, while Section 16 is quantitative in nature. Recall from Remark 1.31 that we will translate qualitative information into quantitative information via certain “self-improving” inequalities. The toy example given in Remark 1.31 is the inequality $C\leq 1+\frac{1}{2}C$ for $C\in[0,\infty]$ , which combined with the qualitative hypothesis $C<\infty$ implies the quantitative bound $C\leq 2$ . In Section 16, we will prove such inequalities with $C$ essentially a comparison constant between norms on the tensor product of two approximate eigenspaces in $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ . For example, suppose given $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\|\cdot\|^{\prime}$ a norm of interest on $\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-5}}^{K}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-5}}^{K}$ . Consider the smallest $C\in[0,\infty]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\otimes\beta\|^{\prime}\leq C\|\alpha\otimes\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}}=\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-5}}^{K}$ . In practice, $\|\alpha\otimes\beta\|^{\prime}$ will depend only on $\alpha\beta$ , so an upper bound on $C$ will mean quantitative control on the multiplication map $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\times\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ . Suppose we wish to prove $C\lesssim 1$ . Before using discrete spectrum, we will typically be able to prove something like

$$ \displaystyle C\lesssim 1+\lambda^{-1}C, $$

where the term $\lambda^{-1}C$ arises when estimating the correction terms from (11.25) in $\|\cdot\|^{\prime}$ , e.g., writing

$$ \displaystyle\|\text{correction terms}\|^{\prime}\leq C\|\text{correction terms}\|_{\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}}\leq\lambda^{-1}C $$

with the second inequality capturing the fact that $\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-5}}^{K}$ is an approximate eigenspace and hence the correction terms are small. Technically, (11.27) is ill-defined as written because the correction terms live in $\mathcal{H}$ rather than $\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}$ , but they are $\mathbf{R}[\lambda,\Delta]$ -linear combinations of images of elements of $\mathcal{H}\otimes\mathcal{H}$ under multiplication, and it is these elements which we estimate in $\|\cdot\|^{\prime}$ . The fact that the term $\lambda^{-1}C$ comes from the correction terms in (11.25) explains why this term does not appear in Section 15. Now, since $\mathcal{H}$ has discrete spectrum, $\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-5}}^{K}$ is finite-dimensional, and any two norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent, so $C<\infty$ . Thus when $\lambda\gg 1$ , we can move the term $\lambda^{-1}C$ to the left hand side in (11.26) to get $C\lesssim 1$ , as desired.

#### Remark 11.16.

The first place where we make this sort of argument is in the proof of Theorem 11.9 in Subsection 16.3. There (16.22) plays the role of (11.26) (c.f. the derivation of (16.23) from (16.22)). It is crucial that discrete spectrum is used there, because Theorem 11.9 fails for the example described in Remark 1.30 with countable spectrum.

In order to use (11.25) to prove Theorem 11.11, we need to make sure the main term $p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha\beta)$ in (11.25) dominates the correction terms uniformly in the relevant ranges of parameters. In particular, we need a lower bound on $|p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)|$ for $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ which is sharp up to a multiplicative constant independent of $n,\lambda,\mu$ . For now, let us suppress the dependence on $\lambda,\mu$ , and focus on getting a lower bound which is sharp uniformly in $n$ . Uniformity in $\lambda,\mu$ will come for free. The polynomials $p_{n}$ are defined by a second order linear recurrence in $n$ with non-constant coefficients (see Proposition 14.5). Equivalently,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p_{n+1}\\
p_{n}\end{pmatrix}=A_{n}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n}\\
p_{n-1}\end{pmatrix} $$

for some explicit $2\times 2$ matrix $A_{n}$ depending on $n$ (and also on $\lambda,\mu$ ). Iterating this,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p_{n+1}\\
p_{n}\end{pmatrix}=A_{n}\cdots A_{1}\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}\\
p_{0}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Thus to estimate $p_{n}$ , it suffices to estimate $A_{n}\cdots A_{1}$ . When $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ , the matrices $A_{m}$ for $m=1,\dots,n$ are diagonalizable, so we can write $A_{m}=Q_{m}D_{m}Q_{m}^{-1}$ with $D_{m}$ diagonal. If $A_{1},\dots,A_{n}$ were commuting matrices, then they would be simultaneously diagonalizable, so we could take $Q_{m}=Q$ independent of $m$ and write

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}\cdots A_{1}=(QD_{n}Q^{-1})\cdots(QD_{1}Q^{-1})=QD_{n}\cdots D_{1}Q^{-1}. $$

Products of diagonal matrices are easily understood, so this would allow us to get a sharp estimate for $A_{n}\cdots A_{1}$ . Unfortunately, $A_{1},\dots,A_{n}$ do not commute. Remarkably, we can still approximate

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}\cdots A_{1}\approx Q_{n}D_{n}\cdots D_{1}Q_{1}^{-1}, $$

and this is good enough. Conditions under which this approximation holds are given in Lemma 16.14, which is the key technical tool in Subsection 16.4. The resulting lower bound for $|p_{n}|$ is Proposition 16.16. Both Lemma 16.14 and Proposition 16.16 are steps toward the main result of Subsection 16.4, which is Proposition 16.13.
