It is this last proposition which shows that the main term in (11.25) dominates the correction terms in the relevant regimes.

This concludes our discussion of Section 16, and thus finishes our outline of Theorem 1.8.

## 12. Weak converse theorem $\implies$ Converse theorem

In Sections 13–16, we will prove Theorem 11.2, the weak converse theorem for multiplicative representations. In this section, we prove Theorem 1.8 given Theorem 11.2. As discussed in Subsection 11.1, the main result needed to deduce Theorem 1.8 from Theorem 11.2 is Theorem 11.3. Theorem 11.3 is in turn an immediate consequence of Theorem 11.4 and Proposition 11.5. We prove Theorem 11.4 in Subsections 12.1 and 12.2, and Proposition 11.5 in Subsection 12.3. Finally, in Subsection 12.4, we finish the reduction of Theorem 1.8 to Theorem 11.2.

### 12.1. Reduction to a topological criterion for homogeneity

In the contrapositive, the following proposition gives a criterion for a $G$ -space $X$ to be compact and homogeneous.

#### Proposition 12.1 (Topological criterion for homogeneity).

Let $G$ be a connected Lie group and $X$ a connected Hausdorff $G$ -space. Suppose $X$ is not of the form $H\backslash G$ for any closed cocompact subgroup $H\subseteq G$ . Then there is a nonempty open set $U\subseteq G$ , and there are infinitely many nonempty open sets $V_{i}\subseteq X$ , such that the product sets $UV_{i}$ are disjoint.

We prove this proposition in the next subsection. Here, we show how it implies Theorem 11.4, which is restated below for convenience.

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.4).

Let $G$ be a connected Lie group, and let $X$ be a connected Hausdorff $G$ -space equipped with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ of full support. Assume $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property. Then $X\simeq H\backslash G$ as $G$ -spaces for some closed cocompact subgroup $H\subseteq G$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 11.4 assuming Proposition 12.1.

Suppose for a contradiction that $X$ is not of the form $H\backslash G$ for any closed cocompact subgroup $H\subseteq G$ . Then let $U,V_{i}$ be as in Proposition 12.1. By shrinking $U$ , take $U$ to be precompact. Let $p,q,\varphi$ be as in the definition of the qualitative Sobolev embedding property (Definition 11.1). Translate $\varphi$ so that it is nonzero at the identity. Then $\varphi\ast\mathds{1}_{U}$ (the convolution of two functions on $G$ ) is positive on $\overline{U}$ , so by compactness, it is bounded below on $U$ by some $\delta>0$ . It is also trivially nonnegative everywhere, so we have $\varphi\ast\mathds{1}_{U}\geq\delta\mathds{1}_{U}$ .

The convolution $\mathds{1}_{U}\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}}$ is strictly positive in $UV_{i}$ and vanishes outside $UV_{i}$ . The $UV_{i}$ have positive measure because $\mu$ has full support. At the same time, the $UV_{i}$ are disjoint subsets of a probability space, so their measures go to zero. Because of this, there exist coefficients $c_{i}\geq 0$ such that $f:=\sum c_{i}\mathds{1}_{U}\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}}$ is in $L^{p}(X,\mu)$ but not in $L^{q}(X,\mu)$ . By the qualitative Sobolev embedding property, we have $\varphi\ast f\in L^{q}(X,\mu)$ . But

$$ \displaystyle\varphi\ast f=\sum_{i}c_{i}\varphi\ast(\mathds{1}_{U}\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}})=\sum_{i}c_{i}(\varphi\ast\mathds{1}_{U})\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}}\geq\delta\sum_{i}c_{i}\mathds{1}_{U}\ast\mathds{1}_{V_{i}}=\delta f $$

pointwise, and the nonnegative function $f$ is not in $L^{q}(X,\mu)$ by construction. This is a contradiction. ∎

### 12.2. Proof of the topological criterion for homogeneity

Let the notation be as in Proposition 12.1. The proofs in this subsection use nets instead of sequences because we are assuming only that $X$ is Hausdorff (and connected). In practice, however, $X$ will be metrizable, so little would be lost by replacing the word “net” with “sequence” everywhere. Assuming metrizability would not shorten the proofs.

For each $x\in X$ , the stabilizer $\Stab_{x}$ is a closed subgroup of $G$ , hence a Lie subgroup.

#### Proposition 12.2.

The function $x\mapsto\dim\Stab_{x}$ from $X$ to $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ is upper semicontinuous.

#### Proof.

Let $x_{n}\to x$ be a convergent net in $X$ . We must show that

$$ \displaystyle\limsup_{n}\dim\Stab_{x_{n}}\leq\dim\Stab_{x}. $$

Denote the $\limsup$ on the left by $d$ . After passing to a subnet, we may assume $\dim\Stab_{x_{n}}=d$ for all $n$ . Then the Lie algebra $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}$ is a $d$ -dimensional subspace of $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , or equivalently a point in the Grassmannian $\Gr_{d}(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}})$ . This Grassmannian is compact, so after passing to a further subnet, we may assume $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}$ converges to some $L\in\Gr_{d}(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}})$ . To prove (12.1), it suffices to show that $\exp(L)\subseteq\Stab_{x}$ . So let $X\in L$ . Since $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}\to L$ , there exist $X_{n}\in\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}$ with $X_{n}\to X$ in $\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Then $\exp(X_{n})\in\Stab_{x_{n}}$ , and $\exp(X_{n})\to\exp(X)$ in $G$ . It follows by continuity that $\exp(X)\in\Stab_{x}$ . Thus indeed $\exp(L)\subseteq\Stab_{x}$ , and (12.1) holds. ∎

Let $d$ be the minimal possible dimension of the stabilizer of a point in $X$ , and let

$$ \displaystyle X^{\min}=\{x\in X:\dim\Stab_{x}=d\}. $$

Then $X^{\min}$ is nonempty by the definition of $d$ , and by Proposition 12.2, $X^{\min}$ is open in $X$ .

#### Proposition 12.3.

The function $x\mapsto\Lie\Stab_{x}$ from $X^{\min}$ to $\Gr_{d}(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}})$ is continuous.

#### Proof.

It suffices to show that every convergent net $x_{n}\to x$ in $X^{\min}$ has a subnet along which $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}\to\Lie\Stab_{x}$ . Since $\Gr_{d}(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}})$ is compact, we may assume after passing to a subnet that $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}$ converges to some $L\in\Gr_{d}(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}})$ . By the same argument as in the proof of Proposition 12.2, we have $\exp(L)\subseteq\Stab_{x}$ , and so $L\subseteq\Lie\Stab_{x}$ . Since $x\in X^{\min}$ , we also have $\dim\Stab_{x}=d$ . Therefore $L$ and $\Lie\Stab_{x}$ have the same dimension, and hence $L=\Lie\Stab_{x}$ . Thus $\Lie\Stab_{x_{n}}\to\Lie\Stab_{x}$ as desired. ∎

An example where $X^{\min}\neq X$ and where $x\mapsto\Lie\Stab_{x}$ is nowhere locally constant is $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ acting on the one-point compactification of the upper half plane.

#### Lemma 12.4 (Local foliation by local orbits).

Fix $x\in X^{\min}$ . Let $K\subseteq G$ be a symmetric compact neighborhood of the identity which is sufficiently small depending on $x$ . Let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ which is sufficiently small depending on $K$ . Define a relation $\sim$ on $W$ by $y\sim z$ when $z=ky$ for some $k\in K$ . Then $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, the quotient map $W\to W/\sim$ is open, and the quotient space $W/\sim$ is Hausdorff.

Note that the notation here is different from other sections: here $K$ is a symmetric compact neighborhood of the identity in $G$ , rather than a maximal compact subgroup of $G$ .

In general, the space $X/G$ of $G$ -orbits need not be Hausdorff. The point of Lemma 12.4 is that we can work with the “local orbits” determined by $K$ instead, and that the “local orbit space” $W/\sim$ is guaranteed to be Hausdorff.

#### Proof of Lemma 12.4.

For notational convenience, fix a metric on $G$ inducing the topology on $G$ . Then choose parameters, including $K$ and $W$ , in the following order.

- (1) Let $B$ be a bounded neighborhood of the origin in $\Lie\Stab_{x}$ .

- (2) Let $K$ as in the statement of Lemma 12.4 be small enough that $K^{2}\cap\Stab_{x}\subseteq\exp(B)$ .

- (3) Choose $\varepsilon>0$ in terms of $K$ , such that whenever $g\in K^{2}$ and $h\in G$ with $\dist(g,h)<2\varepsilon$ , one has $gh^{-1}\in K$ .

- (4) Let $W$ as in the statement of Lemma 12.4 be small enough that the following properties (i),(ii) hold. After stating (i),(ii), we will explain why they hold for $W$ sufficiently small. (i) For each $Z\in B$ and $y\in W$ , there exists $Y\in\Lie\Stab_{y}$ with $\dist(\exp(Y),\exp(Z))<\varepsilon$ . (ii) Whenever $g\in K^{2}$ with $gW\cap W$ nonempty, one has $\dist(g,K^{2}\cap\Stab_{x})<\varepsilon$ .

Let us first explain why (i) holds for $W$ small. From Proposition 12.3, we see that by taking $W$ sufficiently small, $\Lie\Stab_{y}$ can be made arbitrarily close to $\Lie\Stab_{x}$ uniformly for $y\in W$ . Then since $B$ is bounded, one can find $Y\in\Lie\Stab_{y}$ arbitrarily close to any $Z\in B$ , uniformly in $Z$ . In particular, one can arrange $\dist(\exp(Y),\exp(Z))<\varepsilon$ , giving (i).

We now explain why (ii) holds for $W$ small. Suppose for a contradiction that (ii) fails for $W$ arbitrarily small. Then there exists a net $W_{n}$ of neighborhoods of $x$ eventually contained in any given neighborhood of $x$ , together with elements $g_{n}\in K^{2}$ for each $n$ , such that $g_{n}W_{n}\cap W_{n}\neq\emptyset$ and $\dist(g_{n},K^{2}\cap\Stab_{x})\geq\varepsilon$ . Since $K^{2}$ is compact, we may assume after passing to a subnet that $g_{n}$ converges to some $g\in K^{2}$ . This $g$ must satisfy $\dist(g,K^{2}\cap\Stab_{x})\geq\varepsilon$ . Since $g\in K^{2}$ , it follows that $g\not\in\Stab_{x}$ . On the other hand, by continuity, the condition $g_{n}W_{n}\cap W_{n}\neq\emptyset$ yields $gx=x$ in the limit. This is a contradiction. Thus (ii) must hold for $W$ sufficiently small.

With $B,K,\varepsilon,W$ as in (1)-(4), we finally verify the claimed properties of $\sim$ . The relation $\sim$ is reflexive because $K$ contains the identity, and it is symmetric because $K$ is symmetric. For transitivity, suppose $y,z,w\in W$ satisfy $y\sim z$ and $z\sim w$ . Then $w=gy$ for some $g\in K^{2}$ . In particular, $gW\cap W$ is nonempty. Therefore by (ii), we have $\dist(g,K^{2}\cap\Stab_{x})<\varepsilon$ . It follows from (2) that there exists $Z\in B$ with $\dist(g,\exp(Z))<\varepsilon$ . By (i), there exists $Y\in\Lie\Stab_{y}$ with $\dist(\exp(Y),\exp(Z))<\varepsilon$ . Let $h=\exp(Y)\in\Stab_{y}$ . Then by the triangle inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\dist(g,h)\leq\dist(g,\exp(Z))+\dist(\exp(Z),h)<2\varepsilon. $$

Thus by (3), we have $gh^{-1}\in K$ . Since $h\in\Stab_{y}$ , we can write $w=gy=gh^{-1}y\in Ky$ . Hence $y\sim w$ , and $\sim$ is transitive. We conclude that $\sim$ is an equivalence relation.

The quotient map $W\to W/\sim$ is open because the preimage of the image of an open set $V\subseteq W$ is $KV\cap W$ , which is open in $W$ . It follows from the compactness of $K$ that $\sim$ is closed (i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle\{(y,z)\in W\times W:y\sim z\} $$

is a closed subset of $W\times W$ ). Therefore Lemma 12.5 below tells us that $W/\sim$ is Hausdorff. ∎

#### Lemma 12.5 (Criterion for Hausdorff quotients).

Let $Y$ be a topological space, and $\sim$ a closed equivalence relation on $Y$ such that the quotient map $Y\to Y/\sim$ is open. Then $Y/\sim$ is Hausdorff.

This is a standard fact in point-set topology. Taking $\sim$ to be $=$ , it specializes to the more famous fact that $Y$ is Hausdorff if (and only if) the diagonal is closed in $Y\times Y$ .

We write the quotient map $Y\to Y/\sim$ as $y\mapsto\overline{y}$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 12.5.

Denote $S=\{(x,y):x\sim y\}$ . This is closed in $Y\times Y$ by assumption. Let $x,y\in Y$ with $\overline{x}\neq\overline{y}$ in $Y/\sim$ . Our goal is to find disjoint neighborhoods of $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ . Since $(x,y)$ lies in the open set $Y\times Y\setminus S$ , it must be contained in an open subset of $Y\times Y\setminus S$ of the form $U\times V$ (by the definition of the product topology on $Y\times Y$ ). The images of $U$ and $V$ in $Y/\sim$ are open neighborhoods of $\overline{x}$ and $\overline{y}$ , respectively, because the quotient map is open. These neighborhoods are disjoint because $U\times V$ does not intersect $S$ . ∎

We now use Lemma 12.4 to prove Proposition 12.1.

#### Proof of Proposition 12.1.

Choose $x,K,W$ as in Lemma 12.4. Then there are two cases.

Case 1. $\overline{x}$ is a limit point in $W/\sim$ .

Let $U\subseteq K$ be a small open neighborhood of the identity and $V\subseteq W$ a small open neighborhood of $x$ such that $UV\subseteq W$ . Write $\overline{V}$ for the image of $V$ in $W/\sim$ (so $\overline{V}$ does not mean the closure of $V$ ). Since $W\to W/\sim$ is open, $\overline{V}$ is open. Using that the Hausdorff space $\overline{V}$ contains a limit point (namely $\overline{x}$ ), we can find an infinite sequence of disjoint nonempty open sets $\overline{V_{i}}\subseteq\overline{V}$ . Let $V_{i}$ be the intersection of $V$ with the preimage of $\overline{V_{i}}$ . Then the $V_{i}$ are open and nonempty in $X$ , and the $UV_{i}$ are disjoint because their projections to $W/\sim$ are the $\overline{V_{i}}$ , which are disjoint.

Case 2. $\overline{x}$ is isolated in $W/\sim$ .

That $\overline{x}$ is isolated means $Kx\cap W$ is open in $X$ . Let $K/\Stab_{x}$ denote the image of $K$ in $G/\Stab_{x}$ . Then the natural map $K/\Stab_{x}\to Kx$ is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space, so it is a homeomorphism. In particular, a neighborhood of the identity in $K/\Stab_{x}$ maps homeomorphically to $Kx\cap W$ , which is open in $X$ . This means that the map $G/\Stab_{x}\to X$ given by acting on $x$ is a homeomorphism from a neighborhood of the identity to a neighborhood of $x$ . By translation symmetry, it follows that $Gx$ is open in $X$ , and $G/\Stab_{x}\to Gx$ is a local homeomorphism. Since $G/\Stab_{x}\to Gx$ is bijective, we conclude that it is in fact a (global) homeomorphism. Note that $G/\Stab_{x}$ is a smooth manifold, so this shows that $Gx$ is about as nice a topological space as possible — in particular, $Gx$ is locally compact Hausdorff (LCH).

If $Gx$ is non-compact, then it is easy to find nonempty opens $U\subseteq G$ and $V_{i}\subseteq Gx$ with the $UV_{i}$ disjoint — just take the $V_{i}$ to accumulate rapidly at infinity in the LCH space $Gx$ . Thus we may assume $Gx$ is compact. Then $Gx$ is both open and closed in $X$ , so $Gx=X$ because $X$ is connected. Hence $X\simeq G/\Stab_{x}\simeq\Stab_{x}\backslash G$ , and $\Stab_{x}$ is cocompact because $X=Gx$ is compact. This contradicts the assumption in the statement of Proposition 12.1 that $X$ is not of the form $H\backslash G$ for any closed cocompact subgroup $H\subseteq G$ . ∎

Now that Proposition 12.1 is proved, Theorem 11.4 is fully proved as well.

### 12.3. Discreteness of the stabilizer subgroup

In this subsection, we prove Proposition 11.5, restated below. The proof given here is an adaptation of the proof of Theorem 4.5.1 in [47].

#### Proposition (Restatement of Proposition 11.5).

Let $G$ be a noncompact simple Lie group (e.g., $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ ). Let $H\subseteq G$ be a closed cocompact subgroup such that $H\backslash G$ admits a $G$ -invariant probability measure. Then either $H$ is discrete or $H=G$ .

#### Proof.

Since $G$ is non-compact and simple, it contains a unipotent element (this is the only place where non-compactness is used). The closure of the subgroup generated by unipotent elements is a nonempty, closed, connected, normal subgroup of $G$ , so it is equal to $G$ because $G$ is simple.

Since $G$ is simple, it is unimodular. The condition that $H\backslash G$ admits an invariant probability measure then implies that $H$ is unimodular. This means that $\Ad(H)$ acts trivially on $\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{h}$ , where $d=\dim\mathfrak{h}$ . Pick some nonzero element $\omega\in\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{h}$ . We claim that $\Ad(G)$ fixes $\omega$ inside $\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{g}$ . By the previous paragraph, it suffices to check that $\Ad(u)\omega=\omega$ for all unipotents $u\in G$ . Because $u$ is unipotent, $n\mapsto\Ad(u^{n})\omega$ is a polynomial function from the integers to $\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{g}$ . This function lands in $\Ad(G)\omega$ , which is compact because $\omega$ is stabilized by $\Ad(H)$ , and $H$ is cocompact. But bounded polynomials are constant, so $\Ad(u^{n})\omega$ must be independent of $n$ . Equating $n=1$ with $n=0$ , we get $\Ad(u)\omega=\omega$ , proving the claim.

We now know that $\Ad(G)$ acts trivially on $\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{h}\subseteq\wedge^{d}\mathfrak{g}$ . Consequently $\Ad(G)$ preserves $\mathfrak{h}$ . It follows by simplicity that either $\mathfrak{h}=0$ or $\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{g}$ , and hence either $H$ is discrete or $H=G$ . ∎

Having proved Theorem 11.4 and Proposition 11.5, we immediately obtain Theorem 11.3.

### 12.4. Finishing the reduction to the weak converse theorem

Finally, we prove Theorem 1.8 conditioned on Theorem 11.2. So let $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ and $K=\PSO_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ once more. Recall the statement of Theorem 1.8:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 1.8).

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a nontrivial multiplicative representation. Then $\mathcal{H}\simeq L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ , as multiplicative representations, for some cocompact lattice $\Gamma$ in $G$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1.8 assuming Theorem 11.2.

Let $X$ and $\mu$ be as in Theorem 11.2, so in particular the multiplicative representation $\mathcal{H}$ identifies with $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ as unitary representations of $G$ . Then by Theorem 11.3, either $X$ is a point, or $X\simeq\Gamma\backslash G$ as $G$ -spaces for some cocompact lattice $\Gamma$ . If $X$ is a point, then $\mathcal{H}\simeq L^{2}(X,\mu)$ is one-dimensional, contradicting that $\mathcal{H}$ is nontrivial. Therefore $X\simeq\Gamma\backslash G$ . The only $G$ -invariant probability measure on $\Gamma\backslash G$ is Haar, so $\mu$ is the Haar probability measure. Thus $\mathcal{H}\simeq L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ as unitary representations. By Theorem 11.2, this isomorphism can be chosen so that multiplication on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is given by pointwise multiplication on $\Gamma\backslash G$ . We conclude that $\mathcal{H}\simeq L^{2}(\Gamma\backslash G)$ as multiplicative representations. ∎

## 13. $L^{\infty}$ bounds $\implies$ Weak converse theorem

Returning to our usual conventions, let $G=\PSL_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ , let $K=\PSO_{2}(\mathbf{R})$ , and let $\mathcal{H}$ be a multiplicative representation.

Section 12 reduced Theorem 1.8 to Theorem 11.2. In this section we reduce Theorem 11.2 to Theorem 11.6 and Corollary 11.8 (a consequence of Theorem 11.7). Theorems 11.6 and 11.7 will be proved in Sections 14, 15, and 16. For now, we take Theorem 11.6 and Corollary 11.8 for granted.

### 13.1. The commutative C*-algebra generated by $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$

For all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , by the $n=0$ case of Theorem 11.6, $M_{\alpha}$ extends from $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ to a bounded linear operator on $\mathcal{H}$ . Thereby view $M_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ .

#### Proposition 13.1.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $M_{\alpha}^{\ast}=M_{\overline{\alpha}}$ . In particular, if $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , then $M_{\alpha}$ is self-adjoint.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ , it suffices to check that

$$ \displaystyle\langle M_{\alpha}\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\beta,M_{\overline{\alpha}}\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $\beta,\gamma\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . By definition, $M_{\alpha}\beta=\alpha\beta$ and $M_{\overline{\alpha}}\gamma=\overline{\alpha}\gamma$ , so this is immediate from the definition of $\overline{\alpha}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 13.2.

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $M_{\alpha},M_{\beta}$ commute.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ , it suffices to check that

$$ \displaystyle\langle M_{\alpha}M_{\beta}\gamma,\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle M_{\beta}M_{\alpha}\gamma,\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $\gamma,\delta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Indeed, by Proposition 13.1 together with crossing symmetry,

$$ \displaystyle\langle M_{\alpha}M_{\beta}\gamma,\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle M_{\beta}\gamma,M_{\overline{\alpha}}\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\beta\gamma,\overline{\alpha}\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\alpha\gamma,\overline{\beta}\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle M_{\alpha}\gamma,M_{\overline{\beta}}\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle M_{\beta}M_{\alpha}\gamma,\delta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.\qed $$

Let $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ be the closure (with respect to the operator norm topology) of the subalgebra generated by $\{M_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\}$ . Propositions 13.1 and 13.2 imply that $\mathcal{A}$ is a commutative C*-subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ . Since $M_{\mathbf{1}}$ is the identity operator, $\mathcal{A}$ is unital, and since $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ has countable dimension (Proposition 2.5), $\mathcal{A}$ is separable.

The group $U(\mathcal{H})$ of unitary operators on $\mathcal{H}$ acts by conjugation on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ , and for each element of $U(\mathcal{H})$ , its conjugation action is a C*-automorphism of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ . The representation of $G$ on $\mathcal{H}$ is a map $G\to U(\mathcal{H})$ . Pulling the $U(\mathcal{H})$ -action back to $G$ , we obtain an action of $G$ on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ by C*-automorphisms. Our next goal is to show that this $G$ -action preserves $\mathcal{A}$ (Theorem 13.3), and that the action map is continuous (Theorem 13.4).

#### Theorem 13.3.

The C*-subalgebra $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ is $G$ -invariant.

#### Theorem 13.4.

The action map $G\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A}$ , given by $(g,A)\mapsto gAg^{-1}$ , is continuous (where $G$ has the Euclidean topology, $\mathcal{A}$ has the operator norm topology, and $G\times\mathcal{A}$ has the product topology).

To prove these theorems, we will need a few preliminary results.

#### Lemma 13.5.

Let $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and let $v,w\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\langle M_{X\alpha}v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=-\langle M_{\alpha}Xv,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle M_{\alpha}v,Xw\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ , it suffices to check that

$$ \displaystyle\langle M_{X\alpha}\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=-\langle M_{\alpha}X\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle M_{\alpha}\beta,X\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $\beta,\gamma\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Rearranging, we want to show that

$$ \displaystyle-\langle\alpha\beta,X\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle(X\alpha)\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\alpha X\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Using (2.7) to move the $X$ on the left hand side to the first argument in the inner product, we see that this is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle\langle\overline{X}(\alpha\beta),\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle(X\alpha)\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle\alpha X\beta,\gamma\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Now $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ by assumption, so $\overline{X}=X$ , and the above is immediate from the product rule. ∎

#### Proposition 13.6.

Let $X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}$ with $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}\ll 1$ , and set $g=\exp X$ . Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}M_{X^{n}\alpha} $$

(because $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}\ll 1$ , Theorem 11.6 implies that the sum converges absolutely in operator norm). Hence $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ , it suffices to check that

$$ \displaystyle\langle gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}\langle M_{X^{n}\alpha}v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $v,w\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ . For $t\in[0,1]$ , denote $g_{t}=\exp(tX)$ . For fixed $v,w\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ and for each $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , let $F_{\beta}\colon[0,1]\to\mathbf{C}$ be the function

$$ \displaystyle F_{\beta}(t)=\langle g_{t}M_{\beta}g_{t}^{-1}v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

With this notation, (13.1) can be rewritten as

$$ \displaystyle F_{\alpha}(1)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}F_{X^{n}\alpha}(0). $$

In general, by unitarity,

$$ \displaystyle F_{\beta}(t)=\langle M_{\beta}g_{t}^{-1}v,g_{t}^{-1}w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $v,w\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ , it follows from this formula that $F_{\beta}\in C^{\infty}([0,1])$ , and furthermore its derivatives can be computed by the product rule. The first derivative is

$$ \displaystyle F_{\beta}^{\prime}(t)=-\langle M_{\beta}Xg_{t}^{-1}v,g_{t}^{-1}w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle M_{\beta}g_{t}^{-1}v,Xg_{t}^{-1}w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $g_{t}^{-1}v,g_{t}^{-1}w\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ , Lemma 13.5 gives

$$ \displaystyle F_{\beta}^{\prime}(t)=\langle M_{X\beta}g_{t}^{-1}v,g_{t}^{-1}w\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=F_{X\beta}(t). $$

This is valid for all $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , so we can iterate it to see that the $n$ th derivative of $F_{\alpha}$ is $F_{\alpha}^{(n)}=F_{X^{n}\alpha}$ . By the trivial bound

$$ \displaystyle|F_{\beta}(t)|\leq\|\beta\|_{L^{\infty}}\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|w\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

and by Theorem 11.6,

$$ \displaystyle|F_{\alpha}^{(n)}(t)|\lesssim_{\alpha}O(n\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}})^{n}\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|w\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $t\in[0,1]$ . Since $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}\ll 1$ , it follows that the Taylor series for $F_{\alpha}$ at $t=0$ converges absolutely to $F_{\alpha}$ on all of $[0,1]$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle F_{\alpha}(1)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}F_{\alpha}^{(n)}(0)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n!}F_{X^{n}\alpha}(0). $$

This is the desired equation (13.2). ∎

From Proposition 13.6, we deduce Theorem 13.3 with little additional effort. Theorem 13.4 will require one more intermediate result.

#### Proof of Theorem 13.3.

By Proposition 13.6, there is a neighborhood $U$ of the identity in $G$ such that for all $g\in U$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , one has $gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}\in\mathcal{A}$ . Since conjugation by $g$ is a C*-automorphism, the closed subalgebra $\mathcal{A}^{g}$ of $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ generated by $\{gM_{\alpha}g^{-1}:\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\}$ is the $g$ -conjugate of the closed subalgebra generated by $\{M_{\alpha}:\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\}$ , i.e., $\mathcal{A}^{g}=g\mathcal{A}g^{-1}$ . From the definition of $U$ , we know that $\mathcal{A}^{g}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ for $g\in U$ , and hence $g\mathcal{A}g^{-1}\subseteq\mathcal{A}$ for $g\in U$ . Since $G$ is connected, it is generated by any neighborhood of the identity. Thus the $g$ -invariance of $\mathcal{A}$ for $g\in U$ implies that $\mathcal{A}$ is $g$ -invariant for all $g\in G$ . ∎

#### Proposition 13.7.

For each $A\in\mathcal{A}$ , the map $G\to\mathcal{A}$ given by $g\mapsto gAg^{-1}$ is continuous.

#### Proof.

By translation symmetry, it suffices to show that there is a neighborhood $U$ of the identity in $G$ such that for each $A\in\mathcal{A}$ , the map $\Phi_{A}\colon U\to\mathcal{A}$ given by $\Phi_{A}(g)=gAg^{-1}$ for $g\in U$ is continuous. Let

$$ \displaystyle U=\{\exp X:X\in\mathfrak{g}_{\mathbf{R}}\text{ and }\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}\ll 1\}, $$

where the condition $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}\ll 1$ ensures that $X$ satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition 13.6. Then the Taylor expansion in Proposition 13.6 implies that $\Phi_{A}$ is continuous when $A=M_{\alpha}$ for some $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . By the definition of $\mathcal{A}$ , a general $A\in\mathcal{A}$ can be approximated by sums of products of $M_{\alpha}$ ’s. Since conjugation by $g$ is a C*-automorphism, such an approximation translates to an approximation of $\Phi_{A}$ by sums of products of $\Phi_{M_{\alpha}}$ ’s, where the latter approximation takes place in the Banach space of functions $\Psi\colon U\to\mathcal{A}$ with the uniform norm $\|\Psi\|=\sup_{g\in U}\|\Psi(g)\|_{\op}$ . Therefore $\Phi_{A}$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions, and hence is itself continuous. ∎

We will only ever need Proposition 13.7 as opposed to the full strength of Theorem 13.4, but Theorem 13.4 quickly follows from Proposition 13.7, so we give the proof just to make clear that the $G$ -action on $\mathcal{A}$ is well-behaved.

#### Proof of Theorem 13.4.

Let $g\in G$ and $A\in\mathcal{A}$ . Given sequences $g_{n}\to g$ and $A_{n}\to A$ , we must show that $g_{n}A_{n}g_{n}^{-1}\to gAg^{-1}$ . By the triangle inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\|g_{n}A_{n}g_{n}^{-1}-gAg^{-1}\|_{\op}\leq\|g_{n}A_{n}g_{n}^{-1}-g_{n}Ag_{n}^{-1}\|_{\op}+\|g_{n}Ag_{n}^{-1}-gAg^{-1}\|_{\op}. $$

The first term on the right hand side is equal to $\|A_{n}-A\|_{\op}$ , so it goes to zero. The second term goes to zero by Proposition 13.7. ∎

Now, let $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{H}$ be given by evaluation at $\mathbf{1}$ . This is a bounded linear map, and it is $G$ -equivariant because

$$ \displaystyle\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(gAg^{-1})=gAg^{-1}\mathbf{1}=gA\mathbf{1}=g\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(A) $$

for all $g\in G$ and $A\in\mathcal{A}$ .

#### Proposition 13.8.

The map $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{H}$ is injective.

#### Proof.

Let $A\in\mathcal{A}$ be nonzero. We wish to show that $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(A)$ is nonzero. Since $\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ , nonzeroness of $A$ means that there exists $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}$ with $A\alpha\neq 0$ . By density, $\alpha$ may be taken to be in $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then using that $\mathcal{A}$ is commutative, we can write

$$ \displaystyle 0\neq A\alpha=AM_{\alpha}\mathbf{1}=M_{\alpha}A\mathbf{1}=M_{\alpha}\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(A). $$

This forces $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(A)\neq 0$ , as desired. ∎

Finally, we note that Corollary 11.8 has the following easy consequence.

#### Corollary 13.9.

There exists a nonnegative continuous function $\varphi\in L^{1}(G)$ , not identically zero, such that for all $v\in\mathcal{H}$ , the convolution $\varphi\ast v$ lies in the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi$ be as in Corollary 11.8, and let $v\in\mathcal{H}$ . Then $\varphi\ast v\in\mathcal{C}$ , which means that there is an $L^{\infty}$ -Cauchy sequence $\alpha_{n}\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with $\alpha_{n}\to\varphi\ast v$ in $\mathcal{H}$ . The fact that $\alpha_{n}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^{\infty}$ is equivalent to $M_{\alpha_{n}}$ being a Cauchy sequence in $\mathcal{A}$ . Thus the $M_{\alpha_{n}}$ converge to a limit $A\in\mathcal{A}$ . Since $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ is bounded,

$$ \displaystyle\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(A)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\ev_{\mathbf{1}}(M_{\alpha_{n}})=\lim_{n\to\infty}\alpha_{n}=\varphi\ast v. $$

Thus $\varphi\ast v$ is indeed in the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ . ∎

### 13.2. The spectrum of the C*-algebra

By Gelfand duality (Theorem 7.1), $\mathcal{A}$ is isomorphic as a C*-algebra to $C(X)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $X$ unique up to homeomorphism. Fix an isomorphism $\Phi\colon C(X)\to\mathcal{A}$ . Since $\mathcal{A}$ is separable, $X$ is metrizable. The linear functional

$$ \displaystyle f\mapsto\langle\Phi(f)\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

on $C(X)$ is positive because for $f\in C(X)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|f|^{2}\mapsto\langle\Phi(|f|^{2})\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\Phi(f)^{\ast}\Phi(f)\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\Phi(f)\mathbf{1}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\geq 0 $$

(indeed, this functional is the pullback to $C(X)$ of the GNS state on $\mathcal{A}$ associated to $\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{H}$ ). Thus by the Riesz representation theorem, this functional is given by integration against a unique positive measure $\mu$ on $X$ . The measure $\mu$ is a probability measure because

$$ \displaystyle\mu(X)=\int_{X}1\,d\mu=\langle\Phi(1)\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=1, $$

where the last equality is the normalization axiom in the definition of a multiplicative representation. By (13.3),

$$ \displaystyle\|f\|_{L^{2}(X,\mu)}=\|\Phi(f)\mathbf{1}\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\circ\Phi(f)\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $f\in C(X)$ , so $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\circ\Phi$ extends to $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ and gives an isometry $\Psi\colon L^{2}(X,\mu)\to\mathcal{H}$ . Since $\Phi$ is an isomorphism onto $\mathcal{A}$ , the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\circ\Phi$ is the same as the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ , which contains $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ and hence is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ . Thus the image of $\Psi$ is dense in $\mathcal{H}$ , and since $\Psi$ is an isometry, it follows that $\Psi$ is an isomorphism. In summary, we have a diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{2}(X,\mu)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ev_{\mathbf{1}}} $$

where the vertical maps are isomorphisms. The top arrow is the natural map taking a continuous function in $C(X)$ to its $\mu$ -a.e. equivalence class in $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ . It is not obvious a priori that this top arrow is injective, but in fact it is because the bottom arrow is injective by Proposition 13.8.

#### Proposition 13.10.

The measure $\mu$ has full support on $X$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose not. Then there is a nonempty open subset $U\subseteq X$ with $\mu(U)=0$ . By Urysohn’s lemma, there exists a nonzero function $f\in C(X)$ which vanishes outside $U$ . Then $f$ vanishes $\mu$ -a.e., and hence vanishes as an element of $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ . This contradicts that $C(X)\to L^{2}(X,\mu)$ is injective. ∎

Because $C(X)\to L^{2}(X,\mu)$ is injective, we view $C(X)$ as a subspace of $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ from now on.

#### Lemma 13.11.

Let $f\in L^{2}(X,\mu)$ with $\Psi(f)$ in the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ . Then $f\in C(X)$ .

#### Proof.

This is because the vertical arrows in the diagram above are isomorphisms. ∎

By Gelfand duality, the $G$ -action on $\mathcal{A}$ by conjugation induces a $G$ -action on $X$ by homeomorphisms. A priori, the action map $G\times X\to X$ is only continuous when $G$ is given the discrete topology, but Proposition 13.12 below says that it is actually continuous when $G$ has the usual topology. The $G$ -action on $X$ induces a $G$ -action on $C(X)$ by $gf(x)=f(g^{-1}x)$ . The isomorphism $\Phi\colon C(X)\to\mathcal{A}$ is tautologically $G$ -equivariant — the $G$ -action on $X$ is defined to make $\Phi$ equivariant.

#### Proposition 13.12.

The action map $G\times X\to X$ is continuous.

#### Proof.

Suppose for a contradiction that $G\times X\to X$ is not continuous. Then there are convergent sequences $g_{n}\to g$ and $x_{n}\to x$ , and a neighborhood $V$ of $gx$ , such that $g_{n}x_{n}\not\in V$ for all $n$ . By Urysohn’s lemma, there exists $f\in C(X)$ with $f(gx)=1$ and $f|_{X\setminus V}=0$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|f(g_{n}x_{n})-f(gx)|=1 $$

for all $n$ , so

$$ \displaystyle 1=\lim_{n\to\infty}|f(g_{n}x_{n})-f(gx)| \displaystyle\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}|f(g_{n}x_{n})-f(gx_{n})|+\limsup_{n\to\infty}|f(gx_{n})-f(gx)| \displaystyle\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|g_{n}^{-1}f-g^{-1}f\|_{C(X)}+\limsup_{n\to\infty}|g^{-1}f(x_{n})-g^{-1}f(x)| \displaystyle=\limsup_{n\to\infty}\|g_{n}^{-1}\Phi(f)g_{n}-g^{-1}\Phi(f)g\|_{\op}+\limsup_{n\to\infty}|g^{-1}f(x_{n})-g^{-1}f(x)|. $$

The first $\limsup$ vanishes by Theorem 13.4 (in fact Proposition 13.7 suffices), and the second $\limsup$ vanishes because $g^{-1}f$ is a continuous function on $X$ . This is a contradiction. ∎

#### Proposition 13.13.

The measure $\mu$ is preserved by the $G$ -action on $X$ .

#### Proof.

We must show that for all $f\in C(X)$ and $g\in G$ , both $f$ and $gf$ have the same integral with respect to $\mu$ . By the definition of $\mu$ , equivariance of $\Phi$ , and unitarity,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{X}gf\,d\mu=\langle\Phi(gf)\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle g\Phi(f)g^{-1}\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\Phi(f)g^{-1}\mathbf{1},g^{-1}\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\Phi(f)\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\int_{X}f\,d\mu, $$

as desired. ∎

By Proposition 13.13, the group $G$ acts unitarily on $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ by $gf(x)=f(g^{-1}x)$ .

#### Proposition 13.14.

The Hilbert space isomorphism $\Psi\colon L^{2}(X,\mu)\to\mathcal{H}$ is $G$ -equivariant.

#### Proof.

By density, it suffices to show that $\Psi|_{C(X)}=\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\circ\Phi$ is equivariant. This is clear, because both $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ and $\Phi$ are equivariant. ∎

#### Proposition 13.15.

The space $X$ is connected.

#### Proof.

Since $G$ is connected and $G\times X\to X$ is continuous (Proposition 13.12), $G$ preserves each connected component of $X$ . The indicator functions of the components are therefore $G$ -invariant elements of $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ , and they are linearly independent (in particular nonzero) in $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ because $\mu$ has full support (Proposition 13.10). Thus the number of components is at most $\dim L^{2}(X,\mu)^{G}=\dim\mathcal{H}^{G}$ . By the ergodicity assumption in the definition of a multiplicative representation, $\mathcal{H}^{G}=\mathbf{C}\mathbf{1}$ is one-dimensional, so $X$ must be connected. ∎

Combining Corollary 13.9 with what we now know about $X,\mu$ gives

#### Corollary 13.16.

The $G$ -space $X$ with invariant measure $\mu$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property (with $p=2$ and $q=\infty$ in Definition 11.1).

#### Proof.

Let $\varphi$ be as in Corollary 13.9, and let $f\in L^{2}(X,\mu)$ . We wish to show that the convolution $\varphi\ast f$ is in $L^{\infty}(X,\mu)$ . Since $X$ is compact, it suffices to show that $\varphi\ast f\in C(X)$ . Corollary 13.9 says that $\varphi\ast\Psi(f)$ is in the image of $\ev_{\mathbf{1}}$ . By Proposition 13.14, $\Psi$ is equivariant, so $\varphi\ast\Psi(f)=\Psi(\varphi\ast f)$ . Thus by Lemma 13.11, we indeed have $\varphi\ast f\in C(X)$ . ∎

Proposition 13.14 says that $\Psi\colon L^{2}(X,\mu)\to\mathcal{H}$ is an isomorphism of unitary representations of $G$ . Therefore $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ has discrete spectrum, so it makes sense to consider $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , and $\Psi$ restricts to an isomorphism $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We can now extend the diagram above to

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{2}(X,\mu)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ev_{\mathbf{1}}} $$

again with all vertical arrows isomorphisms. The inclusion $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{H}$ in the bottom row factors as

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}.} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\mapsto M_{\alpha}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ev_{\mathbf{1}}} $$

Since the top row is isomorphic to the bottom row, there must be a matching factorization of the inclusion $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow L^{2}(X,\mu)$ . This means that there is a map $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow C(X)$ making the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L^{2}(X,\mu)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{H}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha\mapsto M_{\alpha}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ev_{\mathbf{1}}} $$

commute, with the compositions of the top and bottom rows being the natural inclusions $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow L^{2}(X,\mu)$ and $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{H}$ . Using that both the second map in the top row and the composition of the two maps in the top row are the natural inclusions, we immediately obtain

#### Proposition 13.17.

One has $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\subseteq C(X)$ , and the map $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\hookrightarrow C(X)$ in the diagram (13.4) is the inclusion.

The next proposition says that the pointwise multiplication map $L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\times L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}\to L^{2}(X,\mu)$ identifies via $\Psi$ with the multiplication map $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\times\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}$ .

#### Proposition 13.18.

Let $f,h\in L^{2}(X,\mu)^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $f,h\in C(X)$ , and $\Psi(fh)=\Psi(f)\Psi(h)$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 13.17, we have $f,h\in C(X)$ and hence $fh\in C(X)$ . Since the right square in the diagram (13.4) commutes, we can write $\Psi(fh)=\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\Phi(fh)$ and $\Psi(h)=\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\Phi(h)$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\Psi(fh)=\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\Phi(fh)=\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\Phi(f)\Phi(h)=\Phi(f)\Phi(h)\mathbf{1}=\Phi(f)\ev_{\mathbf{1}}\Phi(h)=\Phi(f)\Psi(h). $$

Since the left square in (13.4) commutes, $\Phi(f)=M_{\Psi(f)}$ . Continuing the above calculation,

$$ \displaystyle\Psi(fh)=\Phi(f)\Psi(h)=M_{\Psi(f)}\Psi(h)=\Psi(f)\Psi(h).\qed $$

We end this section by observing that we have now proved Theorem 11.2 (assuming Theorem 11.6 and Corollary 11.8 of course). Recall the statement:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.2).

There exists a connected compact metrizable $G$ -space $X$ together with a $G$ -invariant probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ of full support, such that $(X,\mu)$ has the qualitative Sobolev embedding property, $\mathcal{H}$ identifies with $L^{2}(X,\mu)$ as unitary representations of $G$ , and the multiplication $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\times\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}\to\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ is given by pointwise multiplication of functions on $X$ .

#### Proof.

Let $X,\mu$ be as above. Then all required properties are explicitly stated and proved above. ∎

## 14. Bulk and tail bounds $\implies$ $L^{\infty}$ bounds

By the results of Sections 12 and 13, Theorem 1.8 follows from Theorem 11.6 and Corollary 11.8. We saw in Section 11 that Corollary 11.8 is a consequence of Theorem 11.7. It therefore remains to prove Theorems 11.6 and 11.7. In this section, we prove these two theorems assuming Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11. These last three theorems are proved in Sections 15 and 16.

### 14.1. Sobolev embedding into $L^{\infty}$

We will deduce Theorem 11.7 from the following proposition. Let $I_{i},\lambda_{i}$ be as in Theorem 11.11.

#### Proposition 14.1.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ for some $i$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i}))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Both to prove Proposition 14.1 and to deduce Theorem 11.7 from Proposition 14.1, we will need the following elementary estimate.

#### Lemma 14.2.

Let $A\geq 0$ and $v\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{A}\|\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\Delta)v\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

On the left hand side, write

$$ \displaystyle\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})=\exp(-\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i}), $$

and then apply Cauchy–Schwarz to get

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\Big(\sum_{i}\exp(-2\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Big(\sum_{i}\exp(2(A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

The first sum on the right is finite because of the polynomial growth property (11.4). Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Big(\sum_{i}\exp(2(A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Since $I_{i}$ has length $\lesssim 1$ , we can replace $\lambda_{i}$ with $\min I_{i}$ at the cost of a factor of $O_{A}(1)$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{A}\Big(\sum_{i}\exp(2(A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\min I_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}. $$

Rewriting this using orthogonality,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{A}\Big\|\sum_{i}\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\min I_{i})\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}(v)\Big\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

For $\mu\geq 0$ , we have the inequality

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i}\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\min I_{i})\mathds{1}_{\mu\in I_{i}}\leq\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\mu). $$

Inserting this above yields the desired estimate. ∎

Let us now see how Proposition 14.1 implies Theorem 11.7. Recall the statement of the theorem:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.7).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 11.7 assuming Proposition 14.1.

By the triangle inequality and Proposition 14.1,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\sum_{i}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\sum_{i}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i}))\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

(note the triangle inequality was valid because $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , so $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}\alpha=0$ for all but finitely many $i$ ). Thus by Lemma 14.2,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By increasing the $O$ -constant, $\lesssim$ can be replaced with $\leq$ . ∎

The remainder of this subsection is dedicated to the proof of Proposition 14.1. The main tool is the “modified $L^{p}$ norm” $\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}$ on $\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , defined as follows for $4\leq p\leq\infty$ : let $\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}$ be the smallest constant $C\in[0,\infty]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq C\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{\frac{4}{p}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{1-\frac{4}{p}}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}. $$

To motivate this definition, note that whenever $f,h$ are functions on a measure space and $4\leq p\leq\infty$ , one has

$$ \displaystyle\|fh\|_{L^{2}}\leq\|f\|_{L^{p}}\|h\|_{L^{2p/(p-2)}}\leq\|f\|_{L^{p}}\|h\|_{L^{4}}^{\frac{4}{p}}\|h\|_{L^{2}}^{1-\frac{4}{p}} $$

by Hölder and log-convexity of $L^{p}$ norms.

The triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}$ is clear. For $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , the first inequality in Proposition 10.3 says that $\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}$ . It follows that $\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}$ is increasing in $p$ . It is trivial to see that the limit as $p\to\infty$ (not including $p=\infty$ ) is

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{p\to\infty}\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}=\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}}=\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}}. $$

In addition to $\|\cdot\|_{\widetilde{L}^{\infty}}$ coinciding with the usual $L^{\infty}$ norm, $\|\cdot\|_{{\widetilde{L}}^{4}}$ coincides with the usual $L^{4}$ norm:

#### Proposition 14.3.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{4}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}$ .

#### Proof.

For any $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}} $$

by $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz (Proposition 10.1), so $\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{4}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}$ . The reverse inequality is due to the fact that equality holds in (14.3) when $\beta=\alpha$ . ∎

The next lemma will allow us to induct on $p$ when working with $\widetilde{L}^{p}$ norms. It is analogous to the $\leq$ direction of the equality $\|f\|_{L^{2p}}^{2}=\||f|^{2}\|_{L^{p}}$ , which holds for any function $f$ on a measure space.

#### Lemma 14.4.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ and $4\leq p\leq\infty$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}. $$

As mentioned in Subsection 11.6, the spectral cutoff $\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}$ is needed because $|\alpha|^{2}\not\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ but $\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We will almost always apply Lemma 14.4 with $\alpha$ a weight vector, in which case $|\alpha|^{2}\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ and $\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})$ .

#### Proof of Lemma 14.4.

For $\beta\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , crossing symmetry allows us to write

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle|\alpha|^{2},|\beta|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\langle\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2}),|\beta|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\lim_{\Lambda\to\infty}\langle\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\beta,\beta\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By Cauchy–Schwarz and the definition of the $\widetilde{L}^{p}$ norm, we get

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{\frac{4}{p}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2-\frac{4}{p}}. $$

Taking square roots,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\beta\|_{L^{4}}^{\frac{4}{2p}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{1-\frac{4}{2p}}. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{|\Delta|\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}^{\frac{1}{2}}, $$

and squaring both sides gives the result. ∎

We are now ready to prove Proposition 14.1.

#### Proof of Proposition 14.1.

Fix $A\gg 1$ and $B\gg_{A}1$ . We will show by induction on $p$ that for any $p\geq 4$ a power of $2$ , any $i$ , and any $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}\leq B\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Then since $A,B$ are fixed constants independent of $p$ , sending $p\to\infty$ and using (14.2) will give the desired bound (14.1).

To begin the proof of the base case $p=4$ of (14.4), we use Proposition 14.3, Theorem 11.9, and the fact that $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ to write

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{4}}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\max I_{i}))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $I_{i}$ has length $\lesssim 1$ , we can replace $\max I_{i}$ with $\lambda_{i}$ at the cost of increasing the $O$ -constant, so

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{4}}\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i}))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Taking $A$ to be at least the $O$ -constant and $B$ to be at least $1$ , we get (14.4) for $p=4$ .

Now make the induction hypothesis that (14.4) holds for some $4\leq p<\infty$ , and let us prove it for $2p$ . By Lemma 14.4, the triangle inequality, and the induction hypothesis,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}\leq\sum_{j}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{j}}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\widetilde{L}^{p}}\leq B\sum_{j}\exp(A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{j})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{j}}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

so by Lemma 14.2,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\lesssim_{A}B\|\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\Delta)(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Let $C,c$ be as in Theorem 11.11. Then splitting $\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta<C\lambda_{i}}+\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\lesssim_{A}B\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta<C\lambda_{i}}\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\Delta)(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}+B\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\Delta)(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating the first term trivially and the second term using that $(A+1)\log_{+}^{2}\mu\leq c\sqrt{\mu}+O_{A}(1)$ for $\mu\geq 0$ (note the $O$ -constant can be taken independent of $c$ because $c\gtrsim 1$ ),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\lesssim_{A}B\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}(C\lambda_{i}))\||\alpha|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}+B\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Rewriting the first term using (10.1) and estimating the second term by Theorem 11.11,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\lesssim_{A}B\exp((A+1)\log_{+}^{2}(C\lambda_{i}))\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{2}+B\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

By Theorem 11.9, the bound $C\lesssim 1$ , and the fact that $I_{i}$ has length $\lesssim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\lesssim_{A}B\exp((A+O(1))\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Since $A\gg 1$ and $B\gg_{A}1$ , we may assume $A$ is greater than the $O(1)$ in the exponential, and $B$ is greater than the implicit constant (importantly, these conditions are independent of $p$ ). Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\widetilde{L}^{2p}}^{2}\leq B^{2}\exp(2A\log_{+}^{2}\lambda_{i})\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Taking square roots yields (14.4) and completes the induction. ∎

### 14.2. Identities from the product rule

To proceed, we need two elementary algebraic identities: Propositions 14.5 and 14.6 below. These identities are crucial, and will be used many times throughout the rest of the paper. The proofs of these propositions are reminiscent of the proofs of Corollary 5.7, Proposition 5.8, and Corollary 5.9.

#### Proposition 14.5.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|E^{n}\varphi|^{2}=p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}), $$

where $p_{n}$ is the polynomial in two variables with real coefficients given by the second order recurrence

$$ \displaystyle p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)=(2\lambda-\mu+2n^{2})p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}p_{n-1}(\lambda,\mu) $$

for $n\geq 1$ , with initial conditions

$$ \displaystyle p_{0}(\lambda,\mu)=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad p_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda-\tfrac{1}{2}\mu. $$

The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ were worked out in Subsection 11.5 (see (11.13), (11.14), and the sentence after (11.14)). These computations are very short, so we redo them here for convenience.

#### Proof.

Since $\varphi$ is real, $|\varphi|^{2}=\varphi^{2}$ , so (14.5) holds for $n=0$ . By (2.6) and the product rule,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(\varphi^{2})=-\overline{E}E(\varphi^{2})=-2\overline{E}(\varphi E\varphi)=2\lambda\varphi^{2}-2|E\varphi|^{2}. $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle|E\varphi|^{2}=\Big(\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Big)(\varphi^{2}). $$

This is (14.5) for $n=1$ . By (2.6), the product rule, and (2.5), we compute for $n\geq 1$

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(|E^{n}\varphi|^{2}) \displaystyle=-\overline{E}E(E^{n}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi) \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}-|\overline{E}E^{n}\varphi|^{2}-\overline{E}E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi-E^{n}\varphi\overline{E}E\overline{E}^{n}\varphi \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}-|(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n-1}\varphi|^{2}+(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi+E^{n}\varphi(\Delta+H^{2}+H)\overline{E}^{n}\varphi \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}|E^{n-1}\varphi|^{2}+2(\lambda+n^{2})|E^{n}\varphi|^{2}. $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}=(2\lambda-\Delta+2n^{2})(|E^{n}\varphi|^{2})-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}|E^{n-1}\varphi|^{2}. $$

Comparing this with (14.6), we conclude by induction that (14.5) holds for all $n$ . ∎

#### Proposition 14.6.

Let $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a lowest weight vector of weight $k\geq 1$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|E^{n}f|^{2}=q_{k,n}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}), $$

where $q_{k,n}$ is the polynomial in one variable with real coefficients given by the second order recurrence

$$ \displaystyle q_{k,n+1}(\mu)=(2(n+k)^{2}-2k(k-1)-\mu)q_{k,n}(\mu)-((n+k)(n+k-1)-k(k-1))^{2}q_{k,n-1}(\mu) $$

for $n\geq 1$ , with initial conditions

$$ \displaystyle q_{k,0}(\mu)=1\qquad\text{and}\qquad q_{k,1}(\mu)=2k-\mu. $$

This proposition is analogous to Corollary 5.9.

#### Proof.

The case $n=0$ of (14.7) is trivial. Computing as in the proof of Proposition 14.5 above,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(|f|^{2})=-\overline{E}E(f\overline{f})=-|Ef|^{2}-|\overline{E}f|^{2}-(\overline{E}Ef)\overline{f}-f\overline{E}E\overline{f}. $$

Since $f$ is a lowest weight vector, $\overline{E}f=0$ and consequently $E\overline{f}=\overline{\overline{E}f}=0$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(|f|^{2})=-|Ef|^{2}-(\overline{E}Ef)\overline{f}=-|Ef|^{2}+(\Delta+H^{2}+H)f\,\overline{f}=-|Ef|^{2}+2k|f|^{2}, $$

where in the last equality we have used that $f$ has Casimir eigenvalue $-k(k-1)$ and weight $k$ . Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle|Ef|^{2}=(2k-\Delta)(|f|^{2}). $$

This is (14.7) for $n=1$ . Now for $n\geq 1$ , write

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(|E^{n}f|^{2}) \displaystyle=-\overline{E}E(E^{n}f\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f}) \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}f|^{2}-|\overline{E}E^{n}f|^{2}-\overline{E}E^{n+1}f\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f}-E^{n}f\overline{E}E\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f} \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}f|^{2}-|(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n-1}f|^{2}+(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n}f\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f}+E^{n}f(\Delta+H^{2}+H)\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f} \displaystyle=-|E^{n+1}f|^{2}-((n+k)(n+k-1)-k(k-1))^{2}|E^{n-1}f|^{2}+2((n+k)^{2}-k(k-1))|E^{n}f|^{2}. $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle|E^{n+1}f|^{2}=(2(n+k)^{2}-2k(k-1)-\Delta)(|E^{n}f|^{2})-((n+k)(n+k-1)-k(k-1))^{2}|E^{n-1}f|^{2}. $$

Comparing with (14.8) yields (14.7) by induction. ∎

The recurrences (14.6) and (14.8) are each analogous to a special case of Corollary 5.7. The coefficients in (14.6) become the coefficients in (14.8) after replacing $\lambda$ with $-k(k-1)$ and $n$ with $n+k$ . Comparing the proofs of Propositions 14.5 and 14.6 makes this clear.

The polynomials $p_{n}$ and $q_{k,n}$ obey the following trivial bounds.

#### Lemma 14.7 (Trivial bound for $p_{n}$ ).

For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $\lambda,\mu\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)|\leq O(\lambda+\mu+n^{2})^{n}. $$

#### Lemma 14.8 (Trivial bound for $q_{k,n}$ ).

For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , $k\geq 1$ , and $\mu\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|q_{k,n}(\mu)|\leq O(k^{2}+\mu+n^{2})^{n}. $$

#### Proof of Lemmas 14.7 and 14.8.

By induction on $n$ , both bounds follow directly from the recursive definitions of $p_{n}$ and $q_{k,n}$ . ∎

### 14.3. Derivative bounds in $L^{\infty}$

In this subsection, we use Theorem 11.7 to prove Theorem 11.6 (still assuming Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11).

From Lemma 14.4 and Theorem 11.7 we obtain the following corollary.

#### Corollary 14.9.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a weight vector. Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since the $L^{\infty}$ and $\widetilde{L}^{\infty}$ norms coincide, the $p=\infty$ case of Lemma 14.4 says that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\liminf_{\Lambda\to\infty}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\|_{L^{\infty}}. $$

Since $\alpha$ is a weight vector, $|\alpha|^{2}\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ , and so $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}(|\alpha|^{2})\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Thus we can apply Theorem 11.7 to conclude. ∎

#### Proposition 14.10.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}<\infty$ .

#### Proof.

By Proposition 2.5, we know that $\alpha$ is a linear combination of automorphic vectors, so by the triangle inequality, it suffices to prove the proposition for $\alpha$ itself an automorphic vector. Replacing $\alpha$ by its complex conjugate if necessary, we may assume $\alpha$ has nonnegative weight $n\geq 0$ . Then by Proposition 2.6, either $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ for some automorphic vector $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ , or $\alpha=E^{n-k}f$ for some lowest weight vector $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ of weight $k$ between $1$ and $n$ . If $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ , then by splitting $\varphi$ into real and imaginary parts and using the triangle inequality, we may assume $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . It follows from Corollary 14.9, together with Proposition 14.5 if $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ or Proposition 14.6 if $\alpha=E^{n-k}f$ , that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))q_{k,n-k}(\Delta)(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By Lemma 14.7 and Corollary 11.13 if $\alpha=E^{n}\varphi$ , or by Lemma 14.8 and Theorem 11.10 if $\alpha=E^{n-k}f$ , we conclude that $\|\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}$ is finite. ∎

We now quantify the second half of the proof of Proposition 14.10, keeping track of the dependence on the weight $n$ .

#### Proposition 14.11.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be an automorphic vector. Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\varphi}O(n)^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

Splitting $\varphi$ into real and imaginary parts and using the triangle inequality, we may assume without loss of generality that $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Let $\lambda$ denote the Casimir eigenvalue of $\varphi$ . Then by Corollary 14.9 and Proposition 14.5 (as in the proof of Proposition 14.10),

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Inserting the trivial bound from Lemma 14.7,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))O(\Delta+\lambda+n^{2})^{n}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

For $n\lesssim_{\varphi}1$ , Proposition 14.10 trivially gives the desired bound (14.9), because the implicit constant in (14.9) is allowed to depend on $\varphi$ (though the $O$ -constant is not). So assume $n\gg_{\varphi}1$ . Take this to mean $n^{2}\geq\lambda+1$ . Then splitting $\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq n^{2}}+\mathds{1}_{\Delta>n^{2}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq n^{2}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))O(n^{2})^{n}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta>n^{2}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))O(\Delta)^{n}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating the first term by ignoring $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq n^{2}}$ and using Corollary 11.13,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\lesssim_{\varphi}O(n)^{2n}+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta>n^{2}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))O(\Delta)^{n}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Dyadically decomposing,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\lesssim_{\varphi}O(n)^{2n}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\geq\frac{1}{2}n^{2}\end{subarray}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[M,2M]}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))O(\Delta)^{n}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Let $c\gtrsim 1$ be as in Corollary 11.13. The summand above is at most

$$ \displaystyle\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}M))O(M)^{n}\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[M,2M]}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Ignoring $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[M,2M]}$ and applying Corollary 11.13, the norm in this product is $\lesssim_{\varphi}1$ . Thus

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\lesssim_{\varphi}O(n)^{2n}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\geq\frac{1}{2}n^{2}\end{subarray}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}M))O(M)^{n}\exp(-c\sqrt{M}). $$

When $M$ is multiplied by $2$ , the summand is multiplied by

$$ \displaystyle M^{O(1)}O(1)^{n}\exp(-c^{\prime}\sqrt{M}), $$

where $c^{\prime}=(\sqrt{2}-1)c\gtrsim 1$ . So once $M$ is bigger than an absolute constant times $n^{2}$ , the sum decays (faster than) geometrically. Thus the first $O(1)$ many terms in the sum dominate. Each of these $O(1)$ many terms is bounded by $O(n)^{2n}$ . Hence

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}\lesssim_{\varphi}O(n)^{2n}, $$

and taking square roots gives (14.9), as desired. ∎

#### Proposition 14.12.

Let $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a lowest weight vector. Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n}f\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{f}O(n)^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

This can be shown in the same way as Proposition 14.11, using Proposition 14.6 in place of Proposition 14.5, and using Theorem 11.10 in place of Corollary 11.13. ∎

Finally, we are ready to prove Theorem 11.6. Recall the statement:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.6).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , let $X\in\mathfrak{g}$ , and let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|X^{n}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(n\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}})^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

For notational convenience, normalize $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}=1$ . Then we want to show $\|X^{n}\alpha\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(n)^{n}$ . As in the proof of Proposition 14.10, by Proposition 2.5 and symmetry under complex conjugation, we may assume without loss of generality that $\alpha$ is an automorphic vector of nonnegative weight $m\geq 0$ . Then by Proposition 2.6, either $\alpha=E^{m}\varphi$ for some automorphic vector $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ , or $\alpha=E^{m-k}f$ for some lowest weight vector $f$ of weight $k$ between $1$ and $m$ . If $\alpha=E^{m}\varphi$ , then by splitting $\varphi$ into real and imaginary parts as usual, we may further assume $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . For $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , denote

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{r}=E^{r}\varphi\text{ and }\varphi_{-r}=\overline{E}^{r}\varphi\qquad\text{or}\qquad f_{r}=E^{r}f. $$

Then by Proposition 14.11 and complex conjugation symmetry, or by Proposition 14.12,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi_{r}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(|r|)^{|r|}\text{ for }r\in\mathbf{Z}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\|f_{r}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim_{\alpha}O(r)^{r}\text{ for }r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}. $$

For $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$ , by the commutation relations (2.2) for $H,E,\overline{E}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle H\varphi_{r}=r\varphi_{r},\qquad E\varphi_{r}=\varphi_{r+1},\qquad\overline{E}\varphi_{r}=-(\lambda+r(r-1))\varphi_{r-1}. $$

Applying complex conjugation, we have again for $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{>0}$ that

$$ \displaystyle H\varphi_{-r}=-r\varphi_{-r},\qquad\overline{E}\varphi_{-r}=\varphi_{-r-1},\qquad E\varphi_{-r}=-(\lambda+r(r-1))\varphi_{-r+1}. $$

For $r=0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle H\varphi_{0}=0,\qquad E\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{1},\qquad\overline{E}\varphi_{0}=\varphi_{-1}. $$

Similarly, for $r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle Hf_{r}=(r+k)f_{r},\qquad Ef_{r}=f_{r+1},\qquad\overline{E}f_{r}=(k(k-1)-(r+k)(r+k-1))f_{r-1} $$

(when $r=0$ , the third equation should be interpreted as $\overline{E}f_{r}=0$ ). Write $X$ as a linear combination of $H,E,\overline{E}$ . Since $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}=1$ , the coefficients in this linear combination are $\lesssim 1$ . By induction on $n$ , using (14.12), (14.13), and (14.14) in case $\alpha=E^{m}\varphi$ , or using (14.15) in case $\alpha=E^{m-k}f$ ,

$$ \displaystyle X^{n}\alpha=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathbf{Z}\\
|r-m|\leq n\end{subarray}}a_{n,r}\varphi_{r}\qquad\text{or}\qquad X^{n}\alpha=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}r\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}\\
|r-m+k|\leq n\end{subarray}}b_{n,r}f_{r} $$

for some coefficients $a_{n,r}$ or $b_{n,r}$ with

$$ \displaystyle|a_{n,r}|\leq O(1)^{n}(n+m+\sqrt{\lambda})^{n+m-|r|}\qquad\text{or}\qquad|b_{n,r}|\leq O(1)^{n}(n+m+k)^{n+m-k-r}. $$

Now, as in the proof of Proposition 14.11, we may assume $n\gg_{\alpha}1$ , because the desired bound (14.10) trivially follows from Proposition 14.10 for $n\lesssim_{\alpha}1$ . In particular, we can assume $n\gg_{m,\lambda}1$ or $n\gg_{m,k}1$ . Then (14.17) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle|a_{n,r}|\leq O(1)^{n}n^{n-|r|}\qquad\text{or}\qquad|b_{n,r}|\leq O(1)^{n}n^{n-r} $$

after increasing the $O$ -constant. Taking $L^{\infty}$ norms in (14.16) and inserting (14.11) and (14.18), we obtain (14.10), as desired (recall we normalized $\|X\|_{\mathfrak{g}}=1$ ). ∎

## 15. Proof of bulk and tail bounds assuming a polynomial Weyl law

At this point, we have reduced Theorem 1.8 to Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11. As mentioned at the beginning of Subsection 11.6, Theorems 11.9 and 11.11 are particularly technical. In this section, to warm up, we prove these three theorems under the assumption that $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law (Definition 1.33). We will be clear about when this assumption is used, and we do not assume it by default. In fact, the proof of Theorem 11.10 does not use this assumption.

### 15.1. Bootstrap inequalities

Combining the results of Section 14.2 with crossing symmetry, we can prove some exact inequalities which will provide the main analytic input for Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11. These inequalities are Propositions 15.1, 15.2, and 15.3.

Let $p_{n}$ and $q_{k,n}$ be as in Propositions 14.5 and 14.6, respectively.

#### Proposition 15.1.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ . For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0. $$

This inequality is (11.20). We recap the proof, which is very short.

#### Proof.

By crossing symmetry, Proposition 14.5, self-adjointness of $\Delta$ , and the fact that the $p_{n}$ have real coefficients,

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle|E^{n}\varphi|^{2},|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle p_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Negating both sides gives the result. ∎

The analog of Proposition 15.1 for lowest weight vectors is

#### Proposition 15.2.

Let $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a lowest weight vector of weight $k\geq 1$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-\langle q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0. $$

#### Proof.

By crossing symmetry, Proposition 14.6, self-adjointness of $\Delta$ , and the fact that the $q_{k,n}$ have real coefficients,

$$ \displaystyle 0\leq\|E^{n+1}f\overline{E}^{n}\overline{f}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle|E^{n}f|^{2},|E^{n+1}f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle q_{k,n}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Negating both sides gives the result. ∎

Our next inequality, Proposition 15.3, is sharper but more complicated than Proposition 15.1. To state it, define

$$ \displaystyle s_{n}(\lambda,\mu)=p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)-(\lambda+n(n+1))p_{n}(\lambda,\mu) $$

and

$$ \displaystyle r_{n}(\lambda,\mu)=\mathds{1}_{\mu\geq 1}\mu^{-1}s_{n}(\lambda,\mu)^{2}-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu). $$

The cutoff $\mathds{1}_{\mu\geq 1}$ in the first term is somewhat arbitrary; we could use $\mathds{1}_{\mu\geq\mu_{0}}$ instead for any fixed $\mu_{0}>0$ without changing much. Note that both $r_{n}$ and $s_{n}$ take real values on real inputs.

#### Proposition 15.3.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ . For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle r_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0. $$

This is stronger than Proposition 15.1 because $r_{n}\geq-p_{n}p_{n+1}$ pointwise. The proof of Proposition 15.3 will use the following simple lemma.

#### Lemma 15.4.

Let $v\in\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ be a vector of weight $1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\overline{E}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Rewrite the square of the right hand side using self-adjointness of $\Delta$ , (2.7), (2.5), and the fact that $v$ has weight $1$ :

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\overline{E}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} \displaystyle=-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-1}E\overline{E}v,v\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-1}(\Delta+H^{2}-H)v,v\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}v,v\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\leq\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}.\qed $$

#### Proof of Proposition 15.3.

By Lemma 15.4, we can lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\overline{E}(E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

By the product rule and (2.5),

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} \displaystyle\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}-(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} \displaystyle=\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|E^{n+1}\varphi|^{2}-(\lambda+n(n+1))|E^{n}\varphi|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Plugging in Proposition 14.5, and then writing the result in terms of $s_{n}$ to simplify notation,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

By self-adjointness of $\Delta$ and real-valuedness of $s_{n}$ , we can rewrite this as

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\geq\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-1}s_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)^{2}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

On the other hand, by the proof of Proposition 15.1,

$$ \displaystyle\|E^{n+1}\varphi\overline{E}^{n}\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\geq\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-1}s_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)^{2}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Subtracting the left hand side from the right hand side and writing the result in terms of $r_{n}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle r_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0, $$

as desired. ∎

### 15.2. Bulk bound

Our aim in this subsection is to prove Theorem 11.9 under the assumption that $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, i.e., to prove

#### Theorem 15.5.

Assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

For $\Lambda\geq 0$ , let $C(\Lambda)\in[0,\infty]$ be the smallest nonnegative constant such that for all automorphic vectors $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\leq\Lambda$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}\leq C(\Lambda)\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

It is clear from the definition that $C(\Lambda)$ is increasing in $\Lambda$ . We will reduce Theorem 15.5 to Proposition 15.8 below, which is stated purely in terms of $C(\Lambda)$ . First, we need a couple easy lemmas.

#### Lemma 15.6.

For every $\Lambda\geq 0$ , the constant $C(\Lambda)$ is finite.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}$ has discrete spectrum, $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}^{K}$ is finite-dimensional. Any two norms on a finite-dimensional space are equivalent, so $\|\cdot\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim_{\Lambda}\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ on $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}^{K}$ . The implicit constant here is an upper bound for $C(\Lambda)$ . ∎

#### Lemma 15.7.

Assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Let $\Lambda\geq 1$ . Then for $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(\Lambda)\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Splitting $\alpha$ into real and imaginary parts, we may assume $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Then by the triangle inequality, the definition of $C(\Lambda)$ , and the polynomial Weyl law,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{\lambda\leq\Lambda}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq C(\Lambda)\sum_{\lambda\leq\Lambda}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(\Lambda)\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Note the second inequality was valid because $\mathds{1}_{\Delta=\lambda}\alpha$ is a real $K$ -invariant automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\leq\Lambda$ . ∎

#### Proposition 15.8.

Assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Then there is an absolute constant $c\in(0,1)$ such that for $\Lambda\gg 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(c\Lambda). $$

This proposition is the technical heart of the proof of Theorem 15.5. We defer the proof of the proposition to the end of this subsection.

#### Proof of Theorem 15.5 assuming Proposition 15.8.

Let $c\in(0,1)$ be an absolute constant as in Proposition 15.8. Then by induction on $\Lambda$ (using Lemma 15.6 for the base case), for $\Lambda\geq 0$ we have

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Lambda)). $$

Now let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . We wish to prove (15.3). Denote $\alpha_{m}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[m-1,m)}\alpha$ , so that $\alpha=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{m}$ . Since $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , this is a finite sum. Thus by the triangle inequality, Lemma 15.7, and (15.5),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\|\alpha_{m}\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}m^{O(1)}C(m)\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}m))\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Applying Cauchy–Schwarz similarly to how it is applied in Lemma 14.2,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim\Big(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}m))\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

We have almost proved (15.3), except we have $\lesssim$ instead of $\leq$ . This is easily remedied by increasing the $O$ -constant. ∎

Recall the functions $p_{n},q_{k,n},r_{n},s_{n}$ defined in Proposition 14.5, Proposition 14.6, (15.2), and (15.1), respectively.

#### Lemma 15.9.

There exist absolute constants $N\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , $a_{0},\dots,a_{N}\geq 0$ , and $c\in(0,1)$ , such that if we let
