$$ \displaystyle R(\lambda,\mu)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_{n}\lambda^{2(N-n)}r_{n}(\lambda,\mu), $$

then for $\mu\geq c\lambda\gg 1$ , we have $R(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0$ and in fact

$$ \displaystyle R(\lambda,\mu)\sim\mu^{2N+1}. $$

We will see that the $c$ in Proposition 15.8 can be taken to be the same $c$ as in Lemma 15.9.

#### Proof of Lemma 15.9.

We claim that $N=1$ , $a_{0}=a_{1}=1$ , and $c=\frac{1}{2}$ work. Let $\mu\geq\frac{1}{2}\lambda\gg 1$ . Using the recursive definition of $p_{n}$ from Proposition 14.5, we compute

$$ \displaystyle p_{0}(\lambda,\mu)=1,\qquad p_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\mu,\qquad p_{2}(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda^{2}-2\lambda\mu+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}+2\lambda-\mu. $$

Plugging these into the definition of $s_{n}$ and then into the definition of $r_{n}$ , and using that $\mu\geq 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle r_{0}(\lambda,\mu)=-\lambda+\frac{3}{4}\mu\qquad\text{and}\qquad r_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=-\lambda^{3}+\frac{19}{4}\lambda^{2}\mu-3\lambda\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{3}-2\lambda^{2}+2\lambda\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle R(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda^{2}r_{0}(\lambda,\mu)+r_{1}(\lambda,\mu)=-2\lambda^{3}+\frac{11}{2}\lambda^{2}\mu-3\lambda\mu^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\mu^{3}-2\lambda^{2}+2\lambda\mu-\frac{1}{2}\mu^{2}. $$

Writing $\mu=t\lambda$ with $t\geq\frac{1}{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle R(\lambda,\mu)=\lambda^{3}\Big[\frac{1}{2}t^{3}-\Big(3+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\Big)t^{2}+\Big(\frac{11}{2}+\frac{2}{\lambda}\Big)t-\Big(2+\frac{2}{\lambda}\Big)\Big]=\lambda^{3}\Big[\frac{1}{2}t^{3}-3t^{2}+\frac{11}{2}t-2+O(\lambda^{-1}t^{2})\Big]. $$

The maximum (in fact the only) real root of the polynomial

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{2}t^{3}-3t^{2}+\frac{11}{2}t-2 $$

is $\approx 0.48$ , which is less than $c=\frac{1}{2}$ . Since $\lambda\gg 1$ and $t\geq\frac{1}{2}$ , it follows that $R(\lambda,\mu)\gtrsim\lambda^{3}t^{3}=\mu^{3}$ . ∎

#### Remark 15.10 (Lemma 15.9 is robust).

The smaller $c$ is, the harder it is to find $N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N}$ satisfying the property desired in Lemma 15.9. Nevertheless, crude numerical experiments show that one can take $c$ much smaller than $1$ and still find satisfactory $N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N}$ . For example, one can check that $c=\frac{1}{37}$ works, with

$$ \displaystyle N=9,\qquad a_{0}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=a_{5}=a_{6}=a_{7}=a_{9}=2,\qquad a_{1}=1,\qquad a_{8}=0. $$

#### Corollary 15.11.

Let $N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N},c$ be absolute constants as in Lemma 15.9. Define $R(\lambda,\mu)$ as in Lemma 15.9. Then for $\lambda\gg 1$ and $\mu\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle(\mu+1)^{2N+1}\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}\mathds{1}_{\mu\leq c\lambda}+R(\lambda,\mu). $$

In particular, for $\lambda\gg 1$ and $\mu\geq 0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle 1\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}\mathds{1}_{\mu\leq c\lambda}+R(\lambda,\mu). $$

In this section, we will only use (15.8), but in the next section, we will need (15.7).

#### Proof.

For $\mu\leq c\lambda$ , we have the trivial bounds

$$ \displaystyle(\mu+1)^{2N+1}\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|R(\lambda,\mu)|\lesssim\lambda^{O(1)}. $$

Thus (15.7) holds when $\mu\leq c\lambda$ . When $\mu>c\lambda$ , (15.7) follows from (15.6). Lastly, (15.7) obviously implies (15.8). ∎

We are now ready to prove Proposition 15.8.

#### Proof of Proposition 15.8.

Fix absolute constants $N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N},c$ as in Lemma 15.9, and define $R(\lambda,\mu)$ as in Lemma 15.9. For example, as is shown in the proof of Lemma 15.9, we can take $N=1$ , $a_{0}=a_{1}=1$ , and $c=\frac{1}{2}$ . Let $\Lambda\gg 1$ be arbitrary. Then we wish to show (15.4).

By the definition of $C(\Lambda)$ and the fact that $C(\Lambda)$ is finite (Lemma 15.6), there exists a nonzero automorphic vector $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\leq\Lambda$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}\gtrsim C(\Lambda)\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

We may assume $\lambda>c\Lambda$ , or else (15.4) follows immediately. Thus in particular $\lambda\gg 1$ . By normalizing $\varphi$ , we may additionally assume $\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ and so $\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}\gtrsim C(\Lambda)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{4}=\|\varphi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Since $1\ll\lambda\leq\Lambda$ , we deduce from (15.8) in Corollary 15.11 that

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By Proposition 15.3 and the nonnegativity of the coefficients $a_{n}$ in the definition of $R$ in Lemma 15.9,

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 0, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By (1.3) and the fact that $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ , Cauchy–Schwarz, the normalization $\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ , and $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz (Proposition 10.1),

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\varphi\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\varphi\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{L^{4}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}. $$

Using Lemma 15.7 to control $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{L^{4}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(c\Lambda)\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}\leq\Lambda^{O(1)}C(c\Lambda)\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{3}. $$

Using the definition of $C(\Lambda)$ and the normalization $\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ to estimate $\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(c\Lambda)C(\Lambda)^{3}. $$

Inserting this into (15.9),

$$ \displaystyle C(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C(c\Lambda)C(\Lambda)^{3}. $$

Since $C(\Lambda)$ is finite by Lemma 15.6, we can cancel factors of $C(\Lambda)^{3}$ on both sides to obtain the desired bound (15.4). ∎

The proof of Theorem 15.5 is finally complete.

### 15.3. First tail bound

In this subsection we prove Theorem 11.10. We recall the statement below, but we need some preliminary results first.

#### Lemma 15.12.

Let $k\geq 1$ , $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , and $\mu\gg k^{2}+n^{2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{n}q_{k,n}(\mu)\geq(0.9\mu)^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

When $n=0$ , we have (15.10) because $q_{k,0}=1$ . For $n\geq 1$ , using the definition of $q_{k,n}$ in Proposition 14.6 and the fact that $\mu\gg k^{2}+n^{2}$ , induction on $n$ gives

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{n}q_{k,n}(\mu)\geq 0.9\mu(-1)^{n-1}q_{k,n-1}(\mu)\geq 0. $$

Iterating this yields (15.10). ∎

For the remainder of this subsection, fix a positive constant $A\lesssim 1$ such that (15.10) holds for all $k\geq 1$ , $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , and $\mu\geq A(k^{2}+n^{2})$ .

For $k\geq 1$ , $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , and $M\geq 0$ , let $\|\cdot\|_{k,n,M}$ be the seminorm on $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ given by

$$ \displaystyle\|v\|_{k,n,M}=\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

This is evidently decreasing in $M$ . By Proposition 2.7, it is finite-valued on $\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ .

#### Proposition 15.13.

Let $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be a lowest weight vector of weight $k\geq 1$ . Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $M\geq A(k^{2}+(n+1)^{2})$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}\leq O(k^{2}+n^{2})^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\|\cdot\|_{k,n,M}$ decreases with $M$ , we may assume $M=A(k^{2}+(n+1)^{2})$ . By the definition of $\|\cdot\|_{k,n,M}$ and self-adjointness of $\Delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)|(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

In view of the definitions of $A$ and $M$ , Lemma 15.12 implies that

$$ \displaystyle-q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\mu)\geq 0 $$

for $\mu\geq M$ , so the above becomes

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}^{2}=-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Writing $-\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}-\mathds{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By Proposition 15.2, the second term on the right (including the minus sign) is non-positive, so

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}^{2}\leq\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}q_{k,n}q_{k,n+1}(\Delta)(|f|^{2}),|f|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating this by the trivial bound Lemma 14.8 and using that $M\lesssim k^{2}+n^{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}^{2}\leq O(k^{2}+n^{2})^{2n+1}\||f|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Since $\||f|^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{4}$ by (10.1), taking square roots gives the desired bound. ∎

#### Proposition 15.14.

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that whenever $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is a lowest weight vector of weight $k\geq 1$ , and whenever $M\gg k^{2}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $A^{\prime}\gg 1$ , to be chosen later. Assume in particular $A^{\prime}\geq A$ . Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ be such that

$$ \displaystyle n^{2}\gtrsim_{A^{\prime}}M\geq A^{\prime}(k^{2}+(n+1)^{2}) $$

(such an $n$ exists because $M\gg k^{2}$ ). Then by Lemma 15.12 and Proposition 15.13,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq(0.9M)^{-n-\frac{1}{2}}\||f|^{2}\|_{k,n,M}\leq O\Big(\frac{k^{2}+n^{2}}{M}\Big)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\leq O(1/A^{\prime})^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Take $A^{\prime}$ to be twice the $O$ -constant. Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 2^{-n}\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

By the definition of $n$ , we have $n^{2}\gtrsim_{A^{\prime}}M$ , and now that $A^{\prime}$ is fixed, we can drop the dependence on $A^{\prime}$ . So we can let $c^{\prime}\gtrsim 1$ be such that $n^{2}\geq c^{\prime}M$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-(\sqrt{c^{\prime}}\log 2)\sqrt{M})\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Thus the desired bound holds with $c=\sqrt{c^{\prime}}\log 2$ . ∎

We now obtain Theorem 11.10 by dyadic decomposition. Recall the statement of the theorem:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.10).

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that whenever $f\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is a lowest weight vector,

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty. $$

#### Proof.

Let $c^{\prime}\gtrsim 1$ be such that one can take $c=c^{\prime}$ in Proposition 15.14. Fix $c=\tfrac{1}{2}c^{\prime}$ . Let $k\geq 1$ be the weight of $f$ . Then by dyadic decomposition,

$$ \displaystyle\|\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim k^{2}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\gg k^{2}\end{subarray}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[M,2M)}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

The first term on the right hand side is finite because $\mathds{1}_{\Delta\lesssim k^{2}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})$ is a bounded operator, so it remains to show that the infinite series is finite. Indeed, by Proposition 15.14,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\gg k^{2}\end{subarray}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[M,2M)}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\gg k^{2}\end{subarray}}\exp(c\sqrt{2M})\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(|f|^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq\|f\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}\\
M\gg k^{2}\end{subarray}}\exp(c\sqrt{2M}-c^{\prime}\sqrt{M}), $$

and this is finite because $c\sqrt{2}<c^{\prime}$ . ∎

### 15.4. Second tail bound

Here we prove Theorem 11.11 assuming $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. The structure of the proof is very similar to that of Theorem 11.10, so it would be reasonable to leave some of the intermediate results to the reader. However, this would not save a huge amount of space, so we err on the side of giving full details.

#### Lemma 15.15.

Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , let $\lambda\geq 0$ , and let $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{n}p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}(0.9\mu)^{n}. $$

#### Proof.

The cases $n=0$ and $n=1$ of (15.12) can be checked directly from the definition of $p_{n}$ in Proposition 14.5. For $n>1$ , using the recurrence (14.6) and the fact that $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ , induction on $n$ gives

$$ \displaystyle(-1)^{n}p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0.9\mu(-1)^{n-1}p_{n-1}(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0. $$

Iterating this gives (15.12). ∎

For the remainder of this subsection, fix a positive constant $A\lesssim 1$ such that (15.12) holds for all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , $\lambda\geq 0$ , and $\mu\geq A(\lambda+n^{2})$ .

For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $\lambda,M\geq 0$ , let $\|\cdot\|_{n,\lambda,M}$ be the seminorm on $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ given by

$$ \displaystyle\|v\|_{n,\lambda,M}=\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

This is decreasing in $M$ and finite-valued on $\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ .

#### Proposition 15.16.

Let $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ be an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ . Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $M\geq A(\lambda+(n+1)^{2})$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}\leq O(\lambda+n^{2}+1)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\|\cdot\|_{n,\lambda,M}$ decreases with $M$ , we may assume $M=A(\lambda+(n+1)^{2})$ . By the definition of $\|\cdot\|_{n,\lambda,M}$ and self-adjointness of $\Delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)|(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

In view of the definitions of $A$ and $M$ , Lemma 15.15 implies that

$$ \displaystyle-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0 $$

for $\mu\geq M$ , so the above becomes

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}=-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Writing $-\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}-\mathds{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By Proposition 15.1, the second term on the right (including the minus sign) is non-positive, so

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\leq\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\varphi^{2}),\varphi^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating this by the trivial bound Lemma 14.7 and using that $M\lesssim\lambda+n^{2}+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\leq O(\lambda+n^{2}+1)^{2n+1}\|\varphi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Writing $\|\varphi^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{4}$ and taking square roots gives the desired bound. ∎

#### Proposition 15.17.

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that whenever $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ , and whenever $M\gg\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Furthermore, if $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, then (15.14) can be upgraded to

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Let $A^{\prime}\gg 1$ , to be chosen later. Assume in particular that $A^{\prime}\geq A$ . Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle n^{2}\gtrsim_{A^{\prime}}M\geq A^{\prime}(\lambda+(n+1)^{2}) $$

(such an $n$ exists because $M\gg\lambda+1$ ). Then by Lemma 15.15 and Proposition 15.16,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 2(0.9M)^{-n-\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}\leq O\Big(\frac{\lambda+n^{2}+1}{M}\Big)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\leq O(1/A^{\prime})^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Take $A^{\prime}$ to be twice the $O$ -constant. Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq 2^{-n}\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

By the definition of $n$ , we have $n^{2}\gtrsim_{A^{\prime}}M$ , and now that $A^{\prime}$ is fixed, we can drop the dependence on $A^{\prime}$ . So we can let $c^{\prime}\gtrsim 1$ be such that $n^{2}\geq c^{\prime}M$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-(\sqrt{c^{\prime}}\log 2)\sqrt{M})\|\varphi\|_{L^{4}}^{2}. $$

Thus (15.14) holds with $c=\sqrt{c^{\prime}}\log 2$ .

Suppose now that $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Then by (15.14) and Theorem 15.5,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\exp(-c\sqrt{M}+O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Since $c\gtrsim 1$ and $M\gg\lambda+1$ , we may assume $M$ is large enough that the quantity inside the exponential satisfies

$$ \displaystyle-c\sqrt{M}+O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)\leq-\tfrac{1}{2}c\sqrt{M}. $$

Then (15.15) holds after replacing $c$ with $\tfrac{1}{2}c$ . ∎

#### Proposition 15.18.

Assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Then there is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that whenever $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ is an automorphic vector with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda\geq 0$ , and whenever $M\gg\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

This follows from a dyadic decomposition argument along the lines of (15.11), using (15.15) in Proposition 15.17 instead of Proposition 15.14. ∎

We are finally ready to prove Theorem 11.11 assuming $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. With this assumption, Theorem 11.11 becomes

#### Theorem 15.19.

Assume $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law. Then there are positive constants $C\lesssim 1$ and $c\gtrsim 1$ , a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals $I_{i}$ of length $\lesssim 1$ , and points $\lambda_{i}\in I_{i}$ for each $i$ , such that the partition has polynomial growth in the sense that

$$ \displaystyle\#\{i:\lambda_{i}\leq X\}\lesssim X^{O(1)}\qquad\text{for}\qquad X\geq 1, $$

and such that for all $i$ and all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial Weyl law, there exists a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals $I_{i}$ of length $\lesssim 1$ , such that the partition has polynomial growth, and such that each interval contains at most one eigenvalue of the Casimir on $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ (not counting multiplicity). One can ensure also that the interval containing $0$ is not the degenerate interval $\{0\}$ . Fix such a partition. Let $\lambda_{i}$ be the midpoint of $I_{i}$ (for concreteness). If $I_{i_{0}}$ is the interval containing $0$ , then $\lambda_{i}\geq\lambda_{i_{0}}$ for all $i$ , and $\lambda_{i_{0}}>0$ because $I_{i_{0}}$ is non-degenerate. Since $\lambda_{i_{0}}$ depends only on $\mathcal{H}$ , this means that $\lambda_{i_{0}}\gtrsim 1$ . Thus $\lambda_{i}\gtrsim 1$ for all $i$ .

Now let $I_{i}$ be an arbitrary interval in the partition. If $I_{i}$ does not contain a Casimir eigenvalue, then $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}=0$ and (15.16) holds vacuously. The only interesting case, then, is that $I_{i}$ does contain a Casimir eigenvalue. Call this eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}^{\prime}$ . By construction, $\lambda_{i}^{\prime}$ is unique, so $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}=\mathcal{H}_{\Delta=\lambda_{i}^{\prime}}^{K}$ . Let $c\gtrsim 1$ be as in Proposition 15.18. Since $\lambda_{i}\gtrsim 1$ and $I_{i}$ has length $\lesssim 1$ , there exists $C\lesssim 1$ (independent of $i$ ) such that $C\lambda_{i}$ is a large enough multiple of $\lambda_{i}^{\prime}+1$ for Proposition 15.18 to give

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\varphi^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\varphi\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} $$

for all automorphic vectors $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ with Casimir eigenvalue $\lambda_{i}^{\prime}$ , or equivalently for all $\varphi\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ . We claim that

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By splitting $\alpha,\beta$ into real and imaginary parts, we may assume $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . By normalizing, we may additionally assume $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}=\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}=1$ . Then the polarization identity $\alpha\beta=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\beta^{2}$ combined with (15.17) gives the claimed estimate (15.18). This is almost the same as (15.16), except with $\lesssim$ instead of $\leq$ . To replace $\lesssim$ with $\leq$ , we simply increase $C$ and decrease $c$ . ∎

## 16. Proof of bulk and tail bounds in general

Recall that Sections 12, 13, and 14 reduced Theorem 1.8 to Theorems 11.9, 11.10, and 11.11. Section 15 proved Theorems 11.9 and 11.11 under the assumption that $\mathcal{H}$ obeys a polynomial law, and proved Theorem 11.10 unconditionally. In this section, we prove Theorems 11.9 and 11.11 unconditionally as well, completing the proof of Theorem 1.8.

Throughout this section, given $\gamma\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , $i\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , and $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ , denote $\gamma_{i}(\lambda)=(\Delta-\lambda)^{i}\gamma$ . It will usually be clear from context what $\lambda$ is, in which case we just write $\gamma_{i}$ . Note that $\gamma_{0}=\gamma$ , and if $\gamma$ is a Casimir eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$ , then $\gamma_{i}=0$ for $i>0$ . In practice, $\gamma$ will be an approximate Casimir eigenvector with approximate eigenvalue $\lambda$ , so $\gamma_{i}\approx 0$ when $i>0$ .

The above notation is used, for example, to define $\alpha_{i}$ and $\beta_{j}$ in the right hand side of (16.1) below, with $\lambda$ taken to be the same $\lambda$ as in the statement of Proposition 16.1.

### 16.1. A refined identity from the product rule

The main result of this subsection is Proposition 16.1, which generalizes Proposition 14.5. The terms $(i,j)\neq(0,0)$ on the right hand side of (16.1) are the correction terms referred to in Subsection 11.7.

#### Proposition 16.1.

Let $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\re E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta=\sum_{i,j}p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\beta_{j}), $$

where $p_{n,i,j}$ , defined for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $i,j\in\mathbf{Z}$ , is the polynomial in two variables with real coefficients given by the recurrence

$$ \displaystyle p_{n+1,i,j}(\lambda,\mu) \displaystyle=[(2\lambda-\mu+2n^{2})p_{n,i,j}-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}p_{n-1,i,j}](\lambda,\mu) \displaystyle\quad+[p_{n,i-1,j}+p_{n,i,j-1}](\lambda,\mu) \displaystyle\quad-(\lambda+n(n-1))[p_{n-1,i-1,j}+p_{n-1,i,j-1}](\lambda,\mu) \displaystyle\quad-p_{n-1,i-1,j-1}(\lambda,\mu) $$

for $n\geq 1$ , with initial conditions

$$ \displaystyle p_{0,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)=\begin{cases}1&\textnormal{if }(i,j)=(0,0),\\
0&\textnormal{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle p_{1,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)=\begin{cases}\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\mu&\textnormal{if }(i,j)=(0,0),\\
\frac{1}{2}&\textnormal{if }(i,j)=(1,0)\textnormal{ or }(0,1),\\
0&\textnormal{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Note by induction on $n$ that

$$ \displaystyle p_{n,i,j}=0\qquad\text{if}\qquad i<0\text{ or }j<0\text{ or }i+j>n. $$

Thus the right hand side of (16.1) is a finite sum over terms indexed by nonnegative integers $i,j$ ; this nonnegativity means that it makes sense to write $\alpha_{i},\beta_{j}$ . The right hand side of (16.1) is also real, so taking the real part on the left is necessary.

Using (16.5) and comparing the recurrences for $p_{n,i,j}$ and $p_{n}$ (where as in previous sections, $p_{n}$ is as in Proposition 14.5), we see that

$$ \displaystyle p_{n,0,0}=p_{n}. $$

It is then clear that Proposition 16.1 is a direct generalization of Proposition 14.5.

#### Proof of Proposition 16.1.

Since $\alpha\beta$ is already real, the case $n=0$ of (16.1) is immediate from the definition of $p_{0,i,j}$ . By (2.6) and the product rule,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(\alpha\beta)=-\overline{E}E(\alpha\beta)=-E\alpha\overline{E}\beta-\overline{E}\alpha E\beta-(\overline{E}E\alpha)\beta-\alpha\overline{E}E\beta=-2\re E\alpha\overline{E}\beta+(\Delta\alpha)\beta+\alpha(\Delta\beta). $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle\re E\alpha\overline{E}\beta=-\frac{1}{2}\Delta(\alpha\beta)+\frac{1}{2}(\Delta\alpha)\beta+\frac{1}{2}\alpha(\Delta\beta). $$

In two of the three terms here, $\Delta$ falls on either $\alpha$ or $\beta$ . Rewriting these two $\Delta$ ’s as $\lambda+(\Delta-\lambda)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\re E\alpha\overline{E}\beta=\Big(\lambda-\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Big)\alpha\beta+\frac{1}{2}(\alpha_{1}\beta+\alpha\beta_{1}). $$

This is (16.1) for $n=1$ . For $n\geq 1$ , use (2.6), (2.5), and the product rule to similarly compute

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta) \displaystyle=-\overline{E}E(E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta) \displaystyle=-E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n+1}\beta-\overline{E}E^{n}\alpha E\overline{E}^{n}\beta-\overline{E}E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta-E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}E\overline{E}^{n}\beta \displaystyle=-E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n+1}\beta-(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n-1}\alpha(\Delta+H^{2}-H)\overline{E}^{n-1}\beta \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta+E^{n}\alpha(\Delta+H^{2}+H)\overline{E}^{n}\beta \displaystyle=-E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n+1}\beta-E^{n-1}(\Delta+n(n-1))\alpha\overline{E}^{n-1}(\Delta+n(n-1))\beta \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+E^{n}\Delta\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta+E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\Delta\beta+2n^{2}E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta. $$

Rearranging,

$$ \displaystyle E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n+1}\beta= \displaystyle-\Delta(E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta)+E^{n}\Delta\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta+E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\Delta\beta+2n^{2}E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta \displaystyle-E^{n-1}(\Delta+n(n-1))\alpha\overline{E}^{n-1}(\Delta+n(n-1))\beta. $$

Replacing the $\Delta$ ’s that fall on $\alpha$ or $\beta$ with $\lambda+(\Delta-\lambda)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n+1}\beta \displaystyle=(2\lambda-\Delta+2n^{2})(E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta)-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}E^{n-1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n-1}\beta \displaystyle\quad+E^{n}\alpha_{1}\overline{E}^{n}\beta+E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\beta_{1} \displaystyle\quad-(\lambda+n(n-1))[E^{n-1}\alpha_{1}\overline{E}^{n-1}\beta+E^{n-1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n-1}\beta_{1}] \displaystyle\quad-E^{n-1}\alpha_{1}\overline{E}^{n-1}\beta_{1}. $$

Taking real parts and comparing with (16.2), we obtain (16.1) by induction on $n$ . ∎

### 16.2. Refined bootstrap inequalities

Recall $r_{n}$ and $s_{n}$ , defined by (15.2) and (15.1). Just as $p_{n,i,j}$ generalizes $p_{n}$ , let $s_{n,i,j}$ be the following generalization of $s_{n}$ . For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $i,j\in\mathbf{Z}$ , define

$$ \displaystyle s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)=[p_{n+1,i,j}-(\lambda+n(n+1))p_{n,i,j}-p_{n,i-1,j}](\lambda,\mu). $$

By (16.5), we have

$$ \displaystyle s_{n,i,j}=0\qquad\text{if}\qquad i<0\text{ or }j<0\text{ or }i+j>n+1 $$

and

$$ \displaystyle s_{n,0,0}=s_{n}. $$

We can now state the two “refined bootstrap inequalities” which we will prove in this subsection. They are Propositions 16.2 and 16.3, and they generalize Propositions 15.1 and 15.3, respectively.

#### Proposition 16.2.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle-\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proposition 16.3.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle r_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\Big( \displaystyle\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\Big). $$

Because of (16.5) and (16.7), the right hand sides are finite sums. If $\Delta\alpha=\lambda\alpha$ , then the right hand sides vanish. Thus Propositions 16.2 and 16.3 indeed generalize Propositions 15.1 and 15.3. A schematic form of the proof of these inequalities is as follows.

#### Proof of Propositions 16.2 and 16.3.

As in the proofs of Propositions 15.1 and 15.3, consider the crossing equation

$$ \displaystyle\langle|E^{n}\alpha|^{2},|E^{n+1}\alpha|^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\|E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

In Propositions 16.4 and 16.5 below, we will write

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}=\MT_{\LHS}+\RT_{\LHS}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\MT_{\RHS}+\RT_{\RHS} $$

(here MT stands for “main term” and RT stands for “remainder term”). In Propositions 16.6 and 16.8 below, we will then bound

$$ \displaystyle|\RT_{\LHS}|\leq\Error_{\LHS}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\RT_{\RHS}|\leq\Error_{\RHS}. $$

Since $\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}$ is a square and hence nonnegative, we have $\LHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq 0$ , so

$$ \displaystyle-\MT_{\LHS}\leq\RT_{\LHS}\leq\Error_{\LHS}. $$

Similarly, combining (16.8), (16.9), and (16.10),

$$ \displaystyle\MT_{\RHS}-\MT_{\LHS}\leq\RT_{\LHS}-\RT_{\RHS}\leq\Error_{\LHS}+\Error_{\RHS}. $$

After inserting the definitions of these quantities from the propositions mentioned above, (16.11) and (16.12) become the inequalities in Propositions 16.2 and 16.3, respectively. ∎

#### Proposition 16.4.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}=\MT_{\LHS}+\RT_{\LHS}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\MT_{\LHS}=\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\RT_{\LHS}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\langle p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}),p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Expanding $|E^{n}\alpha|^{2}$ and $|E^{n+1}\alpha|^{2}$ as in Proposition 16.1,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}=\sum_{i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}\langle p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}),p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

The term where $i=j=i^{\prime}=j^{\prime}=0$ is $\MT_{\LHS}$ , and the remainder is $\RT_{\LHS}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 16.5.

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Let $\lambda\in\mathbf{R}$ . Then for $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\MT_{\RHS}+\RT_{\RHS}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\MT_{\RHS}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-1}s_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)^{2}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\RT_{\RHS}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}),\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 16.5.

By Lemma 15.4, we can lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\overline{E}(E^{n+1}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\alpha)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Applying the product rule and (2.5),

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|E^{n+1}\alpha|^{2}-(\Delta+H^{2}+H)E^{n}\alpha\overline{E}^{n}\alpha)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Splitting $\Delta=\lambda+(\Delta-\lambda)$ , and using that $E^{n}\alpha$ has weight $n$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|E^{n+1}\alpha|^{2}-(\lambda+n(n+1))|E^{n}\alpha|^{2}-E^{n}\alpha_{1}\overline{E}^{n}\alpha)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Applying the trivial inequality $\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}}\geq\|\re v\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ which holds for all $v\in\mathcal{H}$ by Proposition 9.7,

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}(|E^{n+1}\alpha|^{2}-(\lambda+n(n+1))|E^{n}\alpha|^{2}-\re E^{n}\alpha_{1}\overline{E}^{n}\alpha)\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Expanding the three terms on the right hand side as in Proposition 16.1, and then writing the result in terms of the polynomials $s_{n,i,j}$ to simplify notation,

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\Big\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{i,j}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\Big\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}. $$

Expanding the square,

$$ \displaystyle\RHS\eqref{eqn:fund_crossing}\geq\sum_{i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}),\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

The term where $i=j=i^{\prime}=j^{\prime}=0$ is $\MT_{\RHS}$ , and the remainder is $\RT_{\RHS}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 16.6.

With notation as in Proposition 16.4, one has

$$ \displaystyle|\RT_{\LHS}|\leq\Error_{\LHS}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Error_{\LHS}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

This is immediate from the definition of $\RT_{\LHS}$ and the general Lemma 16.7 below. ∎

#### Lemma 16.7.

Let $A,B$ commuting self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space $\mathcal{V}$ . Let $v,w\in\mathcal{V}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle|\langle Av,Bw\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}|\leq\||AB|^{\frac{1}{2}}v\|_{\mathcal{V}}\||AB|^{\frac{1}{2}}w\|_{\mathcal{V}}. $$

Here $|AB|^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is defined using the functional calculus for $AB$ , which is self-adjoint because $A,B$ commute. We are not careful with issues of domain, because in practice $v,w$ will always be in the domains of the relevant operators.

#### Proof.

Write

$$ \displaystyle\langle Av,Bw\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}=\langle ABv,w\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}=\langle\sgn(AB)|AB|v,w\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}=\langle\sgn(AB)|AB|^{\frac{1}{2}}v,|AB|^{\frac{1}{2}}w\rangle_{\mathcal{V}}. $$

The desired bound now follows from Cauchy–Schwarz and the fact that $\sgn(AB)$ is unitary. ∎

#### Proposition 16.8.

With notation as in Proposition 16.5, one has

$$ \displaystyle|\RT_{\RHS}|\leq\Error_{\RHS}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\Error_{\RHS}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

This is immediate from the definition of $\RT_{\RHS}$ and Cauchy–Schwarz. ∎

Propositions 16.2 and 16.3 are now fully proved.

### 16.3. Bulk bound

This subsection is somewhat similar to Subsection 15.2. Our goal is to prove Theorem 11.9.

For $s\in\mathbf{R}$ and $v\in\mathcal{H}^{K}$ , define the Sobolev norm

$$ \displaystyle\|v\|_{H^{s}}=\|(\Delta+1)^{\frac{s}{2}}v\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

In general this may be $+\infty$ , but it is always finite when $v\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\infty}$ . The $H^{0}$ Sobolev norm is just the Hilbert space norm. For $p,s\geq 0$ and $\Lambda\geq 1$ , let $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)\in[0,\infty]$ be the smallest nonnegative constant such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{H^{s}}\leq C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{2}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\qquad\text{for all}\qquad\lambda\in[1,\Lambda]\text{ and }\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-p}}^{K}. $$

It is clear from the definition that $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ is decreasing in $p$ and increasing in $s$ and $\Lambda$ . We will reduce Theorem 11.9 to Proposition 16.11 below, which is analogous to Proposition 15.8.

#### Lemma 16.9.

For all $p,s\geq 0$ and $\Lambda\geq 1$ , the constant $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ is finite.

#### Proof.

Since $\mathcal{H}$ has discrete spectrum, $\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda+1}^{K}$ is finite-dimensional. Thus the multiplication map

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda+1}^{K}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda+1}^{K}\to\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\infty}\hookrightarrow H^{s} $$

is a linear map from a finite-dimensional Hilbert space to a Banach space, and hence is bounded. The operator norm of this map is an upper bound for $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{2}$ . ∎

#### Lemma 16.10.

Let $p,s\geq 0$ and $\Lambda\geq 1$ . Then for all $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\leq\Lambda}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ increases with $s$ , it suffices to prove this for $s=0$ . Choose $\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}$ many points $\lambda_{i}\in[1,\Lambda]$ such that

$$ \displaystyle[0,\Lambda]\subseteq\bigcup_{i}[\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i}^{-p},\lambda_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{-p}]. $$

Choose intervals $I_{i}\subseteq[\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{i}^{-p},\lambda_{i}+\lambda_{i}^{-p}]$ centered at $\lambda_{i}$ , such that the $I_{i}$ partition $[0,\Lambda]$ . Denote $\alpha_{i}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}\alpha$ , so that $\alpha=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}$ and $\alpha_{i}\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda_{i}|\leq\lambda_{i}^{-p}}^{K}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{i}\|\alpha_{i}\|_{L^{4}}=\sum_{i}\|\alpha_{i}^{2}\|_{H^{0}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq C_{p,0}(\Lambda)\sum_{i}\|\alpha_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,0}(\Lambda)\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}.\qed $$

#### Proposition 16.11.

There are absolute constants $p,s\geq 0$ and $c\in(0,1)$ such that for $\Lambda\gg 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda). $$

Before proving Proposition 16.11, we first show how it implies Theorem 11.9. This is almost identical to the deduction of Theorem 15.5 from Proposition 15.8. Recall Theorem 11.9:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.9).

Let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof of Theorem 11.9 assuming Proposition 16.11.

Let $p,s,c$ be absolute constants as in Proposition 16.11. Then by induction on $\Lambda$ (using Lemma 16.9 for the base case), for $\Lambda\geq 1$ we have

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Lambda)). $$

Now let $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ . Denote $\alpha_{m}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta\in[m-1,m)}\alpha$ , so that $\alpha=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\alpha_{m}$ . Since $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}^{\textnormal{fin}}$ , this is a finite sum. Thus by the triangle inequality, Lemma 16.10, and (16.16),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\|\alpha_{m}\|_{L^{4}}\leq\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}m^{O(1)}C_{p,s}(m)\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}m))\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Applying Cauchy–Schwarz as in the proof of Lemma 14.2, we get

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim\Big(\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}m))\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\Big)^{\frac{1}{2}}\lesssim\|\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\Delta))\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

We have almost proved (16.15), except we have $\lesssim$ instead of $\leq$ . This is easily remedied by increasing the $O$ -constant. ∎

In the proof of Proposition 16.11, we will use the following crude bounds for $p_{n,i,j}$ and $s_{n,i,j}$ .

#### Lemma 16.12.

Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $i,j\in\mathbf{Z}$ . Then for $\lambda\geq 1$ and $\mu\geq 0$ , one has

$$ \displaystyle|p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)|\lesssim_{n,i,j}\lambda^{n}(\mu+1)^{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)|\lesssim_{n,i,j}\lambda^{n+1}(\mu+1)^{n+1}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma 16.12.

By induction on $n$ , the polynomial $p_{n,i,j}$ has total degree at most $n$ . From this and the definition (16.6) of $s_{n,i,j}$ , it follows that $s_{n,i,j}$ has total degree at most $n+1$ . Therefore, we obtain (16.17). ∎

We are now ready to prove Proposition 16.11.

#### Proof of Proposition 16.11.

Fix absolute constants $N,a_{0},\dots,a_{N},c$ as in Lemma 15.9. For example, as is shown in the proof of Lemma 15.9, we can take $N=1$ , $a_{0}=a_{1}=1$ , and $c=\frac{1}{2}$ . Set $s=2N+1$ . Let $p\geq 0$ , to be chosen later. Let $\Lambda\gg 1$ be arbitrary. Then we will show that (16.14) holds with these choices of parameters.

By the definition of $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ and the fact that $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ is finite (Lemma 16.9), there exist $\lambda\in[1,\Lambda]$ and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-p}}^{K}$ nonzero, such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{H^{s}}\gtrsim C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{2}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

We may assume $\lambda>c\Lambda$ , or else (16.14) follows immediately. Thus in particular $\lambda\gg 1$ . Now, after normalizing $\alpha,\beta$ , we see that there exist $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-p}}^{K}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}},\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\alpha\beta\|_{H^{s}}\gtrsim C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{2}. $$

Splitting into real and imaginary parts, we may assume in addition that $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Using the polarization identity $\alpha\beta=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\beta^{2}$ , we may further assume that $\alpha=\beta$ . In summary, we conclude that there exists $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-p}}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\alpha^{2}\|_{H^{s}}\gtrsim C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{2}. $$

We can thus estimate

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\|\alpha^{2}\|_{H^{s}}^{2}=\langle(\Delta+1)^{s}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $s=2N+1$ and $1\ll\lambda\leq\Lambda$ , we deduce from (15.7) in Corollary 15.11 that

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim\Lambda^{O(1)}\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}+\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

where $R$ is as in Lemma 15.9. We bound each of the two terms on the right hand side separately.

Let us begin with the first term in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_p,s^4_terms_to_bd}$ . By (1.3) and the fact that $\alpha$ is real, Cauchy–Schwarz, and $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz (Proposition 10.1),

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=\langle\alpha\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2})\|_{L^{4}}\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Recalling from (16.18) that $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1$ , we can ignore factors of $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}$ if we work up to constants. Then using Lemma 16.10 to control $\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2})\|_{L^{4}}$ , we get

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\leq\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{3}. $$

Writing $\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}=\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq\|\alpha^{2}\|_{H^{s}}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and estimating this using the definition of $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\leq c\Lambda}(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{3}. $$

This bound will suffice for the first term in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_p,s^4_terms_to_bd}$ .

For the second term in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_p,s^4_terms_to_bd}$ , writing out the definition of $R$ from Lemma 15.9, recalling that $a_{0},\dots,a_{N}\geq 0$ , and applying Proposition 16.3 yields

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_{n}\lambda^{2(N-n)}\langle r_{n}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\leq\sum_{n=0}^{N}a_{n}\lambda^{2(N-n)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\Big(\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq 1}\Delta^{-\frac{1}{2}}s_{n,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\Big), $$

where we use the notation from Subsection 16.2, so in particular $\alpha_{i}$ denotes the expression $(\Delta-\lambda)^{i}\alpha$ . Crudely estimating the right hand side by Lemma 16.12 (keeping in mind the vanishing conditions (16.5) and (16.7), and the fact that $N$ is an absolute constant),

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{2(N+1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}\\
i+j,i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq N+1\\
\text{not all 0}\end{subarray}}\|(\Delta+1)^{N+\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j})\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|(\Delta+1)^{N+\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Since $s=2N+1$ , we can rewrite this as

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{s+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}\\
i+j,i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq N+1\\
\text{not all 0}\end{subarray}}\|\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}\|_{H^{s}}\|\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\alpha_{j^{\prime}}\|_{H^{s}}. $$

Since $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq\lambda^{-p}}^{K}$ and $\lambda\in[1,\Lambda]$ , we can bound the $H^{s}$ norms in terms of $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ to get

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\Lambda^{s+1}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}\\
i+j,i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq N+1\\
\text{not all 0}\end{subarray}}\|\alpha_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha_{j}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha_{i^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha_{j^{\prime}}\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

By the definition $\alpha_{i}=(\Delta-\lambda)^{i}\alpha$ and the normalization $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1$ from (16.18), we see that $\|\alpha_{i}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim\lambda^{-ip}$ . Combining this with the fact that $\lambda>c\Lambda$ and that not all $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}$ are zero,

$$ \displaystyle\langle R(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim_{p}\Lambda^{s+1-p}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}. $$

This is the bound we need for the second term in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_p,s^4_terms_to_bd}$ .

Inserting (16.20) and (16.21) into $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_p,s^4_terms_to_bd}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\lesssim_{p}\Lambda^{O_{p}(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{3}+\Lambda^{s+1-p}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}. $$

Take $p=s+2$ (anything bigger than $s+1$ would do), and let $A\lesssim 1$ denote the implicit constant. Then the above becomes

$$ \displaystyle C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\leq A\Lambda^{O(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{3}+A\Lambda^{-1}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}. $$

Since $\Lambda\gg 1$ , we may assume $A\Lambda^{-1}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Then since $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ is finite by Lemma 16.9, we can subtract the second term on the right hand side from both sides to get

$$ \displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{4}\leq A\Lambda^{O(1)}C_{p,s}(c\Lambda)C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{3}. $$

Using once again that $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)$ is finite, we can cancel factors of $C_{p,s}(\Lambda)^{3}$ on both sides to conclude the desired bound (16.14). ∎

The proof of Theorem 11.9 is finally complete.

### 16.4. Asymptotics for $p_{n,i,j}$

As above, let $p_{n}$ and $p_{n,i,j}$ be the polynomials in two variables defined in Propositions 14.5 and 16.1, respectively. Recall $p_{n,0,0}=p_{n}$ . The main result of this subsection is Proposition 16.13, which gives a good estimate for $p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)$ with explicit dependence on all parameters (unlike Lemma 16.12, where the dependence on $n$ is implicit).

#### Proposition 16.13.

Let $n,i,j\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with $i+j\leq n$ . Let $\lambda,\mu\geq 0$ . Then one has the trivial bound

$$ \displaystyle|p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)|\leq O(1)^{n}(\lambda+\mu+n^{2})^{n-i-j}. $$

If in addition $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle|p_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)|\leq O(\mu^{-1})^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j}|p_{n}(\lambda,\mu)|. $$

Here $\binom{n}{i+j}$ is a binomial coefficient.

The bound (16.24) follows directly from the recurrence (16.2) and induction on $n$ , where the base case for the induction comes from the initial conditions (16.3) and (16.4). So (16.24) really is “trivial.” Nevertheless, (16.24) is much stronger than the crude bound given in Lemma 16.12. Indeed, when $i=j=0$ , we see from Lemma 15.15 that (16.24) is sharp up to a factor of $O(1)^{n}$ in the regime $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ . The estimate (16.25) says that in this regime, each time $i$ or $j$ is increased by $1$ , we save at least an extra factor of $n/\mu$ .

It remains to establish (16.25), so assume $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ . Writing the recurrence (16.2) for $p_{n,i,j}$ in matrix form,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p_{n+1,i,j}\\
p_{n,i,j}\end{pmatrix}=A_{n}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n,i,j}\\
p_{n-1,i,j}\end{pmatrix}+B_{n}\Big[\begin{pmatrix}p_{n,i-1,j}\\
p_{n-1,i-1,j}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}p_{n,i,j-1}\\
p_{n-1,i,j-1}\end{pmatrix}\Big]+C_{n}\begin{pmatrix}p_{n,i-1,j-1}\\
p_{n-1,i-1,j-1}\end{pmatrix} $$

for $n\geq 1$ , where

$$ \displaystyle A_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}-\mu+2\lambda+2n^{2}&-(\lambda+n(n-1))^{2}\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad B_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-(\lambda+n(n-1))\\
0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad C_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

The initial conditions (16.3) and (16.4) can similarly be written in matrix form as

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}p_{1,i,j}\\
p_{0,i,j}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{cases}\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{1}{2}\mu+\lambda\\
1\end{pmatrix}&\text{if }(i,j)=(0,0),\\[15.00002pt]
\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\\
0\end{pmatrix}&\text{if }(i,j)=(1,0)\text{ or }(0,1),\\[15.00002pt]
\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\end{pmatrix}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}=(-\mu)^{-(n-i-j)}p_{n,i,j}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{p}_{n}=\tilde{p}_{n,0,0}=(-\mu)^{-n}p_{n}. $$

With this normalization, the inequality (15.12) in Lemma 15.15 becomes the lower bound

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n}(\lambda,\mu)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}(0.9)^{n}, $$

and our goal, (16.25), becomes the slightly simpler estimate

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}(\lambda,\mu)|\leq O(1)^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j}\tilde{p}_{n}(\lambda,\mu). $$

The $\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}$ satisfy the modified recurrence

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n+1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}\end{pmatrix}=\tilde{A}_{n}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{n-1,i,j}\end{pmatrix}+\tilde{B}_{n}\Big[\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n,i-1,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{n-1,i-1,j}\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n,i,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{n-1,i,j-1}\end{pmatrix}\Big]+\tilde{C}_{n}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n,i-1,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{n-1,i-1,j-1}\end{pmatrix} $$

for $n\geq 1$ , with

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1-\frac{2\lambda+2n^{2}}{\mu}&-(\frac{\lambda+n(n-1)}{\mu})^{2}\\[5.0pt]
1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tilde{B}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac{\lambda+n(n-1)}{\mu}\\[5.0pt]
0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tilde{C}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

and with initial conditions

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{0,i,j}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{cases}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\\
1\end{pmatrix}&\text{if }(i,j)=(0,0),\\[15.00002pt]
\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\\
0\end{pmatrix}&\text{if }(i,j)=(1,0)\text{ or }(0,1),\\[15.00002pt]
\begin{pmatrix}0\\
0\end{pmatrix}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{n}=\frac{2\lambda+2n^{2}}{\mu}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\varepsilon_{n}=\frac{\lambda+n(n-1)}{\mu}, $$

so that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1-\delta_{n}&-\varepsilon_{n}^{2}\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tilde{B}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varepsilon_{n}\\
0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tilde{C}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}. $$

Since $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ by assumption, we have $0\leq\delta_{n}\ll 1$ and $0\leq\varepsilon_{n}\ll 1$ . Note also that $\delta_{n},\varepsilon_{n}$ are increasing in $n$ , so the entries of $\tilde{A}_{n}$ are monotonic in $n$ . The only properties of $\tilde{B}_{n}$ and $\tilde{C}_{n}$ that we will use are the trivial bounds

$$ \displaystyle\|\tilde{B}_{n}\|_{\op}\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\tilde{C}_{n}\|_{\op}\lesssim 1. $$

If we compute $(\begin{smallmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n+1,i,j}\\ \tilde{p}_{n,i,j}\end{smallmatrix})$ by iterating the recurrence (16.28) until either $i$ or $j$ drop, we find that

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n+1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}\end{pmatrix}= \displaystyle\,\tilde{A}_{n}\tilde{A}_{n-1}\cdots\tilde{A}_{1}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{0,i,j}\end{pmatrix} \displaystyle+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\tilde{A}_{n}\tilde{A}_{n-1}\cdots\tilde{A}_{m+1}\Big[\tilde{B}_{m}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i-1,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i-1,j}\end{pmatrix}+\tilde{B}_{m}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i,j-1}\end{pmatrix}+\tilde{C}_{m}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i-1,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i-1,j-1}\end{pmatrix}\Big] $$

(here when $m=n$ , the empty product $\tilde{A}_{n}\tilde{A}_{n-1}\cdots\tilde{A}_{m+1}$ is taken to be the identity matrix). In order to use this to estimate $\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}$ , we need sharp bounds on products of consecutive $\tilde{A}$ ’s. These bounds will come from the following general linear algebra lemma.

#### Lemma 16.14.

Fix a nonzero vector $u\in\mathbf{C}^{d}$ . Fix a compact subset $\mathcal{K}\subseteq\Mat_{d}(\mathbf{C})$ of $d\times d$ matrices, such that each matrix in $\mathcal{K}$ has $d$ eigenvalues of distinct absolute value, and has eigenvectors all not orthogonal to $u$ . Let $M_{1},\dots,M_{N}\in\mathcal{K}$ be such that the real and imaginary parts of the entries of $M_{n}$ depend monotonically on $n$ . Diagonalize

$$ \displaystyle M_{n}=Q_{n}D_{n}Q_{n}^{-1}, $$

with $D_{n}$ the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of $M_{n}$ in decreasing order of absolute value from top left to bottom right, and $Q_{n}$ the matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $M_{n}$ in the corresponding order, normalized so that each eigenvector has inner product $1$ with $u$ . The assumptions on $\mathcal{K}$ ensure that $D_{n}$ and $Q_{n}$ exist and are uniquely defined. Then

$$ \displaystyle M_{N}\cdots M_{1}=Q_{N}D_{N}\cdots D_{1}Q_{1}^{-1}+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{\op}). $$

In particular,

$$ \displaystyle\|M_{N}\cdots M_{1}\|_{\op}\lesssim_{\mathcal{K},u,d}\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}. $$

We emphasize that the $O$ - and implicit constants in (16.32) and (16.33) are independent of $N$ .

The hypotheses of Lemma 16.14 can be weakened and modified in various ways, but this statement suffices for our purposes. In fact, we will only need to work with real $2\times 2$ matrices with real eigenvalues, but it causes no additional difficulties to prove the lemma for complex $d\times d$ matrices for any $d$ .

#### Proof.

Multiplying by $Q_{N}^{-1}$ on the left and $Q_{1}$ on the right, it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle Q_{N}^{-1}M_{N}\cdots M_{1}Q_{1}=D_{N}\cdots D_{1}+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{\op}). $$

Denoting $Q_{N+1}=Q_{N}$ , the left hand side can be expressed as a telescoping product

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:move_Q_N,Q_1}=\prod_{N\geq n\geq 1}Q_{n+1}^{-1}M_{n}Q_{n}. $$

Write

$$ \displaystyle Q_{n+1}^{-1}M_{n}Q_{n}=Q_{n+1}^{-1}Q_{n}D_{n}. $$

The matrices $D_{n}$ and $Q_{n}$ are smooth functions of $M_{n}\in\mathcal{K}$ . In particular, there is a Lipschitz function $Q\colon\mathcal{K}\to\GL_{d}(\mathbf{C})$ , depending only on $\mathcal{K},u,d$ , such that $Q(M_{n})=Q_{n}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle Q_{n+1}^{-1}Q_{n}=I+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|Q_{n+1}-Q_{n}\|_{\op})=I+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{\op}), $$

where $I$ is the identity matrix (for $n=N$ , denote $M_{N+1}=M_{N}$ ). We thus obtain

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:move_Q_N,Q_1}=\prod_{N\geq n\geq 1}[D_{n}+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{\op})]. $$

Expanding this, treating all terms except the first as error terms, and then refactoring these terms,

$$ \displaystyle\LHS\eqref{eqn:move_Q_N,Q_1}=D_{N}\cdots D_{1}+\Error, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\|\Error\|_{\op} \displaystyle\leq\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}\Big[\prod_{n=1}^{N}(1+O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{\op}))-1\Big] \displaystyle\leq\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}\Big[\exp\Big(O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{N}\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{\op}\Big)\Big)-1\Big]. $$

All norms on finite-dimensional spaces are equivalent, so $\|\cdot\|_{\op}\sim_{d}\|\cdot\|_{1}$ , where $\|M\|_{1}$ is defined to be the sum of the absolute values of the real and imaginary parts of each entry of $M$ . By assumption, the real and imaginary parts of the entries of $M_{n}$ are monotonic in $n$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{\op}\sim_{d}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\|M_{n+1}-M_{n}\|_{1}=\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{1}\sim_{d}\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{\op}. $$

Inserting this above,

$$ \displaystyle\|\Error\|_{\op} \displaystyle\leq\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}[\exp(O_{\mathcal{K},u,d}(\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{\op}))-1] \displaystyle\lesssim_{\mathcal{K},u,d}\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{N}\|_{\op}\|M_{N}-M_{1}\|_{\op}. $$

This establishes (16.34) and concludes the proof. ∎

Let us now apply Lemma 16.14 in dimension $d=2$ with

$$ \displaystyle u=\begin{pmatrix}0\\
1\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathcal{K}=\Big\{\begin{pmatrix}1-s&-t\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}:s,t\in[0,10^{-10}]\Big\},\qquad M_{m}=\tilde{A}_{m}\text{ for }m\leq n $$

(since the variable $n$ is already in use in Proposition 16.13, we index the $M$ ’s by $m$ here instead of $n$ as in Lemma 16.14). Using as always that $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ , it is easy to check that the hypotheses of the lemma are satisfied. As in the lemma, diagonalize

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{A}_{m}=Q_{m}D_{m}Q_{m}^{-1}. $$

Then because $\tilde{A}_{m}\in\mathcal{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle D_{m}\approx\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&0\end{pmatrix}\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_{m}\approx\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
1&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

To be precise, one has for example

$$ \displaystyle D_{m}\in\Big\{\begin{pmatrix}1-s&0\\
0&t\end{pmatrix}:s,t\in[-10^{-5},10^{-5}]\Big\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_{m}\in\Big\{\begin{pmatrix}1-s&t\\
1&1\end{pmatrix}:s,t\in[-10^{-5},10^{-5}]\Big\}. $$

In particular,

$$ \displaystyle\|D_{m}\|_{\op}\sim 1. $$

Now, using (16.33) and the trivial bounds (16.30) to upper bound the products of matrices in (16.31),

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{n+1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}\end{pmatrix}\Big|\lesssim \displaystyle\,\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\Big|\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{1,i,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{0,i,j}\end{pmatrix}\Big| \displaystyle+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\|D_{m+1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\Bigg(\Big|\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i-1,j}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i-1,j}\end{pmatrix}\Big|+\Big|\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i,j-1}\end{pmatrix}\Big|+\Big|\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{m,i-1,j-1}\\
\tilde{p}_{m-1,i-1,j-1}\end{pmatrix}\Big|\Bigg). $$

Denote

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}=|\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}|+|\tilde{p}_{n-1,i,j}| $$

(for the case $n=0$ , set $\tilde{p}_{-1,i,j}=0$ ). For $n=0$ and $n=1$ , the initial conditions for $\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}$ imply

$$ \displaystyle P_{0,i,j}=\mathds{1}_{i=j=0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad P_{1,i,j}\lesssim\mathds{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 0\\
i+j\leq 1\end{subarray}}. $$

For $n\geq 0$ , the recursive estimate (16.37) becomes

$$ \displaystyle P_{n+1,i,j}\lesssim \displaystyle\,\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\,\mathds{1}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\geq 0\\
i+j\leq 1\end{subarray}} \displaystyle+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\|D_{m+1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}(P_{m,i-1,j}+P_{m,i,j-1}+P_{m,i-1,j-1}). $$

Also, it follows trivially from the definitions (16.26) and (16.38) that the vanishing conditions (16.5) hold without change for $P_{n,i,j}$ :

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}=0\qquad\text{if}\qquad i<0\text{ or }j<0\text{ or }i+j>n. $$

Next, we use (16.39), (16.40), and (16.41) to prove

#### Proposition 16.15.

Let $n,i,j\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Let $\lambda,\mu\geq 0$ with $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}\lesssim O(1)^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j}\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op} $$

(note both the scalar $P_{n,i,j}$ and the matrices $D_{m}$ depend on $\lambda,\mu$ , though as usual the implicit constants do not).

As in Proposition 16.13, $\binom{n}{i+j}$ is a binomial coefficient rather than a column vector.

#### Proof.

The case $n=0$ is trivial by (16.39) and (16.41), so it suffices to consider $n\geq 1$ . Fix a large constant $C\gg 1$ . We will show by induction on $i+j$ that for all $n,i,j\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with $n\geq 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}\leq C^{i+j+1}\Big[\sum_{k=0}^{i+j}\binom{n}{k}\Big]\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

First, let us check that this is sufficient to prove the proposition. If $i+j>n$ , then $P_{n,i,j}=0$ by (16.41), so without loss of generality, $i+j\leq n$ . For $k\leq\frac{1}{2}n$ , the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ is increasing in $k$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{i+j}\binom{n}{k}\leq(i+j+1)\binom{n}{i+j}\qquad\text{for}\qquad i+j\leq\frac{1}{2}n. $$

In the complementary range,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{i+j}\binom{n}{k}\leq 2^{n}\leq 4^{i+j}\qquad\text{for}\qquad i+j\geq\frac{1}{2}n. $$

Putting (16.44) and (16.45) together,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{i+j}\binom{n}{k}\lesssim O(1)^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j} $$

(note here it’s important that $i+j\leq n$ , or else the binomial coefficient on the right would vanish). Thus (16.43) implies the desired bound (16.42).

We now turn to proving (16.43). When $i+j=0$ , so $i=j=0$ , it follows from (16.40) and (16.41) that

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,0,0}\lesssim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n-1}\|_{\op}. $$

Since $\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\sim 1$ by (16.36), this is equivalent to

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,0,0}\lesssim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

Since $C\gg 1$ , we may assume $C$ is bigger than the implicit constant, so

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,0,0}\leq C\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

This establishes (16.43) for $i+j=0$ , and hence completes the base case of the induction.

For the induction step, let $i+j\geq 1$ . Again without loss of generality, $i+j\leq n$ . Assume inductively that (16.43) holds for all $n^{\prime},i^{\prime},j^{\prime}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with $n^{\prime}\geq 1$ and $i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}<i+j$ . Using this inductive assumption to estimate the right hand side of (16.40) (with the index $n$ in (16.40) shifted by $1$ ),

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}\lesssim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n-1}\|_{\op}\Big(\mathds{1}_{i+j=1}+\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\Big[2C^{i+j}\sum_{k=0}^{i+j-1}\binom{m}{k}+C^{i+j-1}\sum_{k=0}^{i+j-2}\binom{m}{k}\Big]\Big). $$

Multiplying the right hand side by $\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\sim 1$ , switching the order of summation, and using the “hockey stick identity” for sums over diagonals in Pascal’s triangle,

$$ \displaystyle P_{n,i,j}\lesssim C^{i+j}\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\sum_{k=0}^{i+j}\binom{n}{k}. $$

Again since $C\gg 1$ , we may assume $C$ is bigger than the implicit constant (which is independent of $n,i,j$ ). Then (16.43) holds, and the induction step is complete. ∎

Recall our goal is to prove (16.25), which we have seen is equivalent to (16.27). It in fact suffices to show (16.27) with $\lesssim$ in place of $\leq$ , i.e.,

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}|\lesssim O(1)^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j}\tilde{p}_{n}. $$

This is sufficient because (16.27) trivially holds when $i=j=0$ since then both sides are the same, and when $i+j>0$ , the implicit constant in $\lesssim$ can be absorbed into the $O$ -constant. Now from Proposition 16.15 and the definition of $P_{n,i,j}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}|\lesssim O(1)^{i+j}\binom{n}{i+j}\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

Thus to conclude (16.46) and hence (16.25), it only remains to prove

#### Proposition 16.16.

Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ . Let $\lambda,\mu\geq 0$ with $\mu\gg\lambda+n^{2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n}\gtrsim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

#### Proof.

When $n=0$ , both sides are equal to $1$ . So assume $n\geq 1$ . It follows from the definition $\tilde{p}_{n}=\tilde{p}_{n,0,0}$ , the recursive formula (16.31), and the fact that $\tilde{p}_{n,i,j}=0$ if $i<0$ or $j<0$ , that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\end{pmatrix}\tilde{A}_{n}\cdots\tilde{A}_{1}\begin{pmatrix}\tilde{p}_{1}\\
\tilde{p}_{0}\end{pmatrix}. $$

Plugging in the initial conditions for $\tilde{p}_{0},\tilde{p}_{1}$ and applying (16.32) from Lemma 16.14,

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\end{pmatrix}Q_{n}D_{n}\cdots D_{1}Q_{1}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\\
1\end{pmatrix}+O(\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\|\tilde{A}_{n}-\tilde{A}_{1}\|_{\op}). $$

Combining (16.35) with the fact that $\lambda/\mu\ll 1$ , we can crudely estimate

$$ \displaystyle Q_{1}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\\
1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\
b\end{pmatrix}\qquad\text{with}\qquad a\geq 0.4\text{ and }|b|\leq 0.6. $$

Then again by (16.35),

$$ \displaystyle D_{n}\cdots D_{1}Q_{1}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\\
1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a^{\prime}\\
b^{\prime}\end{pmatrix} $$

with

$$ \displaystyle a^{\prime}=\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\,a\geq 0.4(1-10^{-5})^{n}\qquad\text{ and }\qquad|b^{\prime}|\leq 0.6\times 10^{-5n}. $$

Since $n\geq 1$ , we have in particular

$$ \displaystyle a^{\prime}\gtrsim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|b^{\prime}|\leq\frac{1}{2}a^{\prime}. $$

By (16.35) one last time,

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}0&1\end{pmatrix}Q_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}. $$

Thus

$$ \displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}0&1\end{pmatrix}Q_{n}D_{n}\cdots D_{1}Q_{1}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\lambda}{\mu}\\
1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a^{\prime}\\
b^{\prime}\end{pmatrix}=a^{\prime}+b^{\prime}\geq\frac{1}{2}a^{\prime}\gtrsim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}. $$

Inserting this into (16.48),

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{p}_{n}\gtrsim\|D_{1}\|_{\op}\cdots\|D_{n}\|_{\op}(1-O(\|\tilde{A}_{n}-\tilde{A}_{1}\|_{\op})). $$

By (16.29),

$$ \displaystyle\|\tilde{A}_{n}-\tilde{A}_{1}\|_{\op}\lesssim\delta_{n}+\varepsilon_{n}^{2}\ll 1. $$

Thus we may assume that the term $O(\|\tilde{A}_{n}-\tilde{A}_{1}\|_{\op})$ in (16.49) is $\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Then (16.49) reduces to the desired lower bound (16.47). ∎

The proof of Proposition 16.13 is now complete.

### 16.5. Second tail bound

In this subsection we prove Theorem 11.11.

Throughout this subsection, fix a positive constant $A\lesssim 1$ such that (15.12) holds for all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , $\lambda\geq 0$ , and $\mu\geq A(\lambda+n^{2})$ , and such that (16.25) holds for all $n,i,j\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ with $i+j\leq n$ , all $\lambda\geq 0$ , and all $\mu\geq A(\lambda+n^{2})$ .

For $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $\lambda,M\geq 0$ , recall the seminorm $\|\cdot\|_{n,\lambda,M}$ on $\mathcal{H}^{K}$ defined by (15.13). Let $C_{n,\lambda,M}\in[0,\infty]$ be the smallest constant such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{n,\lambda,M}\leq C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}} $$

for all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ . Since $\|\cdot\|_{n,\lambda,M}$ decreases with $M$ , so does $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ .

#### Lemma 16.17.

For all $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ and $\lambda,M\geq 0$ , the constant $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ is finite.

#### Proof.

The same argument used to prove Lemma 16.9 works here. ∎

The key technical result toward Theorem 11.11 is the following proposition, which is analogous to Proposition 15.16 combined with Theorem 11.9.

#### Proposition 16.18.

Let $n\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , let $\lambda\geq 0$ , and let $M\gg\lambda+n^{2}+1$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\leq O(\lambda+n^{2}+1)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)). $$

#### Proof.

Since $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ decreases with $M$ , we may assume $M=A^{\prime}(\lambda+(n+1)^{2})$ for some fixed $A^{\prime}\gg 1$ to be chosen later. Assume $A^{\prime}\geq A$ and $A^{\prime}\geq 1$ . By the definition of $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ and the fact that $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ is finite (Lemma 16.17), there exist $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ nonzero, such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\beta\|_{n,\lambda,M}\gtrsim C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

After normalizing $\alpha,\beta$ , we see that there exist $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}},\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\alpha\beta\|_{n,\lambda,M}\gtrsim C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}. $$

Splitting into real and imaginary parts, we may assume in addition that $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Using the polarization identity $\alpha\beta=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta)^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\alpha^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\beta^{2}$ , we may further assume $\alpha=\beta$ . In summary, we conclude that there exists $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}\cap\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}$ with

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\alpha^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}\gtrsim C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}. $$

We can thus estimate

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim\|\alpha^{2}\|_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}=\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)|(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

In view of the definitions of $A$ and $M$ , Lemma 15.15 implies that

$$ \displaystyle-p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\mu)\geq 0 $$

for $\mu\geq M$ , so (16.52) becomes

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim-\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Writing $-\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}-\mathds{1}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim\langle\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle p_{n}p_{n+1}(\lambda,\Delta)(\alpha^{2}),\alpha^{2}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating the first term by the trivial bound Lemma 14.7 and writing $\|\alpha^{2}\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{4}$ , and estimating the second term by Proposition 16.2 together with (16.5),

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim O(M)^{2n+1}\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{4}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j\leq n\\
i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq n+1\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}\prod_{(\ell,m)\in\{(i,j),(i^{\prime},j^{\prime})\}}\||p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m})\|_{\mathcal{H}}, $$

where the sum is over nonnegative integers $i,j,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}$ , and where we use the notation from Subsection 16.2, so in particular $\alpha_{\ell}$ denotes the expression $(\Delta-\lambda)^{\ell}\alpha$ . Splitting $\mathds{1}=\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}+\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}$ , each term in the product is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta<M}|p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m})\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}|p_{n,i,j}p_{n+1,i^{\prime},j^{\prime}}(\lambda,\Delta)|^{\frac{1}{2}}(\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m})\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

Estimating the first term by (16.24) and the second term by (16.25) (the latter being valid because of the definitions of $A$ and $M$ ),

$$ \displaystyle\eqref{eqn:muliplicand_bd}\leq O(M)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\|\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\Big[O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\binom{n}{i+j}\binom{n+1}{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\Big]^{\frac{1}{2}}\|\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m}\|_{n,\lambda,M} $$

(by (16.24), the exponent $n+\frac{1}{2}$ in the first term could be improved to $n+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2}(i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime})$ , but this would not improve the final result). By $L^{4}$ -Cauchy–Schwarz (Proposition 10.1), Theorem 11.9, the fact that $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ , and the normalization condition $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1$ in (16.51),

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha_{\ell}\|_{L^{4}}\|\alpha_{m}\|_{L^{4}}\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))\|\alpha_{\ell}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)). $$

By the definition of $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ , the fact that $\alpha\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ , and the normalization $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha_{\ell}\alpha_{m}\|_{n,\lambda,M}\leq C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\|\alpha_{\ell}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\alpha_{m}\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}\lesssim C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}. $$

Inserting these bounds into (16.55),

$$ \displaystyle\eqref{eqn:muliplicand_bd}\lesssim O(M)^{n+\frac{1}{2}}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+\Big[O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\binom{n}{i+j}\binom{n+1}{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\Big]^{\frac{1}{2}}C_{n,\lambda,M}^{2}. $$

By the triangle inequality and the elementary inequality $(A+B)^{2}\lesssim A^{2}+B^{2}$ , we deduce that the product in $\RHS\eqref{eqn:C_n,l,M_to_insert}$ is bounded by

$$ \displaystyle O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\binom{n}{i+j}\binom{n+1}{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

Thus from (16.53) we get

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim O(M)^{2n+1}\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}^{4} \displaystyle+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j\leq n\\
i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq n+1\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)) \displaystyle+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j\leq n\\
i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq n+1\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\binom{n}{i+j}\binom{n+1}{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

To bound the first term on the right hand side, we estimate $\|\alpha\|_{L^{4}}\lesssim\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))$ by Theorem 11.9 and the normalization $\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\lesssim 1$ . The sum in the second term on the right hand side consists of $(n+1)^{O(1)}\leq O(1)^{n}$ many identical terms, and this factor of $O(1)^{n}$ can be absorbed into the factor of $O(M)^{2n+1}$ in the summand. Thus

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+\Big[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i+j\leq n\\
i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}\leq n+1\\
\textnormal{not all }0\end{subarray}}O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\binom{n}{i+j}\binom{n+1}{i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}\Big]C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

We wish to bound the sum in brackets. Denoting $k=i+j$ and $k^{\prime}=i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}$ , we can express this as a weighted sum over $k$ and $k^{\prime}$ , where each term is weighted by the number of ways to write $k=i+j$ and $k^{\prime}=i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}$ . This weight is equal to $(k+1)(k^{\prime}+1)\leq O(1)^{k+k^{\prime}}$ , so it can be absorbed into the factor of $O(M^{-1})^{i+j+i^{\prime}+j^{\prime}}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+\Big[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\leq n\\
k^{\prime}\leq n+1\\
\textnormal{not both }0\end{subarray}}O(M^{-1})^{k+k^{\prime}}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k^{\prime}}\Big]C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

Using the identity

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k\leq n\\
k^{\prime}\leq n+1\end{subarray}}X^{k+k^{\prime}}\binom{n}{k}\binom{n+1}{k^{\prime}}=(1+X)^{n}(1+X)^{n+1}=(1+X)^{2n+1} $$

to simplify the sum in brackets,

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\lesssim O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+[(1+O(M^{-1}))^{2n+1}-1]C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

Since $M=A^{\prime}(\lambda+(n+1)^{2})$ with $A^{\prime}\geq 1$ , the expression in brackets is $\lesssim\frac{n}{M}\leq M^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ . Thus, absorbing implicit constants into factors of $O(1)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\leq O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda))+O(M^{-\frac{1}{2}})C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}. $$

Choose $A^{\prime}$ large enough that the quantity $O(M^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ is $\leq\frac{1}{2}$ . Then the second term on the right can be subtracted from both sides to give

$$ \displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}C_{n,\lambda,M}^{4}\leq O(M)^{2n+1}\exp(O(\log_{+}^{2}\lambda)) $$

(note this subtraction is valid because $C_{n,\lambda,M}$ is finite by Lemma 16.17). Now that $A^{\prime}$ has been fixed, we have $M\lesssim\lambda+n^{2}+1$ . Substituting this into (16.56), multiplying both sides by $2$ , and taking square roots, we obtain the desired bound (16.50). ∎

#### Proposition 16.19.

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that for any $\lambda\geq 0$ , any $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ , and any $M\gg\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\exp(-c\sqrt{M})\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is almost identical to that of Proposition 15.17, except with Proposition 16.18 replacing the combination of Proposition 15.16 and Theorem 11.9. ∎

#### Proposition 16.20.

There is a positive constant $c\gtrsim 1$ , such that for any $\lambda\geq 0$ , any $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{|\Delta-\lambda|\leq 1}^{K}$ , and any $M\gg\lambda+1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq M}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

Similarly to Proposition 15.18, this follows from a dyadic decomposition argument along the lines of (15.11), except using Proposition 16.19 instead of Proposition 15.14. ∎

We are finally ready to prove Theorem 11.11. Recall the statement:

#### Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 11.11).

There are positive constants $C\lesssim 1$ and $c\gtrsim 1$ , a partition of $[0,\infty)$ into intervals $I_{i}$ of length $\lesssim 1$ , and points $\lambda_{i}\in I_{i}$ for each $i$ , such that the partition has polynomial growth in the sense that

$$ \displaystyle\#\{i:\lambda_{i}\leq X\}\lesssim X^{O(1)}\qquad\text{for}\qquad X\geq 1, $$

and such that for all $i$ and all $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\mathds{1}_{\Delta\geq C\lambda_{i}}\exp(c\sqrt{\Delta})(\alpha\beta)\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{H}}\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{H}}. $$

#### Proof.

For $i\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 0}$ , let $I_{i}=[i,i+1)$ , and let $\lambda_{i}$ be the midpoint of $I_{i}$ . Then each $I_{i}$ has length $\leq 1$ , and together the $I_{i}$ make up a partition of $[0,\infty)$ of polynomial growth. Let $c\gtrsim 1$ be as in Proposition 16.20. Since $\lambda_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}$ , the condition $M\gg\lambda_{i}+1$ is equivalent to $M\gg\lambda_{i}$ . Thus by Proposition 16.20, there exists $C\lesssim 1$ such that for $M\geq C\lambda_{i}$ , the estimate (16.57) holds whenever $\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal{H}_{\Delta\in I_{i}}^{K}$ . In particular, taking $M=C\lambda_{i}$ gives (16.58). ∎

All implications shown in (1.16) have now been established, so Theorem 1.8 is proved.
